title: The instinctive synthesis
statement: The court identifies all relevant factors, discusses their significance, and at the end makes a value judgment as to the appropriate sentence from its synthesis of the factors. It is discretionary; weight cannot be allocated in advance; there is no single correct sentence, and reasonable minds may differ.

The instinctive synthesis
The court identifies all relevant factors, discusses their significance, and at the end makes a value judgment as to the appropriate sentence from its synthesis of the factors. It is discretionary; weight cannot be allocated in advance; there is no single correct sentence, and reasonable minds may differ.

title: Cautions identified by the Court of Appeal
statement: Do not synthesise the factors by proceeding in stages; over-referencing statistics or current practices may distort the synthesis; statistics are a very crude indicator and must not be given great weight; referring to offending as 'low', 'mid-range' or 'high' risks assessing practices for that category without the circumstances of the case, which limits the synthesis — treat comparable cases as yardsticks.

title: Quantified discounts, s 6AAA and the standard sentence
statement: Quantifying a sentence discount is inconsistent with the instinctive synthesis, except that s 6AAA requires the court to identify any discount given for a guilty plea. The standard sentence is just another factor and does not interrupt the instinctive synthesis.

title: Two-tier sentencing is prohibited (what it is, and is not)
statement: Prohibited: first identifying a 'benchmark sentence' based solely on, for example, the weight of narcotics, the maximum term, a co-offender's sentence or the scaled 'seriousness' of the offending, and then making proportional deductions from it (or then making differing orders for cumulation between co-offenders); the method has been rejected in Victoria and by the High Court. It is not a prohibition on sequential reasoning or even arithmetic deductions in certain cases.

title: Exercising the discretion judicially
statement: The court must act reasonably and justly, according to legal principle and statute, in the public interest, not arbitrarily or by giving effect to private opinion; it must not frustrate the legislative intent, and should not attempt to remedy what it considers inadequate provision by the legislature, the executive or social institutions.

title: Procedural fairness: notice of facts and issues the sentence will rest on
statement: A court may not sentence on a fact it considers important (such as prevalence, or whether a factor is aggravating or mitigating) without identifying it and giving the parties an opportunity to address it; it cannot sentence on material not before it in open court, and error has been found where the court sought out facts or directed the prosecution to tender evidence; agreement of the parties on a point of law (such as the maximum) does not bind it; and it cannot sentence on the basis that a more serious or uncharged offence was committed, though uncharged offending may be narrative context.

title: No adverse inference from the offender not giving evidence on disputed facts
statement: Where facts are disputed, a court may not draw an adverse inference from the offender's failure to give evidence on the plea except in rare and exceptional circumstances.

title: Submissions on range: prosecution may not, defence may (Barbaro)
statement: The prosecution may make submissions on the type of disposition but not on the range of permissible durations; such submissions were rejected by the High Court. The proscription does not apply to the defence; if the defence submits a range, the prosecution may respond on whether it is open by reference to comparable cases and current practices. A wrong prosecution range submission vitiates the discretion only if it influenced the court.

title: Duties of counsel relevant to the estimate
statement: Counsel must not mislead, withhold adverse authorities, stay silent on an irregularity, or fail to check the maximum penalty. The prosecution must present the facts adequately and identify comparable cases with informed submissions (a schedule alone is not enough); the court must review that material independently. Defence must identify the relevant factors and all reasonably open alternatives and adduce evidence of prerequisites for a sanction.

title: Findings must be consistent with the verdict or plea

title: What a guilty plea admits
statement: A guilty plea admits the essential facts of the crime but no more — not automatically the depositions or the prosecution opening. Unless legislation directs otherwise, the prosecution must establish facts beyond those admitted by the plea to the criminal standard; otherwise they cannot be used adversely.

title: Fact-finding on a contested plea (Formosa) and the standard of proof
statement: The Crown opening conventionally constitutes the agreed factual basis; depositions and exhibits are the basic materials; a party wanting another matter considered must raise it and, if necessary, prove it by admissible evidence; absent a legislative direction to the contrary, facts used adversely must be established beyond reasonable doubt; facts used favourably, on the balance of probabilities. Whether a fact is adverse depends on the use made of it.

title: Burden of proof and proof of mitigation
statement: The party relying on a further fact generally bears the burden. Whether a fact is adverse or favourable depends on the use made of it. If no mitigating circumstances are raised, the court proceeds as if there are none; failure to prove mitigation does not prove aggravation (or vice versa); both must be proved by evidence and mitigation cannot be inferred from an absence of evidence. But the court may not approach a fact with a predetermined view that it will not be accepted absent formal proof.

title: No sentencing for a more serious offence than the one pleaded to
statement: On a plea to an alternative offence the court cannot consider aggravating circumstances that might warrant conviction for a more serious offence; it may sentence only for the offence convicted of, not for uncharged acts. (Uncharged offending may be mentioned as narrative context; uncharged conduct may aggravate within the limits in factor.uncharged_conduct; offences taken into account under s 100 and representative or course-of-conduct charges are dealt with in sentence.other_offences_into_account and charges.*.)

title: Criminal record and pending charges
statement: Previous convictions are relevant to several sentencing purposes and may affect the punishment open under statute; the offender must admit them or they must be proved. Children's Court orders may be given in evidence only if made in the past 10 years. The court should be advised of pending charges so it may consider deferring sentence or, if applicable, ask whether the offender wishes admitted subsequent offences to be taken into account (s 100).

title: Pre-sentence, drug and alcohol, medical and third-party reports
statement: A pre-sentence report must be ordered if the court is considering a CCO, YJC or YRC order (not for a CCO whose sole condition is less than 300 hours of unpaid work; 11.1 says “300 hours or less”: flag.cco_work_only_300_hours); disputed parts cannot be relied on until the dispute is heard; the report does not control the sentence. Medical reports should not offer opinions on sentencing principles or purposes; unsolicited third-party reports should not be considered. A pre-sentence report determines suitability for the order, that the necessary facilities are available, and appropriate conditions. If a CCO is under consideration and a drug or alcohol dependency contributed to the offending, the court may order a drug and alcohol assessment report (same purpose, distribution and dispute process as a pre-sentence report).

title: Character and work references
statement: Weight is entirely for the court; there is a tendency to disfavour references from people with no knowledge of the charged offence.

title: Victim impact statements
statement: A victim impact statement informs the court of the crime's impact and the victim's concerns; it is not to punish the offender or produce an unjust sentence. 'Victim' means anyone who suffered injury, loss or damage (including grief, distress, trauma) as a direct result of the offence, whether or not foreseeable; it is not interpreted narrowly. If harm in the statement is disputed and would increase the sentence, causation must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. Weight is for the judge; the victim's attitude cannot govern sentencing, though a favourable statement must be given appropriate weight; unsupported assertions about the victim’s attitude need not be given any weight.

title: Dispositions available on a finding of guilt (with / without conviction)
statement: Subject to the Act’s terms and any provision relating to a crime, on finding a person guilty a court may: with conviction: imprisonment; detention and treatment as a security patient; drug treatment order; youth justice or youth residential centre order; discharge. With or without conviction: CCO; fine; adjournment on conditions. Without conviction: dismissal. Plus any other sentence or order authorised by statute.

title: Whether to record a conviction
statement: The court must consider all the circumstances, including the nature of the offence, the character and history of the offender, and the impact of a conviction on economic or social wellbeing or employment prospects.

title: Deferral of sentence (up to 12 months)
statement: The Magistrates' or County Court may defer sentencing for up to 12 months if in the interests of justice and the offender agrees, eg to assess or demonstrate rehabilitation or allow participation in a program.

title: Order of formulation
statement: Generally impose a separate sentence on each charge (an aggregate sentence may be available: agg.*); then consider cumulation, concurrency and totality by reference to a base sentence (ordinarily the most severe individual sentence); state the head sentence, any non-parole period (and commencement dates for federal sentences); declare time already served in custody and have it noted.

title: Mandatory licence disqualification orders at formulation
statement: The court must make licence disqualification orders on a finding of guilt and conviction (2.4.3; 16.1 says “found guilty or convicted”: flag.licence_guilty_or_convicted; (app policy) with no conviction recorded the order is still listed, with a caution) for manslaughter, negligently causing serious injury, culpable driving causing death, or dangerous driving causing death or serious injury arising out of driving, and for (aggravated) intentionally or recklessly exposing a protected worker to risk by driving.

title: Representative charges
statement: A representative charge does not increase the maximum or permit a disproportionate sentence, but generally results in a heavier sentence than an isolated incident: it removes the 'isolated incident' mitigation and the acts are directly relevant to objective gravity. It requires the offender's express and unequivocal assent; without it, uncharged acts that would warrant further or more serious convictions cannot aggravate.

title: Rolled-up charges
statement: A rolled-up charge bundles identifiable offences (by agreement, on a plea). The court considers all circumstances (extended period, multiple victims, totality of harm), but the maximum is that for a single charge. An aggregate sentence may be imposed. 2.4.5 says it qualifies as a CCE offence only if one constituent transaction is $50,000 or more; 9.4 says the transaction must exceed $50,000 (flag.cce_value_threshold). The CCE test is applied by cce.regime.

title: Course of conduct charges
statement: Available for sexual offences (same complainant) and listed fraud-related offences; a single offence with the same maximum as the substantive offence, but the sentence must reflect the totality of the conduct and is likely to be higher than for a single incident.

title: Commencement and order of service
statement: A sentence generally commences on the day imposed; imprisonment is served concurrently with other uncompleted sentences unless the court orders otherwise or legislation provides otherwise (presumptive cumulation: cum.presumption_cumulation); a cumulative part starts on completion of the sentence it is cumulative on. Terms without a non-parole period are served first, then the non-parole period, then the balance.

title: Taking other offences into account (s 100)
statement: Admitted pending charges (not treason or murder) on the prescribed form may be taken into account; the sentence cannot exceed the maximum for the offence(s) formally sentenced, cannot be lessened, and is hardened; as general policy, the procedure should not be used to dispose of serious offences (caution only).

title: What reasons for sentence should contain
statement: Usually: findings of fact and the reasons for them; aggravating and mitigating factors; the impact on the victim(s); the offender's circumstances that materially bear on the sentence; conclusions on the parties' primary arguments — the route to the conclusion. Explain unusual factors (different sentences for instances of the same offence; an unusual or no non-parole period; why significant assistance did not attract a discount). Discuss statutory matters rather than reciting the statutory words (a recitation is generally insufficient); avoid intemperate or formulaic language.

title: Statements of reasons required by statute
statement: Required statements include: aggregate sentence (decision, reasons, effect, in open court); indefinite sentence; orders needing consent or an undertaking (purposes, effect, consequences of non-compliance, variation); a less severe sentence because of cooperation (noted in the record; scope: flag.s5_2AB_past_vs_future_cooperation); and, where a less severe sentence is imposed because of a guilty plea, the sentence and non-parole period that would otherwise have been imposed (for multiple offences, for the total effective sentence). For dispositions outside s 6AAA(1), whether the court must or may state the notional sentence is stated inconsistently (flag.s6aaa_scope_2_4_9_vs_7_1_4).

title: Correction of errors; sentencing after retrial
statement: Courts may correct clerical and similar errors (s 104A) and reopen to correct a penalty contrary to law (s 104B); a penalty is not contrary to law merely because it was reached through erroneous reasoning or a factual error (s 104B(6)). After a retrial the court must have regard to the earlier sentence; exceeding it will be rare.

title: Sentencing after a retrial: regard to the earlier sentence
statement: When sentencing after a retrial the court must have regard to the sentence previously imposed; it is not bound by it, but a second sentence may permissibly exceed the first only rarely. The parties must be put on notice where a less favourable sentence than on the previous occasion is at risk (method.notice_specific_duties).

title: Open court: sitting in camera needs statutory authority or a recognised exception
statement: For a court to sit in camera there must be statutory authorisation or a recognised exception; it has no inherent power to exclude the public and should not. There is a narrow exception where proceeding in public would defeat the exercise of the court’s jurisdiction (e.g. disruption by rioters). A judge should not receive information capable of affecting the sentence in chambers. A court may still protect confidential information (e.g. concealing witnesses’ names, not reading documents aloud), but if it sits in camera or receives unpublished documents it must say so in its published reasons.

title: A very wide discretion, exercised judicially and within the limits Parliament sets
statement: The sentencing discretion is very wide but must be exercised judicially: the court must not frustrate the legislative intent, must have regard to the scope, subject matter and purpose of legislation, and should not try to remedy what it sees as inadequate provision by the legislature, the executive or social institutions. Parliament has limited the discretion, for example by mandatory penalties, required custodial terms and minimum non-parole periods, and preconditions for youth justice and youth residential centre orders.

title: Procedural fairness: required in all circumstances; a sentence within range is no answer
statement: Procedural fairness is required in all circumstances; relief for a breach should be refused only when it is clear the breach could not possibly have affected the sentence, and a sentence within range is no answer to a denial of procedural fairness. The ultimate issue is whether there was a fair hearing (an objective test; no fault need be shown), and the key question is often what the circumstances require. Each party must have a reasonable opportunity to present its case; what is reasonable depends on the nature of the decision, the complexity of the issues and submissions, the significance of an adverse decision to the party, and the court’s competing demands.

title: Notice: when the court must alert the parties
statement: If the court takes a different view of the law from the parties’ joint position (e.g. the maximum), it must say so and hear submissions. The parties cannot prevent the court obtaining further material (such as a pre-sentence report). Great care is needed before departing from agreed facts. For material not provided by the parties, the court should make doubly sure counsel have access to it or that all parties agree to its use. A change in the court’s previously expressed view of a factor should be notified. If further facts are needed and provided, a hearing must be permitted even if the plea is reopened. Where the parties agree an approach, the court must warn them not to assume it will be followed if it finds it problematic. Notice is also required where a less favourable sentence than on a previous occasion is at risk (remittal or retrial) or where the course of the plea reasonably suggests a non-custodial sentence.

title: Unrepresented offenders: assessing what a fair hearing requires
statement: Managing unrepresented litigants requires balancing the interests of justice against the efficient use of public resources, with patience and judgment about adjournments. Where an unrepresented defendant disputes the facts, the court must be alive to the possibility that the plea is inconsistent with the dispute and should advise reconsideration. The court must assess the person’s capacity to formulate and communicate their case, and where there may be an arguable legal point they cannot articulate it should seek to elicit and clarify it.

title: Disclosing concerns without apprehended bias
statement: A judge may disclose concerns about aspects of the case (failing to do so can itself deny procedural fairness), but should take care not to create a perception that it may not bring an impartial and unprejudiced mind to its task: gratuitous or intemperate remarks should be avoided. Tentative views on matters the parties may then address do not show bias; the number, intrusiveness and tone of interjections may.

A judge may disclose concerns about aspects of the case (failing to do so can itself deny procedural fairness), but should take care not to create a perception that it may not bring an impartial and unprejudiced mind to its task: gratuitous or intemperate remarks should be avoided. Tentative views on matters the parties may then address do not show bias; the number, intrusiveness and tone of interjections may.

title: Prosecution duties at sentencing (detail)
statement: The prosecution must, among other things, correct matters put on the plea that it believes to be in error and give an adequate presentation of the facts (what is fair, reasonable and practical; not limited to the facts of the offence — e.g. criminal history and relevant post-offence conduct). The court is entitled to rely on its summaries as accurate. Unlike the defence, it cannot make unsworn, unproved assertions. A plurality of the High Court has said it may be incumbent on the prosecution to seek limiting orders for cooperation material that cannot be disclosed; other members doubt this is permissible without legislation (flag.prosecution_limiting_orders_hca_split). It must identify comparable cases (the court must review them independently), give a fair test of the defence case and help the court avoid appealable error; failure may support an appellate court’s residual discretion not to intervene on a Crown appeal. Submissions by the prosecution on the range of durations are impermissible statements of opinion (method.barbaro).

title: Defence duties: candour, and submissions for a CCO
statement: The defence must not mislead the court, affirmatively or by omission, but need not volunteer detrimental facts (such as bad character or prior convictions) unless its other submissions would mislead without them (e.g. asserting good character from an absence of priors). Arguing for a CCO requires submissions on the formulation of conditions that address the offender’s needs and the causes of the offending, not just a recital of personal circumstances.

title: The court alone decides the sentence and finds the facts; facts beyond the plea need proof
statement: The court alone decides the sentence and must find the relevant facts, subject to limits (above all, the verdict or plea). Any dispute about facts beyond the essential ingredients admitted by the plea is resolved by the ordinary criminal principles: unless legislation directs otherwise, the prosecution must establish such facts to the criminal standard, failing which they cannot be used against the offender.

title: Guilty pleas: obtaining an unequivocal plea; unrepresented accused; withdrawal
statement: If the court considers a plea is not genuine it must obtain an unequivocal plea or direct a not guilty plea. It should make certain an unrepresented defendant understands a guilty plea (especially where a viable defence appears) and, for a serious offence, adjourn to allow legal advice. If the evidence does not support the charge it should advise withdrawal, but it cannot compel it; if the accused refuses, the plea is final, subject to leave to change it before the matter is finalised. If an unrepresented accused insists on proceeding after an opportunity to obtain advice, the plea may be taken but set aside if circumstances later give cause for concern. When the prosecution accepts a plea, the court cannot reject it unless it is not genuine or an abuse of process.

title: Pleas to alternative or lesser offences
statement: If a plea to a lesser alternative offence is not accepted, the trial proceeds on both counts; the plea is taken before the jury and may be used in evidence, but no conviction is recorded on the lesser offence until the verdict on the more serious one. If the plea to an alternative offence is accepted, the court is not bound by the facts that persuaded the Crown to accept it, but cannot consider aggravating circumstances that might warrant conviction for a more serious offence.

title: When the Evidence Act applies at sentencing; what proof contested facts need
statement: The Evidence Act 2008 does not automatically apply to sentencing. It applies only if the court so directs on a party’s application concerning proof of a fact, the court determines the proceeding involves proof of the fact, and the fact will be significant in determining the sentence; the court must so direct where appropriate in the interests of justice. Even without a direction, the law of evidence applies to contested fact finding. A contested factual assertion must be proved by admissible evidence, though not necessarily on oath or after cross-examination. Uncontested facts may be proved by admissions, agreed statements or bar-table submissions, but the court need not accept assertions that may rest on unreliable instructions.

title: Burden of proof at sentencing: who bears it, notice, and the effect of reasonable doubt
statement: There is no general burden of proof in sentencing unless a party asserts further facts; that party generally bears the burden, and the opposing party must have notice and an opportunity to be heard. Giving the offender the benefit of any reasonable doubt about adverse facts may in practice oblige the court to sentence on the view most favourable to them. Whether a fact is adverse or favourable depends on the use made of it. Failure to prove mitigation does not prove aggravation, or vice versa.

title: Proving prior convictions and subsequent offending
statement: The court must ask whether the offender admits the convictions in the criminal record; if admitted it may sentence accordingly, otherwise the prosecution may prove them (typically by an Evidence Act s 178 certificate). In the higher courts the record may be provided after the indictment is filed and before the hearing (or later in the interests of justice). In a summary proceeding where the accused is found guilty in their absence, a record served at least 14 days before may be admitted. Children’s Court orders can be proved only if made in the past 10 years. Subsequent offending cannot be proved by the CPA record process but may be admitted or proved by certificate. A conviction under appeal to the County Court may count as a previous conviction.

title: Using depositions: no oath requirement; conflicts with agreed facts; co-offender material
statement: Depositions need not have been given on oath or tested by cross-examination. If they conflict with an agreed statement of facts the court should raise it with the parties. Depositions about admitted prior convictions, or a co-offender’s depositions or record of interview where parity is in issue, may be used as evidence subject to objection, but not if they relate to an offence more serious than the one before the court.

title: Reports: distribution, disputes, drug and alcohol pre-release reports, third-party and medical reports
statement: A pre-sentence report must be filed by the specified time and copies given to the parties a reasonable time before sentencing; if distribution has not occurred the court should give time and hear submissions. If a party files a notice disputing a report, the court must not sentence on the disputed part until that party can lead evidence and cross-examine the author. Where, on receiving a drug and alcohol assessment report (itself discretionary: findings.reports), the court is satisfied the offender has a drug or alcohol dependency and the sentence is imprisonment of no more than three months followed by a CCO commencing on release, the court must then order a drug and alcohol pre-release report (prepared by an approved agency, specifying treatment; no dispute process). Unrequested third-party reports should not be considered. Medical reports are shown to the prosecutor; “without objection” does not mean the Crown concurs with their substance.

title: Victim impact statements: who is a victim, content, admissibility, reading aloud and weight
statement: A statement may be made on behalf of a victim under 18, incapable of making it, or not an individual. “Victim” is not read narrowly: the impact of the crime is regarded more broadly than on the immediate victim; a victim need not be the target or related to them; the harm need only be the direct result of the offence (not necessarily immediate or proximate; foreseeability is irrelevant). The statement must address only the offence of which the offender is convicted; if that impact cannot be distilled in a multi-offender, multi-charge case, it should not be admitted. The statutory admissibility regime must be observed, with some flexibility on the plea; on objection the court should rule the part inadmissible or make clear it will not be relied on. The statement is filed and served a reasonable time before sentencing. If it is to be read aloud, the court must ensure only admissible, appropriate and relevant parts are read — a mandatory obligation it cannot waive. It is one consideration only: the court may not disregard it or the victim’s attitude entirely, but that attitude cannot govern the sentence.

title: Effect of a finding of guilt without conviction; what counts as a “sentence”
statement: The Act does not define “sentence”; the Criminal Procedure Act’s definition includes, among other things, reporting orders (or orders that a person is not a registrable offender) under the Sex Offenders Registration Act 2004, and the Court of Appeal applies it to cumulation and concurrency orders and non-parole periods. Unless an Act provides otherwise, a finding of guilt without conviction is not a conviction for any purpose, but it does not prevent other orders authorised by legislation, and it has the effect of a conviction for appeals, variation or contravention proceedings, subsequent offending and later proceedings for the same offence.

title: Deferral of sentence: review, re-offending, custody and orders at the adjourned hearing
statement: When deferring sentence the court may set a review date (and reserve the review to itself); on review it may take no action or cancel the order and sentence. If the offender is found guilty of another offence during deferral, the hearing may be brought forward. The offender may be released on undertaking or bail, and a pre-sentence report may be ordered. At the adjourned hearing the court has regard to the report, the offender’s behaviour during deferral and other relevant matters; custody during deferral can be dealt with as pre-sentence detention; mandatory licence orders remain; a warrant may issue for non-appearance. The common law power to remand at large has not developed in Victoria.

title: Formulation: time served reckoned unless otherwise directed; correcting a declaration; complex orders
statement: Where imprisonment or detention is imposed, custody in relation to the proceedings for that offence must, unless the court directs otherwise, be reckoned as time served; the period may be advised by the informant or proved, must be declared and noted, and can later be corrected if the declaration was in error. Formal orders are usually pronounced at the end of the remarks; with complex orders the court commonly states their intended effect and invites submissions before they are entered.

title: Multiple and mixed indictments: identifying indictments; relating State and federal orders
statement: Each of several indictments should have a unique identifying number (the court adds one if needed and announces it), and the remarks should identify which indictment each sentence relates to; after the orders the court announces the overall result. On a mixed indictment, care is needed in orders relating federal and State sentences (e.g. commencement dates) and in stating total terms.

title: Representative charges: what they permit and require
statement: A representative charge does not mean sentencing for uncharged acts: those acts are directly and highly relevant to the objective gravity of the charged offence, which is heightened because the conduct is not isolated and the impact on the victim is likely greater. It differs from taking other charges into account, rolled-up and course of conduct charges. The conduct must accurately and explicitly reflect the parties’ agreement, identified in some detail (detailed articulation is not required); if the prosecution summary reflects the agreement, the court should not go behind it. The prosecution may not use an incident charged separately, or acts outside the charged period; the essence is that the other acts cannot be particularised as separate charges. The offender’s assent must be express and unequivocal; without it, additional uncharged acts that would warrant conviction for another or more serious offence must not be treated as aggravating.

title: Rolled-up and course of conduct charges: single charge, single maximum
statement: A rolled-up charge, though the court considers all its circumstances (period, number of victims, total harm), is still a single formal charge with the single-charge maximum. A course of conduct charge (a relevant sexual or fraud-related offence involving more than one incident) allows serial offending to be prosecuted where details of each instance are not available: the incidents must together amount to a course of conduct (time, place, purpose), each must be an offence under the same provision (for a sexual offence, the same complainant), and incidents need not be proved with the specificity of a single charge. It is a single offence with the substantive offence’s maximum, but the sentence must reflect the totality of the conduct, so it is likely to be higher than for one incident.

title: Commencement of sentences; CCO start; order of service
statement: A sentence generally commences on the day it is imposed (if the offender is not in custody, on arrest under the warrant). Unless otherwise ordered or legislated, imprisonment is concurrent with other uncompleted sentences. A cumulative sentence (or part) commences on completion of the sentence it is cumulated on; State cumulation needs no commencement date, but a State term imposed on a person serving a Commonwealth sentence must be directed to commence immediately after the federal term or its non-parole/pre-release period (2.4.7), or no later than that point (8.4.1) — a later date is an error on both readings; an earlier one is a caution (flag.cth_sentence_commencement_fixed_or_latest). A CCO commences on the date specified, no later than three months after the order; a CCO combined with imprisonment starts on release. A PSD declaration treats the sentence as commenced on first entering custody, but the formal commencement date is the date of sentence. Terms are served in order: terms without a non-parole period, the non-parole period, then the balance; an earlier sentence is suspended if needed to follow that order.

title: Taking other offences into account (s 100): exclusions and prerequisites
statement: Treason and murder cannot be taken into account under the State scheme. Before considering pending charges the court must be satisfied that a prescribed form listing them has been prepared and given to the offender, and it is appropriate to ask whether the offender admits them and wants them considered. As a general policy the procedure should not be used to dispose of serious offences. Contested other charges are irrelevant, though admitted collateral matters may be relevant; admitted further offending may negate, reduce or qualify an inference that would otherwise mitigate.

title: Reasons: when required, adequacy, statutory statements, publication and revision
statement: There is a common law duty to give reasons for sentence. Reasons are not required in every case (e.g. a routine penalty for a routine offence), but where the duty exists, failure is an error of law (though the Act provides that a failure to give reasons does not invalidate the sentence). Their extent and detail depend on the circumstances: the nature of the case, the complexity of the issues, the evidence and the parties’ submissions. Reasons may be short and need not state the obvious or identify every consideration; nor must a court always explain rejecting alternative options, particularly those not reasonably practicable. Findings should not rest on speculation. Statutory statements: the announcement before an aggregate sentence (without needing notional separate sentences); orders requiring consent or an undertaking (explaining purposes, effect, consequences of non-compliance and variation); cooperation (facts and details recorded); s 6AAA (recorded). Where legislation directs a matter be considered, it should be discussed, not merely recited. Remarks may refer to objective and informed community expectations. Where cooperation is involved, two sets of reasons (one restricted) should be published. A transcript may be revised for meaning, but not altered in substance.

title: Correcting sentences: common law, s 104A, CPA s 412 limits, and reopening under s 104B
statement: At common law a court may correct an order to give effect to its intention but may not vary an order it intended to make. Under the Act it may amend for clerical mistakes, accidental slips or omissions, material mistakes in figures or descriptions, or defects in form (without an open-court hearing unless the interests of justice require). CPA s 412 provides very generally that a court may amend any sentence or order to correct any defect in substance or form, but it is not a “cure all”: it does not abrogate functus officio, correct substantive errors, revive an entered sentence, or apply where there was no error when pronounced. Section 104B (from 2015) allows reopening where a penalty was contrary to law or a required penalty was not imposed; the court must consider elapsed time and the consequences already suffered, and the new penalty runs from the original date unless otherwise ordered. Section 104B does not yet seem to have been tested.

title: Sentencing in the offender’s absence
statement: A trial for an indictable offence must be conducted in the accused’s presence, including sentencing, but the court may proceed in their absence if they waive the right (absconding on bail is prima facie waiver). Reluctance to proceed where the accused absconds before trial does not mean the power to proceed to sentence will be exercised sparingly; it depends on the circumstances. If the judicial officer who imposed the sentence goes out of office or is incapacitated, and it appears probable to the Chief Justice, Chief Judge or Chief Magistrate that they will not be able to deliver sentence within a reasonable time, a second judicial officer may be nominated to do so.

title: Open court principle
statement: Hearings should be public; sitting in camera needs statutory authority or a recognised exception (narrowly, where proceeding in public would defeat the jurisdiction). A judge should not receive sentence-relevant information in chambers. Confidential information may be protected by procedures, but closed hearings or unpublished documents must be noted in the published reasons.

Hearings should be public; sitting in camera needs statutory authority or a recognised exception (narrowly, where proceeding in public would defeat the jurisdiction). A judge should not receive sentence-relevant information in chambers. Confidential information may be protected by procedures, but closed hearings or unpublished documents must be noted in the published reasons.

title: Judicial duties and procedural fairness: a fair hearing on any adverse information
statement: The court must exercise its discretion judicially and ensure procedural fairness: a party facing an adverse determination on any information must be made aware of it and given a reasonable opportunity to respond. A sentence within range is no answer to a denial of procedural fairness; the test is objective. What is reasonable depends on the decision, the complexity of the issues and submissions, the significance to the party, and the court’s resources. For the app: any adverse matter it relies on that the user has not supplied must be surfaced as an assumption for the user to answer.

title: Unrepresented offenders: the court’s special responsibilities
statement: The court must ensure an unrepresented accused understands the charge and that the plea is their decision (with the chance to seek advice), knows of bail if relevant, is informed (if the case proceeds) of the seriousness and possible penalties, can put mitigation, call witnesses and dispute facts (and reconsider a plea inconsistent with a dispute), is told of any onus to prove mitigating facts, and is invited to address relevant matters. If imprisonment is possible and no submissions are made, the court should ask about character and history.

title: Neutrality and apprehended bias
statement: The judge should be neutral and not inquisitorial, but may (and sometimes must) disclose concerns; tentative views that the parties can address do not show bias, but intrusive interjections may create a reasonable suspicion of prejudgment.

title: Acceptance of a guilty plea: must be free, voluntary and unequivocal
statement: A plea must be freely made and unequivocal — a true admission (not from ignorance, fear, duress, mistake or for technical advantage), though it may be partly motivated by a discount. If not genuine, the court must obtain an unequivocal plea or enter not guilty. If the evidence does not support the charge the court should advise withdrawal but cannot compel it. A plea accepted by the prosecution cannot be rejected unless not genuine or an abuse of process. For the app: if the user’s facts disclose a possible defence or deny an element, flag it — the app does not decide guilt.

title: Depositions as sentencing material
statement: Depositions (committal transcript and statements, or the hand-up brief) are basic sentencing materials, need not be sworn or tested, and are reviewed broadly; conflicts with an agreed statement of facts should be raised with the parties; disputed items may be notified and evidence called. Depositions about admitted priors, or a co-offender’s depositions or record of interview where parity is in issue, should not be considered if they relate to an offence more serious than the one before the court.

title: What the principles are (and are not)
statement: Proportionality, parsimony, totality, parity and the prohibitions on double punishment and crushing sentences are guiding or limiting principles of broad application. They are not a blueprint, do not dictate a path of reasoning, and are taken together with gravity, purposes, the circumstances of offence and offender, and policy considerations.

What the principles are (and are not)
Proportionality, parsimony, totality, parity and the prohibitions on double punishment and crushing sentences are guiding or limiting principles of broad application. They are not a blueprint, do not dictate a path of reasoning, and are taken together with gravity, purposes, the circumstances of offence and offender, and policy considerations.

title: Proportionality
statement: The sentence should be proportionate to the gravity of the offence in light of the circumstances, including the maximum penalty, the harm, the method and the offender's culpability; it constrains both leniency and severity. The maximum defines the limit for the worst class of offending but is a guidepost. A longer term cannot be imposed merely to cure a condition (including addiction), to protect the community or for preventative detention. It applies to the total effective sentence, parity, mitigation, aggregation, cumulation and the non-parole period. There is no single proportionate sentence and sentencing is not a stepped process that first fixes a proportionate term. Legislation qualifies the principle to some degree (serious offenders under s 6D; indefinite sentences), but proportionality remains a fundamental consideration: departure is sparing and must be reasoned (see principle.proportionality_detail).

title: Parsimony and the hierarchy of sanctions (s 5(3)–(7))
statement: The sentence must be no more severe than necessary to achieve the purposes (type and length). In general, imprisonment cannot be imposed unless the purposes cannot be achieved by any other sentence, nor where a drug treatment order or CCO will serve; a drug treatment order not where a CCO suffices; a CCO not where a fine will do; a fine not where a dismissal, discharge or adjournment is sufficient. No single less severe sentence is mandated, and reasons for rejecting a non-custodial term are not required.

title: Totality
statement: For multiple offences the aggregate must be a just and appropriate measure of the total criminality. Preferred approach: appropriate individual terms, then wholly or partly concurrent orders — not cumulation of artificially reduced sentences. Steps: an appropriate term for each charge (highest as base — but see Barbat, fn 450); decide cumulation; then stand back and consider the appropriate total effective sentence, moderating cumulation if needed. The secondary "moderate and cumulate" approach is available where the preferred approach is not possible. Totality applies to offences that may overlap or be cumulated on an existing custodial sentence, to sentences imposed at the same time and to offences committed on different occasions and in different States (authority conflicts on whether interstate offending must be close in time and similar in kind, so care is needed), and to the head sentence and the non-parole period.

title: Totality, serious offenders (ss 6D, 6E) and parole offending (ss 5(2AA), 16(3B))
statement: Section 6D affects totality much as it affects proportionality: the court must be satisfied the offender will remain a danger beyond the period totality would permit. Totality must not be applied as if s 6E (presumptive cumulation for serious offenders) did not exist. For offending on parole: the court must not speculate on future executive action (s 5(2AA)), but where parole has been cancelled it considers the whole of the prior sentence with the new one so that the combination is not disproportionate to the aggregated criminality; absent exceptional circumstances the new sentence is cumulative (s 16(3B)) and totality cannot be applied inconsistently with that. Where parole has not been cancelled at the time of sentencing, no s 16(3B) order (cumulation or concurrency) may be made without breaching s 5(2AA) (see flag.parole_not_cancelled_at_sentence: s 77(7A) deems cancellation at sentence).

title: Double punishment
statement: A person must not be punished twice for the same criminal conduct: where offences share elements, the common elements must not be punished twice. Approach it as common sense, not semantics. If one offence is wholly subsumed in another, do not sentence for the subsumed offence (even concurrently). A single act causing separate harms (especially to different people) may be punished separately. The test is whether one sentence includes punishment also included in the other. Aggregate sentences rarely raise the issue.

title: Avoiding a crushing sentence
statement: A court should not impose a crushing sentence (one destroying any reasonable expectation of a useful life after release) unless there are special circumstances — eg crimes arousing deep public revulsion, a persistent unrepentant offender, multiple grave crimes, or community protection. It is an expression of the rehabilitation principle; a richly deserved sentence is not disturbed because the offender may feel crushed; age is relevant but cannot support an inappropriate sentence. The Manual also says there is no sentencing principle that requires a crushing sentence to be avoided, describing it as a particular expression of the rehabilitation principle (principle.crushing_detail); the two statements are recorded in flag.crushing_sentence_principle ((app policy) a possibly crushing total is a caution, never an error).

title: Parity between co-offenders
statement: Like cases should be treated alike: any significant difference between co-offenders' sentences should be capable of a rational explanation (an evaluation by impression). Relevant differences include age, background, criminal history, health, character and role (instigator, recruiter or principal vs aider and abettor or subordinate); also significant assistance to police and prosecution (possibly even where the non-cooperating offender was subordinate), an early plea (not a “marked” disparity — but see Sikoulabout, fn 589), adult vs juvenile (parity has only a limited application), armed vs unarmed, differences in criminal history, moral culpability and gain, dependence on or domination by the other in a personal or familial relationship, and personal factors (rehabilitation, specific deterrence, impact of custody, mercy). Compare all components including non-parole periods. Where parity requires modification, err on the side of leniency. Using a co-offender's sentence as a starting point and adjusting is an inappropriate two-step process.

title: The purposes of sentencing (s 5(1))
statement: Just punishment; deterrence of the offender and others; rehabilitation; denunciation; protection of the community. They overlap, can point in different directions, and which (if any) is paramount is a discretionary matter in all the circumstances.

The purposes of sentencing (s 5(1))
Just punishment; deterrence of the offender and others; rehabilitation; denunciation; protection of the community. They overlap, can point in different directions, and which (if any) is paramount is a discretionary matter in all the circumstances.

title: Just punishment and denunciation
statement: Just punishment reflects the moral sense of the community; it synthesises the offender's circumstances, the gravity of the crime and current sentencing practices (not mechanically). It is significant for homicide (especially domestic), causing serious injury (especially family violence), culpable or dangerous driving, armed robbery, aggravated burglary and sex offences (especially against children or vulnerable people). Denunciation communicates society's condemnation of the conduct (not the person). The victim's rehabilitation is relevant. Denunciation and retribution have less relevance for a mentally disabled offender unable to appreciate condemnation; a deliberate affront by an able offender cannot expect leniency; for grave crimes rehabilitation of a youth gives way.

title: Deterrence: points common to general and specific deterrence
statement: Deterrence is tempered by proportionality; it applies to the head sentence and the non-parole period (an unduly low non-parole period may destroy its effect); it may be achieved by non-custodial sentences. Mental illness or impairment may moderate or eliminate it (not automatically; moderation preferred), depending on symptoms and capacity; a condition arising from the reaction to discovery of the crime does not reduce it. Ideological or martyrdom motivation may make deterrence less relevant.

title: General deterrence
statement: General deterrence plays a role in almost every case but must not overwhelm the other purposes to produce a disproportionately harsh sentence, and must not target an ethnic community. Particularly important for homicide (domestic), indictable driving, child sexual offending, family violence, armed robbery, aggravated burglary, white collar crime, drug trafficking, prevalent offences, OHS offences, people smuggling and terrorism; and where public safety is at risk (street violence, drug/alcohol-fuelled or unprovoked violence, vulnerable victims, police, emergency workers, good Samaritans) or a court order (bail, parole, intervention order) is breached — there it “takes priority”. In some circumstances it may be moderated for an elderly offender (mercy may reduce its weight where death in prison is possible), but it remains important irrespective of advancing age. It has minimal relevance for a child, continues to have (moderated) relevance for an adult sentenced for offending committed as a child, is usually far less important than rehabilitation for youthful offenders except as seriousness rises, and may be given reduced weight for investigative or prosecutorial delay (not victim reluctance). Whether it applies to charges that could have been dealt with in the Children’s Court is unclear (flag.general_deterrence_childrens_court_charges).

title: Specific deterrence
statement: Criminal history is probably the most significant consideration; generally, the greater the risk of reoffending, the more weight. Persistent recidivism may preclude a moderate sentence; good character or a low risk of reoffending reduces but does not exclude it; offending while subject to another court order (bail, parole, an intervention order) requires it to be emphasised; it may assume great significance where the offence is a significant escalation of prior offending; it is less significant where the offender is genuinely remorseful, but good rehabilitation prospects do not make it irrelevant; a plea alone does not establish remorse.

title: Rehabilitation
statement: Steps towards rehabilitation should be given due weight, but the court does not set a period of rehabilitation or impose a disproportionate sentence to facilitate it. Rehabilitation has two parts — remorse and reform — both must be demonstrated. Relevant: plea, conduct of the defence, motive, delay not attributable to the offender, criminal record, youth (usually far more important than general deterrence), addiction, mental impairment. In serious, grave or violent offending other purposes may predominate. It may justify a lower non-parole period, but it is wrong to assume the head sentence reflects punishment and the non-parole period rehabilitation. A youthful first offender should not, if it can be avoided, be given a custodial sentence; alternatives like a youth justice centre are preferred to adult prison. Where an offender has had every opportunity to rehabilitate and has not done so, other purposes may take precedence; rehabilitation between absconding and new offending may be given slight weight.

title: Protection of the community
statement: Protection is usually by incapacitation but not only by imprisonment; prior convictions showing a continuing attitude of disobedience for the law, reluctance to undergo treatment or an incurable disorder fuelling offending may raise its importance (possibly to primary importance). It is limited by proportionality — no disproportionate sentence to extend protection. Legislative exceptions arguably elevate protection above proportionality: s 6D (serious offenders) is permissive — the court “may” impose a disproportionate term, is not required to, and need not disregard proportionality; before doing so it must be satisfied the offender will remain a danger beyond a proportionate term, with reasons — and indefinite sentences.

title: Why the principles are “fundamental” — and their limits
statement: The principles (proportionality, parsimony, totality, double punishment, crushing sentences, parity) are treated as fundamental because their application does not depend on the circumstances of the offence or offender and, subject to conditions and exceptions, they can make some claim to universal application. They are guiding or limiting principles, not a closed system: they are taken together with gravity, purposes, circumstances and policy in the synthesis.

title: Proportionality: the maximum, its statutory qualifications, and no “stepped” proportionate term
statement: The maximum defines the absolute limit for the worst class of the offence but is only a guidepost; a lengthy term cannot be imposed merely to cure a condition (including addiction), to protect the community or for preventative detention. Legislation qualifies the principle: for a serious offender sentenced for a relevant offence, the Supreme or County Court must treat community protection as paramount and may impose a disproportionate sentence where necessary — but proportionality remains fundamental and departure must be sparing and reasoned; an indefinite sentence is confined to very exceptional cases. Proportionality applies to every aspect (total effective sentence, parity, mitigation, aggregation, cumulation, non-parole periods). Individual sentences must not be made artificially inadequate to accommodate cumulation; each count gets an appropriate and proportionate sentence. Sentencing is not a stepped process that first fixes a proportionate term: a range of proportionate sentences is usually open and there is no single one.

title: Parsimony: what the hierarchy requires; reasons; supervision orders
statement: Before imposing imprisonment the judge must be satisfied that no other sentence is appropriate; the sentence must be no more severe than necessary (in type and length). The statutory hierarchy does not mean there is a single less severe sentence that must be imposed; in general it means imprisonment cannot be imposed unless the purposes cannot be achieved by any other sentence. The court need not give reasons for rejecting a non-custodial term or note parsimony expressly. Parsimony also applies to supervision orders under the Crimes (Mental Impairment and Unfitness to be Tried) Act.

title: Totality: the preferred and secondary approaches, and when totality applies
statement: There must be appropriate relativity between the totality of the criminality and the total effective sentence. Individual sentences should not be made artificially inadequate to accommodate cumulation (they may be “modest”). The strongly preferred approach — appropriate individual terms, the highest as base, cumulation for each count, then “stand back” and moderate cumulation if the total infringes totality — should be departed from only for a special feature of the case; it is not mandatory, other consistent approaches are permissible and a different approach does not itself show error. Where it cannot be followed, the secondary “moderate and cumulate” approach (reduced individual terms, partly cumulated) may be used, e.g. where the offender has previously served substantial periods of imprisonment and conventional terms could produce a disproportionately long sentence, multiple serious offences, or where s 16(3B) precludes concurrency. The preferred approach exists so that each sentence reflects its offence, remaining sentences stay appropriate if one is set aside, and artificial disparity claims are avoided. A single court may achieve totality by concurrency (wholly or partly) or by disproportionately low terms. Totality applies when sentencing for offences that may overlap or be cumulated on an existing custodial sentence, to sentences imposed at the same time and to offences on different occasions and in different States (authority conflicts on whether interstate offending must be close in time and similar in kind: care), to head sentence and non-parole period, and where the current sentence derives from a parole breach. Usually the court considers what would have been just had all offences been sentenced together; where that is not apt (Sayer), totality applies distinctly and prior sentences and custody remain part of the offender’s circumstances (but see Mendoza-Cortez, fn 469).

title: Totality and the serious offender provisions (ss 6D, 6E)
statement: Section 6D affects totality much as it affects proportionality: the court must be satisfied the offender will remain a danger beyond the period totality would permit. Section 6E makes cumulation presumptive for serious offenders; the court must not undermine that policy by applying totality as if the legislation did not exist (but see DPP (Vic) v VH, fn 473), and it is wrong to “direct otherwise” simply to achieve what totality would have required. Guidance on resolving the s 6E/totality tension is limited: as objective gravity increases so might the degree of cumulation, or the secondary (moderated individual sentences) approach may be used.

title: Totality and offending on parole: s 5(2AA), cancellation, s 16(3B) and the “whole sentence”
statement: For totality, s 5(2AA) bars considering whether custody will be affected by executive action — e.g. whether parole might be granted at the end of the non-parole period (in fixing the non-parole period itself, 8.3.3.2 lets the court consider the possibility of release on parole: npp.no_executive_speculation; flag.parole_consideration_3_3_3_vs_8_3_3_2). Because it is prospective, it bars totality only where parole has not been revoked at sentence; once revoked (including automatic cancellation under the Corrections Act — s 77(6) “on conviction” for listed offences committed on parole for such an offence; s 77(7A) at the time of sentencing when a prison sentence is imposed for parole offending), the whole sentence may be considered. A long line of Court of Appeal cases held that only the additional period the offender must serve because of the cancellation was considered; Koumis held that the entire period imposed for the prior offending (the time served before release on parole and the balance after cancellation) should be considered, and DPP v Bowen affirmed that view — so that the combined effect is not disproportionate to the aggregated criminality. Under s 16(3B), absent exceptional circumstances, sentences for offending on parole are cumulative on the period served because of cancellation (the offender normally serves the balance first), and totality must not be applied inconsistently with that intention — but viewed as a whole the terms cannot exceed what totality and the purposes require; neither the head sentence nor the non-parole period for the later offences may be disproportionate to the total criminality (the further statement that “the parole sentence has no role to play” beyond that rests on Dickson and Waugh, from the line Bowen overtook: caution, flag.parole_no_role_rests_on_disapproved_line). “Exceptional circumstances” is a relative and protean concept; re-offending on parole from a life sentence has been held exceptional (warranting concurrency), without precluding cumulation among the later offences. If parole has not been cancelled at sentence, no s 16(3B) order can be made without breaching s 5(2AA) (when that case arises once s 77(7A) operates is unclear: flag.parole_not_cancelled_at_sentence). Totality is significant but not controlling.

title: Totality and crushing sentences are different tests
statement: A crushing sentence does not inherently offend totality; the two are not the same, and a sentence may offend totality without being crushing — although some authority treats avoiding a crushing sentence as a very significant part, or the second limb, of the totality analysis (fn 502; flag.crushing_within_totality).

title: Double punishment: the test
statement: Punishment should reflect only what the offender did, not how offence boundaries are drawn: an offender may be prosecuted for conduct constituting several offences but not punished more than once for the same act or omission. The enquiry is one of common sense, not semantics. A wholly subsumed offence should not be sentenced at all, even concurrently. A single act causing separate harms (especially to different people) may be punished separately, and some cumulation may be called for where one action constitutes two distinct harms. The test is whether one sentence includes an element of punishment also included in another; with no common elements or facts, no question arises. An aggregate sentence is unlikely to raise the risk. The area is complex and hard to reduce to firm guidelines.

title: Crushing sentences: what the principle is, and is not
statement: There is no principle that a crushing sentence must be avoided: it is an expression of the principle that a sentence should promote rehabilitation where possible, and in grave cases little weight can be given to rehabilitation. It is wrong to set a minimum by the need to ensure “some measure of life after release”. Age (advanced or youthful) may be significant but cannot support an inappropriate sentence. Extreme length alone does not make a sentence crushing, and there are no hard and fast rules. An offender may by their crimes forfeit the expectation of a useful life after release, and community protection may justify a sentence the offender sees as crushing (s 6D may produce one: purpose.community_protection_detail). A crushing term is of greater concern for older offenders. The authority for the “no principle” statement (fn 564) is incomplete in the Manual (flag.citation_incomplete_fn564). The Manual also says a court should not impose a crushing sentence unless there are special circumstances (principle.crushing_sentence; the two statements: flag.crushing_sentence_principle).

title: Parity: scope, comparison and how to apply it
statement: Parity is an aspect of equal justice (like treated alike) but does not require strict comparison or the same sentence. The court must assess the individuals and circumstances; a comparative analysis of culpability is indispensable. Co-offenders are preferably sentenced together by the same judge; otherwise the later judge should learn the earlier sentence and its circumstances. A substantial discount to one offender must be considered for the other and may require some reduction, but an excessively lenient sentence cannot justify an inappropriately low one. Further justified differences include gender-related burdens (not gender itself), an agreed statement of facts, and positive participation in the Koori Court with a year under its supervision. Parity applies to all co-offenders (not just the lowest sentence) and to everyone in a common criminal enterprise (but see Huu, fn 605) (participants need not act at the same time or know of each other). Related offending may be relevant, weighted by nexus, similarity and personal factors; a sufficient nexus may require close conformity even without a common enterprise. Parity is harder to apply as the crimes differ. Percentages of non-parole periods and head sentences may help. Parity may require a substantially lower penalty. A common criminal enterprise is a course of criminal activity of multiple unlawful acts of the same or similar nature, related to the same criminal purpose. If co-offenders are not sentenced together, an appellate court is not justified in interfering on parity grounds on that account (fn 581). For adult and juvenile co-offenders parity has only a limited application, but the youthful offender’s sentence remains part of the background for the adult.

title: Parity on appeal: Crown appeals, re-sentencing and co-appellants
statement: Parity arguments have very little chance of success where the co-offenders were sentenced for multiple counts, or where one was sentenced for several counts and the other for only one. The DPP may appeal only one co-offender’s sentence. Normally, given the limited and specific nature of a Crown appeal, the court is constrained from intervening even if it considers the sentence manifestly inadequate; parity may limit intervention but does not require the court to decline to intervene; on re-sentence the co-offender’s sentence must be taken into account, but parity cannot require a wholly inappropriate sentence. Parity is relevant to the residual discretion, which the court may decline to exercise where giving full weight to parity would produce unjustifiable disparity amounting to an affront to justice. A reduction for one appellant re-opens the discretion for co-offenders who appealed, without requiring a reduction.

title: Parity on appeal: marked disparity and a justifiable sense of grievance
statement: Disparity on appeal is approached like manifest excess; intervention needs disparity so marked as to produce a legitimate and justifiable sense of grievance in the objective observer (i.e. the differential was not reasonably open). Parity arguments rarely succeed where the co-offenders were sentenced for multiple counts, or where one was sentenced for several counts and the other for only one. In Crown appeals parity may limit intervention, but does not require a wholly inappropriate sentence. If one offender’s sentence is reduced, the discretion reopens for appealing co-offenders, without requiring a reduction.

title: Weighing the purposes: they overlap and may point in different directions
statement: Sentencing is difficult because each purpose must be given appropriate weight, and the purposes overlap and cannot be considered in isolation. More than one purpose is often furthered, and which (if any) is paramount depends on all the circumstances and is a matter for the court’s discretion.

title: Just punishment and denunciation: content and limits
statement: Retribution does not mean “an eye for an eye”: the court recognises what accords with the moral sense of the community, and the law must be administered in a way the community can understand and regard as fair and just. Determining a just sentence is not mechanical, and guidelines for the synthesis cannot be set without impeding the discretion. Denunciation communicates, through the type or duration of the sentence, society’s condemnation of the conduct; the court speaks with reference to community expectations and values and must vindicate them and be seen to do so. The sentence must acknowledge the personal damage to the victim (whose rehabilitation may be harder than the offender’s). Denunciation and retribution have less relevance for an offender with a mental disability who cannot appreciate the condemnation; an intelligent offender whose conduct is a deliberate affront cannot expect leniency. For a youthful offender, rehabilitation must give way in crimes of great gravity or violence, and significantly so for an intended terrorist act.

title: Deterrence: no non-parole period, and impairment arising after the offending
statement: Where imprisonment is imposed with no minimum term, deterrence is given the most weight; if deterrence predominates it may, rarely, be appropriate to make little or no allowance for mitigating factors. A mental impairment or illness that develops after the offending may require moderation of general and specific deterrence: the court asks, at sentence, whether the offender is an “appropriate vehicle” for deterrence (the offender should not be used as a model for others) — but not where the condition resulted from the discovery of the crime and fear of a long prison term (the offender is the author of their predicament). Deterrence may be less relevant where the offender is motivated by an ideology or religion that calls for martyrdom (but see MHK, fn 672).

title: General deterrence: how it operates and where its weight changes
statement: General deterrence depends on community awareness of sentences; if outcomes are not known they lose their deterrent effect (courts rely on the media and government to communicate them). It imposes a severity the offender’s criminality does not itself warrant, so it must not cause injustice; it has separately contributed only if the sentence was increased above what specific deterrence alone would justify. It must not be used to target a specific ethnic community. It is important in familial offending (a person should be able to leave a relationship without fear), and of paramount concern for offending in custody. For an elderly offender it is considered in light of the greater burden of prison and public perception. It is significant regardless of provocation or motive. It has minimal relevance when sentencing a child, and the matters in CYFA s 362(1) preclude it from being considered when a child is sentenced under that Act; it is unclear whether it applies where charges that might have been dealt with in the Children’s Court are dealt with in a superior court — it likely applies if punishment beyond that Act (or s 32(3)(b)) is needed (flag.general_deterrence_childrens_court_charges). For youthful offenders rehabilitation is usually more important, but not automatically: in murder there is much less room for youth, and where a youthful offender carries out or plans extreme violence, youth is diminished quite substantially in weighing general deterrence. For an adult sentenced for offending committed as a child, its weight depends on multiple factors, including the seriousness of the offence and offending, remorse and rehabilitation prospects; where general deterrence is a significant purpose there is less scope for leniency based on youth.

title: Specific deterrence: offending on orders, remorse and restitution
statement: Offending while subject to another court order (bail, parole, an intervention order) requires specific deterrence to be emphasised. Good rehabilitation prospects do not make specific deterrence irrelevant. Without genuine remorse, specific deterrence is particularly important; an offer of restitution may indicate remorse but is of limited consequence if not spontaneous or made only after discovery. Being on summons for another offence that did not lead to conviction is not relevant to specific deterrence.

title: Rehabilitation: remorse and reform, indicators, and its place in the sentence
statement: Steps towards rehabilitation should be given due weight. Rehabilitation has two parts — remorse and reform — both of which must be demonstrated; less weight is given where genuine remorse is lacking or there is merely no further offending (but see TC, fn 751). Remorse is shown by post-offence conduct; it is error to reject it merely because it is inconsistent with a lack of remorse at the time of offending. A guilty plea may indicate remorse, but a not guilty plea is not itself a basis for finding no prospects; a spurious defence may reflect poorly. An absence of motive can make prospects hard to assess. Delay not attributable to the offender increases the emphasis on rehabilitation, so that rehabilitation under way is not halted. Rehabilitation is usually far more important than general deterrence for young offenders, but not automatically. Mental impairment does not mean an offender is incapable of rehabilitation. A short custodial term may reflect a rehabilitative aspect; a youthful first offender should if possible be given the opportunity to reform rather than custody. Only regret for the harm caused — not sorrow at being caught and punished — is remorse for sentencing purposes.

title: Protection of the community: indicators, s 6D, and dangerousness assessed at sentence
statement: Prior convictions showing a continuing disobedience of the law, reluctance to engage in treatment, or an incurable disorder that fuelled the offending may increase the importance of community protection. Under s 6D, when imprisonment is justified for a serious offender’s relevant offence, protection of the community becomes the principal purpose; because protection is always relevant, this has little impact except where mitigating factors call for a shorter term. The serious-danger assessment for an indefinite sentence is made at the time of sentencing, not as a prediction of dangerousness at the end of the sentence; on an application for review of the indefinite term (ss 18H, 18M) it is made as at the time of review. Invoking s 6D may produce a crushing sentence, which may have to be accepted if necessary to protect the community (as may an elderly offender’s likely death in jail).

The serious-danger assessment for an indefinite sentence is made at the time of sentencing, not as a prediction of dangerousness at the end of the sentence; on an application for review of the indefinite term (ss 18H, 18M) it is made as at the time of review. Invoking s 6D may produce a crushing sentence, which may have to be accepted if necessary to protect the community (as may an elderly offender’s likely death in jail).

title: Comparing sentence types: the “loose hierarchy” of s 5(4)–(7) and the ordering the hard checks use
statement: Sections 5(4)–(7) create a loose hierarchy of sentencing options (3.2): imprisonment may not be imposed where a drug treatment order or a conditional CCO will serve the purposes; a drug treatment order cannot be imposed where a CCO will suffice; a CCO must not be imposed where a fine will do; and a fine cannot be imposed if a dismissal, discharge or adjournment is sufficient. The hierarchy does not mean there is a single less severe sentence that must be imposed. (app policy) Where a hard check must compare two sentence types (the s 6AAA notional sentence; a sentence indication), it uses this order: imprisonment (including a combination sentence) > CCO > fine > adjourned undertaking, discharge or dismissal (these three are not ranked among themselves). A comparison involving any other order (a DATO — the Manual does not say whether it is the “drug treatment order” of 3.2 — youth detention, CSTO, RTO, MTMO, indefinite sentence), or between the last three, is not settled by the Manual → caution, never error.

title: Victorian summary offences: imprisonment capped at two years

Summary offences may or may not be punishable by imprisonment, and need care in combination with offences attracting a custodial term.

title: Victorian indictable offences triable summarily; two-year cap per offence; five-year cumulative cap
statement: Victorian indictable offences (statutory and common law) triable summarily include those listed in Schedule 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2009, Level 5 or Level 6 offences, offences punishable by Level 5 or 6 imprisonment or fine, and offences punishable by up to 10 years, a fine of 1200 penalty units, or both. title: The maximum is the absolute ceiling for each sentence — and the two departures (indefinite sentence; CCE offender)
statement: Unless an indefinite sentence is available, the maximum penalty fixed by Parliament is absolutely the highest term that may be imposed for the offence. The ceiling applies to each individual sentence: cumulation can produce a total exceeding the maximum for a single charge. The Magistrates’ Court limits are lower ceilings, never higher ones.

title: Commonwealth offences in the Magistrates’ Court: summary trial and sentencing limits (outside the app’s Victorian scope)
statement: Commonwealth indictable offences that may not be tried summarily are effectively those relating to treason, espionage or advocating terrorism or violence. title: Imprisonment requires a recorded conviction
statement: A sentence of imprisonment can only be imposed if a conviction is recorded.

title: When imprisonment is available for the offence
statement: A statutory offence is punishable by imprisonment only if that sanction is expressly provided for, generally by a prescribed maximum penalty. Almost all indictable offences are punishable by imprisonment; possession of a small quantity of cannabis is punishable only by a fine. Where a statutory offence is created but no maximum penalty is specified, the maximum is presumptively two years imprisonment. Common law offences are punishable by imprisonment, with a maximum set by statute or “at large”. Summary offences may or may not be punishable by imprisonment.

title: Imprisonment is the sanction of last resort
statement: A sentence requiring confinement cannot be imposed unless the court considers that the sentencing purposes cannot be met by another sentence. Courts are traditionally reluctant to imprison some offenders, such as those with mental impairments or who are gravely ill. The principle is subject to the statutory schemes: for Category 1 and 2 offences, and for mandatory minimum offences, imprisonment must be imposed unless an exception is engaged.

title: A sentence must be imposed for each offence (unless aggregate)
statement: A court must impose a sentence for each offence, unless it imposes an aggregate sentence. The total custodial term (head sentence / total effective sentence) is produced by orders for cumulation or concurrency.
