title: Individual sentences reflect each charge, not a formula
statement: Individual sentences should not be imposed mechanistically (for example as a fixed proportion of the maximum); a court should ensure they reflect the criminality of the specific offences and are appropriate to the gravity of each charge. Particular care is required with numerous offences, although within limits a broad-brush approach (the same sentence for offences of the same type) may be adopted, for example for an ongoing course of fraudulent conduct or similar and repetitive offending; the sentences then need only be roughly proportional to the gravity of the offending and any amounts taken.

title: What the non-parole period is
statement: The non-parole period is the minimum term justice requires the offender to serve before being eligible for parole; it does not fix the release date.

title: Non-parole period must be fixed for imprisonment of two years or more
statement: For imprisonment of two years or more the court must fix a non-parole period unless it considers that the nature of the offence or the circumstances of the offender make it inappropriate. These criteria are not exclusive: the court must also have regard to the head sentence and the sentencing purposes and principles. Historically, avoiding an interaction between parole and a CCO was not a basis to decline; more recently the Court of Appeal has said that, at least for an arson offence, imprisonment without a non-parole period could be appropriate so that there is no risk of serving a CCO while on parole. For a sentence between one and two years the court may fix one (but not if the sentence is combined with a CCO: npp.none_with_cco_12m_2y). No non-parole period is fixed for an indefinite sentence. A failure to fix a non-parole period does not invalidate the sentence.

title: No non-parole period when a 12 month–2 year sentence is combined with a CCO
statement: If the sentence is between 12 months and two years and is combined with a CCO, the court cannot fix a non-parole period; a CCO and a non-parole period are alternatives in those circumstances. title: Minimum non-parole period for standard sentence offences (s 11A(4))
statement: When sentencing for a standard sentence offence within the scheme (sso.scope), or for multiple offences including one, the court must, unless it considers it is not in the interests of justice, fix a non-parole period of at least 30 years for a life term, 70% of the relevant term if it is 20 years or more, and 60% if it is 20 years or less. Reasons must be given for a shorter non-parole period. As printed, a term of exactly 20 years falls in both limbs; and for short terms the floor cannot be met together with the 12-month and six-month restrictions in 8.3.1.

Reasons must be given for a shorter non-parole period. title: The 'usual' non-parole period (60–75%) and reasons for departing
statement: In practice non-parole periods usually fall between 60% and 75% of the head sentence; this is an important guide, but there is "no usual non-parole period", different standards may apply for longer and shorter sentences, and the range ceases to be of much guidance where the head sentence is around 10 years or more. A non-parole period outside the range does not vitiate the sentence but may attract greater appellate scrutiny, so an unusual non-parole period should be explained (a failure to give reasons is not itself error). Where a court states an intention to impose a proportionately short (or long) non-parole period, one within the usual range may show that the intention was not given effect, though that is exceptional.

title: Do not speculate on executive action (parole)
statement: The court must not consider the possibility or likelihood that the time spent in custody will be affected by executive action of any kind (including release on parole), and in fixing the non-parole period must consider that the offender may have to serve every day of the head sentence. It may nonetheless consider the possibility of release on parole, the rehabilitative potential of parole and the offender’s suitability for parole in fixing the non-parole period: the prohibition primarily excludes considering that parole may be cancelled when assessing totality, and the head sentence must be one that would be appropriate whether or not the offender is released on parole. (3.3.3 states the prohibition without this qualification: flag.parole_consideration_3_3_3_vs_8_3_3_2.)

title: Offender already serving a non-parole period: fix a new single non-parole period
statement: If the offender is serving the non-parole period of a prior sentence (the “parole sentence”) and receives a further term, the court must fix a new single non-parole period for all sentences; it supersedes the earlier one and must not make the offender eligible for parole earlier than if the new sentence had not been imposed. It is wrong to approach the new sentence as if there must be an “overall minimum term” made up of the time remaining on the parole sentence and a non-parole period for the new sentence. The requirement does not apply where the prior sentence was originally a straight sentence without parole eligibility, where the original non-parole period has been completed, or to an offender sentenced at one time for offences across multiple indictments. The new single non-parole period is not a “sentence of imprisonment” for the purposes of determining when a sentence commences. Courts are encouraged to commence it from the date of the new sentence (on appeal, the date of the order under appeal); the date must be expressly stated; and where it runs from the new sentence date the court must make an allowance for the parole sentence already served. Its length reflects the standard considerations for fixing a non-parole period. Pre-sentence detention already considered by the first court: psd.new_single_npp.

title: One non-parole period for multiple offences; preferably stated in months/years
statement: For multiple offences the non-parole period applies to the aggregate period of incarceration for all offences (one non-parole period). A court ordinarily fixes it by stating the term in months or years, which is preferable to nominating a specific date; selecting a date may cause confusion and lead to error. No non-parole period is fixed for an indefinite sentence.

title: Select the longest individual sentence as the base; attribute punishment to every charge
statement: The longest (ordinarily most severe) individual sentence should be the base sentence; cumulation orders add to it. Imposing the total effective sentence on one charge with total concurrency for the rest is problematic.

title: Cumulation orders reflect seriousness, episodes and victims; totality governs
statement: Cumulation orders must reflect differences in the seriousness of each offence, different episodes and each victim; uniform sentences or uniform cumulation orders across offences of a type may indicate a failure to consider each charge and risk an excessive head sentence. Totality is the fundamental principle. There is no formal minimum length of a cumulation order, though orders measured in days or weeks are rare and most are measured in months. Subject to totality there is no maximum period of cumulation (except the Magistrates’ Court five-year limit for several offences committed at the same time: cum.magistrates_5_years); cumulation can produce a total exceeding the base sentence and even the maximum for a single charge.

title: Sentences are concurrent unless ordered otherwise
statement: The principal rule presumes sentences are served concurrently; if no order is made they are concurrent by operation of law. The court exercises a sound discretion whether to cumulate (for some or all counts, in whole or in part). There must be good reason to depart from the applicable presumption; where cumulation is the default, a prison offence, escape, breach of parole or offending on parole requires “exceptional circumstances” to displace it (cum.presumption_cumulation). The sentence may be expressed as cumulation or concurrency whichever is presumed; the underlying requirement is that its individual elements are clear (stating any deviation from the presumption is preferable but not strictly required).

title: Categories where cumulation is the default
statement: The default is cumulation rather than concurrency for terms of imprisonment for: defaulting on a fine or payment of money (only for uncompleted terms relating to a similar default); a prison offence or escape; a serious offender convicted of a relevant offence; an offence committed while on parole or for breaching parole; an offence committed while on bail; a young offender whose later offending was escape or property damage to specified correctional facilities; the four offences of (aggravated) intentionally or recklessly exposing an emergency worker, custodial officer or youth justice custodial worker to risk by driving; and damaging an emergency vehicle. All remain subject to fundamental principles, in particular totality. For a prison offence, escape, breach of parole or offending on parole, “exceptional circumstances” must be found to displace the prima facie cumulation of new sentences with the previous sentence. For fine or payment defaults, a serious offender convicted of a relevant offence, offending on bail, and specified offences against emergency workers and custodial officers, the court has a wide discretion whether to order concurrency and totality can justify departing from the presumption. The Manual does not say which of the two groups the young-offender category or damaging an emergency vehicle belongs to. For offending on parole the default applies only where parole has been cancelled before sentencing (3.3.3; flag.parole_not_cancelled_at_sentence). Where the parole is from a life sentence, no term may be cumulated on the life term (cum.life_parole), and re-offending on life parole is itself an exceptional circumstance warranting a concurrent term (3.3.3).

title: No cumulation on a life sentence (imposed now, already imposed or being served, or paroled from)
statement: Additional sentences of imprisonment cannot be imposed on a person already sentenced to, or serving, a life sentence other than concurrently with the life sentence (21.4.1). Cumulation may still be ordered between the sentences for offences committed during release on parole, independently of whether any cumulation is ordered with the parole sentence. Re-offending while on parole for a life sentence is itself an exceptional circumstance warranting a concurrent term (3.3.3), so the parole cumulation default (cum.presumption_cumulation) does not require a further finding. (app policy) A life sentence imposed on another charge at the same sentencing is treated as within “already sentenced to” only as a caution, not an error.

title: Aggregate sentence: when available and its ceiling
statement: An aggregate sentence may be imposed for two or more offences founded on the same facts or forming part of a series of the same or similar character (the joinder test), including representative or rolled-up charges; it cannot exceed the total effective sentence that separate sentences could have produced. It is a “term of imprisonment”, so any order for cumulation or concurrency may be made in respect of it; more than one aggregate sentence may be imposed in one proceeding, grouping offences in any way the court considers just and convenient (not necessarily following the indictment). The court must announce in open court the decision, its reasons and the effect of the aggregate term, but need not identify the separate events or announce the sentences it would have imposed for each offence. In the Magistrates’ Court it is not clear whether an aggregate sentence may exceed two years (mc.two_year_max_summary).

title: Pre-sentence detention must be declared as time served
statement: Time in custody after charge and before sentence for the offence must be taken into account and declared as time already served when the offender is sentenced to imprisonment or detention for that offence (s 18). If the offender is charged with a series of offences committed on different occasions and has been in continuous custody since arrest, the whole custodial period from the arrest must be taken into account, even if they are not convicted of the offence underlying the first arrest or any other offence. The court may "otherwise order", but the discretion should not be exercised without good reason (and never because it intends a combination imprisonment and CCO sentence); the declaration is then "nil days". A declaration is made in either case and entered in the records of the court.

title: New single non-parole period: pre-sentence detention already considered by the first court (s 14(2)(d))
statement: In fixing a new single non-parole period for an offender already serving an earlier non-parole period, the later court must not take into account a PSD period considered by the first sentencing court. A PSD declaration made at the first sentence continues to operate, and the new single non-parole period should not include the PSD declared on the first occasion. The later court must also declare a further PSD period unrelated to any PSD already declared by the first court; the correctional authorities aggregate the two declared periods.

title: Custody that is not declarable under s 18
statement: Section 18 does not apply to custodial periods of less than one day (applied practically where the only custody is the day of sentencing); imprisonment or detention in a designated mental health service of less than one day (most commonly a sentence “to the rising of the court”); periods already declared under another sentence or Court Secure Treatment Order; custody while already serving another sentence or youth detention (including after parole is cancelled); detention for other offending pending extradition; or immigration detention pending trial. Time served under a quashed sentence on resentence on appeal is declarable.

title: Imprisonment combined with a CCO: one year after deducting pre-sentence detention (except arson)
statement: The maximum length of imprisonment on a combination imprisonment and CCO sentence is one year plus time served as pre-sentence detention: except for arson, the sum of all terms of imprisonment cannot exceed one year after deducting any pre-sentence detention. The limit is enforced once, by cco.combination_one_year and order.cco.combination_time_served (which also state the arson exception and the Magistrates’ Court limit).

title: Renzella discretion and 'dead time'
statement: Courts have a common law discretion to take into account custody not covered by a s 18 declaration (eg residential rehabilitation or immigration detention), weighted by its burden: it is not equivalent to real incarceration and does not necessarily attract the same deduction. It forms part of the instinctive synthesis and is not a mathematical exercise. "Dead time" (custody that in hindsight should not have been served) is reflected by reducing the base sentence or moderating cumulation, by the amount the court considers appropriate. Time served under a previous sentence is not declarable PSD; the court must make clear that it took the earlier sentence into account through totality. Previous detention should be taken into account at the earliest opportunity, not left to a later court (though the discretion has been exercised for custody in the distant past). The discretion does not operate where the offender is on parole from a life sentence.

title: Indefinite sentence: availability, threshold and procedure
statement: An adult convicted of a 'serious offence' by the Supreme or County Court may be sentenced to an indefinite term, regardless of the maximum penalty, on the court’s own initiative or the DPP’s application. No non-parole period is fixed; the court fixes a “nominal sentence” equal to the non-parole period of the fixed term it might have imposed. As preventative detention at odds with proportionality, the power is exercised sparingly, in the exceptional case. Before imposing it the court must consider whether the Court Secure Treatment Order provisions apply (if so, it must make that order instead) and be satisfied to a high degree of probability that, at sentencing, the offender is a serious danger to the community (the prosecution bears the burden). In deciding serious danger it must consider: whether the nature of the serious offence is exceptional; anything relevant in the transcript of any proceeding for a serious offence; any medical, psychiatric or other relevant report; the risk of serious danger if no indefinite sentence is imposed and the need to protect the community; and anything else it thinks fit. Procedure: DPP notice (day of conviction or within five working days) and application (within 10 working days); explanation to the offender within five working days of conviction; adjournment of at least 25 working days after conviction; evidence and submissions, victim impact statements and pre-sentence reports considered; reasons given and recorded; any period detained under a Court Assessment Order deducted from the nominal sentence where the psychiatrist’s report was made under it.

title: Indefinite sentence: review, discharge and appeal
statement: An indefinite sentence must be reviewed on the DPP’s application as soon as practicable after the nominal sentence is served, on the offender’s application three years after that review, and then at intervals of not less than three years. Unless satisfied to a high degree of probability that the offender still poses a danger to the community, the reviewing court must discharge the indefinite sentence, make the offender subject to a re-integration program and issue a warrant as if for a five-year term; otherwise the indefinite sentence continues. A review is not “imposing sentence”, so the reviewing court should assume the authorities will responsibly exercise their statutory powers. The offender may appeal a refusal to discharge and the DPP may appeal a discharge.

title: Suspended sentences abolished (by offence date and court)
statement: Suspended sentences are not available for offences committed after: 1 September 2013 (all offences heard in the County or Supreme Court); 1 May 2011 (serious or significant offences heard in those courts); 1 September 2014 (all offences heard in the Magistrates' Court at first instance); 1 September 2013 (Magistrates' Court following a transfer from a higher court). “Serious” and “significant” offences (as defined before 1 September 2014) include: murder; manslaughter; child homicide; defensive homicide; intentionally or recklessly causing serious injury; threats to kill; rape; assault with intent to rape; incest (except where both participants were over 18 and consented); sexual penetration of a child under 16; persistent sexual abuse of a child under 16; abduction or detention; abduction of a child under 16; kidnapping; armed robbery; aggravated burglary; arson; arson causing death; trafficking a large commercial or a commercial quantity of a drug of dependence. The Manual does not set out the suspended sentence regime for earlier offending.

title: Category 1 offences: imprisonment without a CCO
statement: For most Category 1 offences a court must impose a sentence of imprisonment and must not attach a CCO. An exception applies to Category 1 offences that are also mandatory minimum offences against protected officials (9.1.2.3), and it is confined: (a) if special reasons are found on a charge of intentionally or recklessly causing serious injury, or intentionally or recklessly causing injury (ss 16–18; and, per fn 2005, ss 317AC/317AD), the court must sentence under s 5(2GA): imprisonment (without a CCO) or a mandatory treatment and monitoring order, Residential Treatment Order or Court Secure Treatment Order, the therapeutic orders only on the stated conditions (whether imprisonment combined with a mandatory treatment and monitoring order is open is unresolved: flag.mtmo_combination_sentence); (b) for an offender under 21 at sentence, where the court does not find special reasons and a pre-sentence report supports it, a youth justice centre order of at least the minimum non-parole period may be made instead (not for gross violence charges); (c) for ss 15A/15B (gross violence) against a protected official with special reasons found, imprisonment without a CCO is open, and whether any other disposition is open is unresolved (flag.gross_violence_protected_special_reason). For a Category 1 offence that carries no mandatory minimum a special reason never opens another disposition; for the other Category 1 offences that carry one, whether a special reason permits a disposition other than imprisonment without a CCO is unresolved (flag.category1_special_reason). The offence tables state the rule for Category 1 offences committed on or after 20 March 2017 as a “custodial sentence (other than a sentence of imprisonment imposed in addition to making a community correction order)”.

title: Category 2 offences: imprisonment unless an exception is established
statement: For Category 2 offences a court must impose imprisonment (without a CCO) unless: (a) the offender assisted or undertook to assist law enforcement authorities in the investigation or prosecution of an offence (information supplied to bring others to justice or prevent other crimes; an admission is not enough); (b) the offender proves on the balance of probabilities impaired mental functioning at the time of offending (not substantially caused by self-induced intoxication) causally linked to the offence that substantially and materially reduces culpability; (c) the offender proves on the balance of probabilities impaired mental functioning that would subject them to “substantially and materially greater” than ordinary burdens or risks of imprisonment (an extant mental illness at sentence is needed, not a mere possibility; where an offender with complex mental health needs submits evidence of them, the prosecution is best placed to adduce evidence that they can be met in custody); (d) the court proposes a Court Secure Treatment Order or Residential Treatment Order; or (e) there are substantial and compelling circumstances that are exceptional and rare and that justify not imposing imprisonment (cat2.substantial_compelling_test).

title: Category 2 'substantial and compelling, exceptional and rare' test
statement: The Category 2 exceptions closely follow the special-reason test, including the weight given to general deterrence and denunciation, limits on considering good character, plea, rehabilitation or parity, and a need to have regard to Parliament’s intention that imprisonment should ordinarily be imposed for offences of this type. The residual exception is a category of limited scope: a stringent, non-discretionary test, a higher hurdle than Verdins, which the Court of Appeal has said will not often, if ever, be satisfied — though that observation only describes the apparent operation of the legislation, and the difficulty may vary with the offence. Two steps: are there substantial and compelling circumstances (weighty enough to justify no custody), and are they exceptional and rare (wholly outside the run-of-the-mill factors typical of the offending)? General deterrence and denunciation have primacy; personal circumstances get less weight than the gravity of the offending; previous good character, early plea, rehabilitation prospects and even parity must not be considered (the special-reason test instead excepts a lack of previous convictions: flag.good_character_category2_vs_special_reason). It is evaluative: minds may reasonably differ, an accumulation of detail may compel the conclusion, and each case turns on its own facts.

title: Manslaughter (gross violence or single punch): 10-year minimum non-parole period
statement: From 1 November 2014, a 10-year minimum non-parole period applies to manslaughter in circumstances of gross violence or by a single punch or strike, if the prosecution gives notice that it intends to apply for the minimum and the elements are proved beyond reasonable doubt (mmnpp.gross_violence_definition). It does not apply if the offender was under 18 at the time of the offence, or the court finds special reasons; and for a single punch or strike it does not apply to a person who intentionally directed, assisted or encouraged the offence, or who intentionally directed, assisted or encouraged another offence knowing it was probable the charged offence would occur. The Court of Appeal has observed that a minimum fixed only for the non-parole period skews the sentencing discretion and may lead to an unacceptably short period of supervision on parole.

title: Manslaughter: gross-violence and single-punch elements (9.1.2.1)
statement: For the manslaughter minimum, gross violence requires proof beyond reasonable doubt that the offender (1) caused the victim’s death in company with two or more people, or entered into an agreement, arrangement or understanding with two or more people to engage in the conduct that caused the death; and (2) planned in advance to have and use an offensive weapon or firearm and did use it to cause the victim’s death, or planned in advance to engage in the conduct that caused the death when at the time of planning a reasonable person would have foreseen it would be likely to result in death, or caused two or more serious injuries to the victim during a sustained or prolonged attack. A single punch or strike requires proof beyond reasonable doubt that the death was caused by a punch or strike taken to be a dangerous act, that the offender intended it to be delivered to the head or neck, that the victim was not expecting it, and that the offender knew the victim was not expecting (or was probably not expecting) it; the unexpected punch or strike must be the one that caused death and was intended (the victim need not expect any punch at all). These elements are given for manslaughter only: for causing serious injury in circumstances of gross violence (9.1.2.2) gross violence is part of the offence charged.

title: Offences against emergency workers, custodial officers and youth justice custodial workers on duty
statement: Protected officials are emergency workers, custodial officers and youth justice custodial workers on duty (including persons employed or engaged by a State, Territory or the Commonwealth to perform similar functions while on duty in Victoria). Minimum non-parole periods: intentionally or recklessly causing serious injury in circumstances of gross violence 5 years; intentionally causing serious injury 3 years; recklessly causing serious injury 2 years; intentionally or recklessly causing injury 6 months. The minimum applies only if it is proved beyond reasonable doubt that a victim was such a worker on duty and that the offender knew or was reckless as to that. It does not apply if: the accused was found guilty on the basis of intentionally directing, assisting or encouraging (on either limb) and proves on the balance of probabilities that their involvement was minor; the offender was under 18 at the time of the offence; or the court finds special reasons. Instead of imprisonment with the minimum, a youth justice centre order of at least the minimum may be made if the offender is under 21 at sentence, the court does not find special reasons, and on a pre-sentence report it believes the offender has reasonable prospects for rehabilitation or is particularly impressionable, immature or likely to be subjected to undesirable influences in an adult prison (not for gross violence charges). If special reasons are found on a charge of intentionally or recklessly causing serious injury or injury (ss 16–18; for ss 15A/15B against a protected official: flag.gross_violence_protected_special_reason), the court must impose imprisonment (without a CCO) or make a mandatory treatment and monitoring order, Residential Treatment Order or Court Secure Treatment Order (whether imprisonment combined with a mandatory treatment and monitoring order is open is unresolved: flag.mtmo_combination_sentence); a therapeutic order only if the offender proves on the balance of probabilities impaired mental functioning at the offence, causally linked to it and substantially and materially reducing culpability, not caused substantially by self-induced intoxication, and the court has received and had regard to a psychiatrist’s or registered psychologist’s report and is satisfied the order is appropriate. The Manual gives no commencement date for these minimums.

title: Aggravated home invasion / aggravated carjacking: 3-year minimum non-parole period
statement: A court must impose imprisonment with a non-parole period of at least three years for aggravated home invasion or aggravated carjacking unless the offender was under 18 at the time of the offence or the court finds special reasons. title: 'Special reason' to depart from a mandatory minimum
statement: Victorian mandatory minimum provisions provide an exception where the court finds a special reason: it may then decline to impose imprisonment (Category 1 offence) or impose a non-parole period below the minimum. A special reason may exist in four circumstances: (1) the offender assisted or undertook to assist authorities in the prosecution or investigation of an offence; (2) the offender proves on the balance of probabilities a mental impairment at the time of offending, causally related to it, that substantially and materially reduces culpability (not where caused substantially by self-induced intoxication), or that would cause substantially greater than ordinary burdens or risks of imprisonment; (3) the court intends to impose a Court Secure Treatment Order or Residential Treatment Order; (4) substantial and compelling reasons, exceptional and rare, justify not imposing imprisonment — for which the court must regard general deterrence and denunciation as primary, give less weight to personal circumstances than to the nature and gravity of the offending, not consider prior good character (other than a lack of previous convictions or findings of guilt), early plea, rehabilitation prospects or parity, and have regard to Parliament’s intention that a custodial term should ordinarily be imposed. The offender carries the burden, which is heavy and not lightly discharged. The reason must be stated in writing and recorded. For the protected-official injury offences (ss 16–18) and the protected-worker driving offences, a special reason confines the disposition to imprisonment (no CCO) or a therapeutic order (s 5(2GA): cat1.custodial_required; whether imprisonment combined with a mandatory treatment and monitoring order is open is unresolved: flag.mtmo_combination_sentence); for ss 15A/15B against a protected official the disposition other than imprisonment without a CCO is unresolved (flag.gross_violence_protected_special_reason).

title: Standard sentence scheme: when it applies
statement: An offence is a standard sentence offence if the Act creating it or prescribing its maximum specifies a period as the standard sentence. The scheme became effective on 1 February 2018 and applies only to offences committed after that date; it does not apply to offenders under 18 at the time of offending, or to offences heard and determined summarily. Conspiring, inciting or attempting to commit a standard sentence offence is not itself a standard sentence offence. The Manual does not settle an offence committed on 1 February 2018 itself, or charged over a period spanning that date.

Conspiring, inciting or attempting to commit a standard sentence offence is not itself a standard sentence offence. The Manual does not settle an offence committed on 1 February 2018 itself, or charged over a period spanning that date.

title: Standard sentence: a guidepost, not a starting point
statement: The standard sentence is the sentence for an offence in the middle of the range of seriousness, taking into account only the objective factors (the nature of the offence, not the offender’s personal circumstances; the scheme does not exclude mitigating factors from sentencing). The key requirement is that the court take it into account as a relevant sentencing factor: a legislative guidepost like the maximum, which must not be given too much weight; it does not permit two-stage sentencing, and the court does not start from it and work up or down. Seriousness is assessed as it always has been, as part of the instinctive synthesis. The notional mid-range can be very difficult to identify for offences covering a wide range of conduct (e.g. sexual penetration of a child under 12). Only sentences imposed under the scheme may be used as current sentencing practices (principles from earlier cases remain usable); a sentence that exceeds pre-scheme practice is not for that reason manifestly excessive.

title: Standard sentence offences: state how the sentence relates to the standard sentence
statement: The court must give reasons for the sentence, for any non-parole period shorter than s 11A(4), and state how the sentence relates to the standard sentence by identifying the facts, matters and circumstances bearing on its judgment; it must not classify the offence against a hypothetical mid-range instance. The manual gives an adequate and an inadequate model statement.

title: Serious offenders (arson, drug, sexual, violent)
statement: When the Supreme or County Court imprisons a 'serious offender' for a 'relevant offence': (1) protection of the community is the principal purpose (the other purposes are not excluded; its weight depends on the assessed risk of re-offending, which the court must assess), and a sentence longer than proportionate may be imposed — rarely, and with reasons for assessing a continuing risk; such a sentence generally widens the gap between head sentence and non-parole period; (2) terms for relevant offending are served cumulatively on any uncompleted sentence unless the court directs otherwise (a prima facie rule: good reason, but not exceptional circumstances, is needed for concurrency; totality still applies); (3) the status is recorded. Serious offenders: serious arson offender (a serious arson offence); serious drug offender (a drug offence); serious sexual offender (two or more sexual offences; persistent sexual abuse of a child under 16; the incidents of a sexual offence in a course of conduct charge; or at least one sexual and one violent offence from the same course of conduct); serious violent offender (a serious violent offence). Relevant offences: arson / drug / sexual or violent / serious violent offence respectively. Each qualifying conviction (in the current hearing or earlier) must have resulted in imprisonment or youth justice centre detention, and must be proved beyond reasonable doubt; Commonwealth, interstate or overseas convictions count if substantially similar and resulting in imprisonment or detention. The status is acquired only after sentence for a qualifying offence, and no serious offender may be a young offender (under 21 when committing the relevant offence). The provisions apply only to relevant offences (not other charges on the indictment) and not to Commonwealth offences. There is no particular relationship with the indefinite sentence scheme. The offence chapters list the qualifying offences: for drug offences, the State offences listed in 28.7 (trafficking or cultivating a large commercial or commercial quantity, and conspiracy, incitement, aiding or abetting, or a preparatory act for them); certain Commonwealth import/export and possession convictions can qualify an offender found guilty of a Victorian Schedule 1 drug offence (28.7: guide.drugs.statutory_schemes); for arson, the listed arson offences (27.5.1: guide.property.statutory_schemes).

title: Continuing criminal enterprise offenders
statement: A CCE offender sentenced for a CCE offence (listed in Schedule 1A: three classes of offences relating to property, financial advantages, goods, gains or losses valued at $50,000 or more) may be liable to imprisonment of twice the maximum term or 25 years, whichever is less. A rolled-up charge qualifies only if at least one constituent transaction exceeds $50,000 (not where the value exceeds $50,000 only by virtue of the rolled-up value); 2.4.5 and 27.5.1 say “$50,000 or more” (flag.cce_value_threshold). CCE offender: a CCE offence plus two or more relevant offences in another trial or hearing; two CCE offences plus one; or three or more CCE offences (a relevant offence is a CCE offence found guilty of within 10 years before the latest offence, including offences before the definition commenced). Because the scheme depends on findings of guilt, it applies immediately to the qualifying offences. The raised maximum remains only one consideration; it does not compel a given sentence or require an automatic increase. Uniform penalties for CCE offences and different uniform penalties for non-CCE offences, without explanation, are likely to show error. The status must be recorded. The scheme is wholly separate from the serious offender scheme: it only adjusts the maximum.

title: Head sentence and non-parole period are one sentence; the total effective sentence is not a “sentence” for appeal
statement: The term “head sentence” has no statutory basis; it distinguishes the total custodial term from other parts such as the non-parole period, but the two are not distinct punishments — they are one sentence. Because the total effective sentence results from the individual sentences and orders for cumulation and concurrency, it is not a “sentence” for appeal under s 287 of the Criminal Procedure Act.

title: Why a non-parole period is fixed, and what it does
statement: A minimum term is fixed because mitigating considerations or rehabilitation may make it undesirable for the offender to serve the entire term in prison. It fixes a time after which the Parole Board or other authorised entities may decide if and when the offender is released.

title: Failure to fix a non-parole period: correction on application vs appeal
statement: Failure to fix a non-parole period does not invalidate the sentence, and a reviewing court may correct such a failure on application — but only for sentencing irregularities. A deliberate decision not to fix one is within the court’s discretion and is not a basis for a reviewing court to fix one; the remedy is an application for leave to appeal.

title: Total effective sentence, the base sentence, and cumulation across several indictments
statement: When imprisoning for more than one offence the court must generally fix a total effective sentence, usually by individual sentences and orders for cumulation or concurrency. A Victorian judge must select a base sentence, usually the longest individual sentence: using a shorter one risks distorting the process (e.g. undeserved primacy to a lesser offence). With several indictments in one proceeding, the court may cumulate directly towards the total, or cumulate to notional totals for each indictment and then between them; both are correct, the second being more appropriate where each indictment addresses discrete offending.

title: Renzella discretion: the Act is not exclusive; immigration detention; “dead time”; overlap with totality
statement: Section 18 is not the exclusive measure of how pre-sentence detention may be considered. The weight of immigration detention depends on the burden it imposed. “Dead time” is not defined; the Court of Appeal describes it as custody that, with hindsight, should not have been served. In some cases there is no practical difference between the Renzella discretion and totality, both being concerned with fairness and a just sentence.

title: Indefinite sentence review: applications, reports, disputes, presence and appeal standard
statement: On an offender’s review application the court must give the DPP a copy, make directions within 10 working days and hear it within 25 working days. A different judge may review, and may order reports about the period since sentence or last review; reports go to the parties, who may file their own and must exchange them. A disputed report (or part) cannot be considered until the parties may lead evidence and cross-examine its author. On review the parties may lead admissible evidence and make submissions. The offender must be present unless their conduct makes it impracticable (or absence will not prejudice them and is in the interests of justice). On appeal the Court of Appeal may confirm, or set aside and make the proper order; it is an appeal in the strict sense requiring House v The King error.

title: Federal offences: a different regime (the app is limited to Victorian offences)

Federal offences: a different regime (the app is limited to Victorian offences)
If any charge is a Commonwealth offence, Victorian rules do not simply apply: cumulation is effected by commencement dates and State sentences cannot be cumulated on Commonwealth ones; certain federal offences carry a minimum non-parole period of three-quarters of the head sentence; Boulton does not apply, and s 44 does not apply to federal offenders (so no combination sentence for a single federal offence); mixed indictments need separate, consistent sentences. The app must flag federal charges as outside its scope rather than estimate them. A Victorian sentence for an offender already serving a Commonwealth sentence is within scope: cum.commonwealth_sentence_commencement.

title: Offender already serving a Commonwealth sentence: direct when the Victorian term commences (s 16(4))
statement: If an offender is already serving a sentence for a Commonwealth offence, the court must direct when the new term commences: no later than immediately after completion of the Commonwealth sentence if no non-parole or pre-release period was fixed, or immediately after the end of any non-parole or pre-release period fixed as part of the Commonwealth sentence. A State sentence cannot be cumulated on a Commonwealth sentence by a cumulation order.

title: Youth justice centre order (YJC) / youth residential centre order (YRC)
statement: If a custodial sentence is appropriate for a young offender on conviction (or appeal) in a higher court, the court may make a YJC or YRC order instead of imprisonment; these are not sentences of imprisonment. (The Manual also gives a Magistrates’ Court maximum for these orders: see yjc.maximum.) Purposes: punish while promoting rehabilitation and separating the young offender from experienced adult offenders.

title: Community Correction Order (CCO)
statement: A CCO is available if the offence is punishable by more than five penalty units, the court has a pre-sentence report (unless the only condition is unpaid community work of 300 hours or less — 11.4.2.1 says “less than 300 hours”: flag.cco_work_only_300_hours), and the offender consents. A Victorian CCO may be made with or without recording a conviction. It is a significant punishment that can serve all sentencing purposes; proportionality and suitability govern it.

title: Mandatory treatment and monitoring order (a type of CCO)
statement: If, sentencing for offending against protected workers, the court finds special reasons and that a mandatory treatment and monitoring order is appropriate, it must make a CCO with a judicial monitoring condition and either a treatment and rehabilitation condition or a justice plan condition. This does not limit the other conditions the court may attach or its power to impose a combination sentence (11.9); but 9.1.2.3 (ss 16–18) and 9.1.2.4 (ss 317AC, 317AD) say that, on a special reason for a protected-official charge, the court must “either” imprison without a CCO “or” make an MTMO, RTO or CSTO, so whether the two may be combined there is unresolved (flag.mtmo_combination_sentence → caution). The mandatory conditions may not be cancelled or varied unless the varied conditions are at least as onerous.

title: Fine
statement: A fine may be imposed with or without conviction, in addition to or instead of another sentence; not for Level 1 offences; for Level 2 offences only in addition to imprisonment (unless otherwise stated or a body corporate); not if a dismissal, discharge or adjournment would achieve the purposes. Main purposes: punishment and deterrence. A fine includes costs but not restitution or compensation, costs of such applications, costs between parties in a civil proceeding, third-party costs, or payments to a charitable or community organisation. The Manual’s own penalty tables print “Level 1 – life and fine not exceeding 5000 penalty units” for some DPCSA offences, which the 12.1 bar does not reconcile (flag.level1_fine_dpcsa); and it does not say whether the Level 1/2 rules apply to life or 25-year maxima printed without a level (flag.fine_unlabelled_life_25_maximum).

title: Dismissal without conviction
statement: Solely a non-conviction order. The discretion arises only when the charge is proved and the plea was a proper one. The Manual then says the offence 'must' be able to be characterised as 'trifling', the circumstances clearly indicating it would be manifestly unfair and unreasonable to penalise and stigmatise the offender (e.g. trivial offending, or a conviction that might disqualify the offender from their profession), but also that dismissals "may also be granted" where strong steps towards rehabilitation, or previous good character and post-offence conduct, would make a conviction disproportionate. Whether these are alternative grounds or the trifling requirement always applies is not resolved (flag.dismissal_trifling_requirement). No conditions may be attached, but compensation or restitution may be ordered separately. A dismissed charge cannot be revived. A dismissal is not a conviction for any purpose except as the Act provides: it has the same effect as a recorded conviction for appeals against sentence, variation or breach proceedings, proceedings for a subsequent offence, and subsequent proceedings for the same offence (so a prior dismissal can count in later sentencing: intake.criminal_history).

title: Discharge on conviction
statement: Conviction recorded and the offender discharged without conditions (a finding of guilt and a recorded conviction are required first). Sometimes appropriate for low culpability, minor conduct subsumed in a more serious offence, or compelling personal circumstances (e.g. finances precluding a fine, or to let rehabilitation and treatment continue); a serious offence may call for more to denounce the conduct despite mitigation. No conditions may be attached, but compensation or restitution may be ordered separately.

title: Release on adjournment (adjourned undertaking), with or without conviction
statement: The court may adjourn and release the offender on an undertaking with conditions, with or without conviction, for up to five years. It is only available if the offender first agrees to give the undertaking (agreement given because imprisonment is a realistic alternative is still valid). Mandatory conditions: attend court if called on (and at any adjourned hearing), be of good behaviour, observe any special conditions; a justice plan condition may be attached (lasting for the adjournment or two years, whichever is shorter; the CCO condition is worded differently: flag.justice_plan_request). The court must be satisfied of guilt and have regard to the nature of the offence, the offender’s character and past history, and the impact of a conviction on economic or social wellbeing or employment, balanced with general deterrence; it should expressly say whether a conviction is recorded. An adjourned undertaking is a “sentence”. Usually made for minor offences, but not if that would breach the fundamental principles or purposes; it may be imposed for serious offences in exceptional circumstances (e.g. marginally excessive self-defence in a family violence context, serious psychiatric illness, the wellbeing of children or a partner as carer, unusual child pornography possession, assistance to authorities), and other mitigation may also lead to one (e.g. significant delay, intellectual disability or mental health issues, youth or advanced age, an unwilling accomplice, immigration detention). On compliance the offender is discharged (if convicted) or the charge dismissed (if not).

title: Residential Treatment Order (RTO)
statement: Detention for up to five years in a residential treatment facility, designed for people with an intellectual disability who have committed serious sexual or other violent offences. Eligible offences: sexual assault, sexual assault by compelling sexual touching, or a “serious offence”, which includes (the Manual does not say the list is complete: flag.rto_serious_offence_list) (murder, manslaughter, child homicide; causing serious injury offences; threats to kill; rape, rape by compelling sexual penetration, assault with intent to commit a sexual offence; familial sexual penetration offences; sexual abuse or penetration of a child under 16; kidnapping and abduction for sexual purposes; armed robbery; repealed equivalents; conspiracy, incitement or attempt). Only if the DHS Secretary specifies that the offender is suitable for admission and the planned services are available. Not if a less restrictive sanction is more suitable; an intention to impose one may constitute special reasons for not imposing a mandatory term. Eligible offences cannot be a gateway for ineligible ones, which need separate sanctions that do not interfere with the RTO; separate RTOs cannot be cumulated (additional orders are redundant). Length: a sentence, so no more severe than necessary; it may exceed the minimum period recommended in a pre-sentence report and need not track the imprisonment otherwise appropriate, so long as it is proportionate. Pre-sentence detention cannot be declared for the RTO offence if already declared for other offences dealt with at the time. If the order is cancelled and the offender re-sentenced, a new s 6AAA declaration must be made if relevant.

title: Court secure treatment order (and court assessment order)
statement: Orders for mentally ill offenders, only if no less restrictive means are reasonably available. A court secure treatment order (CSTO) requires: (1) that but for the mental illness the court would have imposed imprisonment; (2) consideration of the person’s current mental condition, physical and mental health, forensic history and social circumstances; (3) a psychiatrist’s examination and report (with any other evidence) satisfying the court that the person has a mental illness (actual, not merely apparent as for a court assessment order), needs treatment to prevent serious deterioration or serious harm, will receive it, and has no less restrictive means reasonably available; (4) a report from the authorised psychiatrist of the service recommending the order and stating facilities are available. The illness need not have caused the offending. All relevant sentencing considerations apply. Duration must not exceed the imprisonment that would otherwise have been ordered (so that notional term must be considered); a life-duration order is possible for offences punishable by life. A non-parole period must be fixed “as if it were a term of imprisonment” (the Manual does not say how this works with the ch 8 rules — no non-parole period under 12 months (8.3.1), a discretion between one and two years and, for two years or more, an exception where an npp is inappropriate (8.3: npp.must_fix_two_years): flag.csto_npp_short_terms). On discharge, the unexpired period takes effect as imprisonment served in prison unless paroled, so the offender may serve some or virtually all of it in prison.

title: Drug and Alcohol Treatment Order (DATO) — Drug Court only
statement: Made only by the Drug Court Division of the Magistrates' or County Court. Eligibility: plea of guilty to at least one imprisonable offence within the Drug Court’s jurisdiction; conviction; dependency on drugs or alcohol that contributed to the offence (balance of probabilities); otherwise an unsuspended prison term would be appropriate (no more than 2 years in the Magistrates’ Court, 4 years in the County Court); assessment report ordered and received; appropriateness; written agreement to the order and to comply with the treatment and supervision part. Excluded: schedule 1 sexual offences (24.5 says a Drug Court order is not available for “a sexual offence”, citing the same provision, s 18Z(1)(a)(i), and the Manual does not list schedule 1: a DATO is excluded (error) where the user states the offence is a schedule 1 sexual offence; otherwise the exclusion is unresolved, a caution — for the 24.1.1, 24.1.2 and 24.1.4 offences the app does not propose a DATO unless the user states the offence is not a schedule 1 sexual offence (app policy, following 24.5’s words), and for the child abuse material and sexual servitude offences the user is asked: flag.dato_sexual_offence_scope), offences involving the infliction of actual bodily harm (but the Magistrates’ Drug Court may make a DATO where satisfied the harm was of a minor nature: fn 2834), offences under ss 10–10AE; an offender on parole or subject to a higher court sentence. Prior imprisonment, prior dependency-driven offending or prior non-compliance with bail or sentence does not bar a DATO. One DATO may cover multiple offences, but an offender can be subject to only one DATO at a time. The custodial part is a term of imprisonment equal to the sentence that would otherwise be imposed (no non-parole period; automatically suspended; maximum 2 years Magistrates’ Court, 4 years County Court); it must not be lengthened merely to allow treatment, nor artificially decreased to fit under the maximum. It will generally be prudent to declare eligible pre-sentence custody when the DATO is imposed. Purposes include recovery through judicially supervised therapeutic rehabilitation, community protection from substance-driven offending and reducing health risks; rehabilitation and community protection have greater importance than the other purposes.

title: Driver licence cancellation and disqualification
statement: Licence cancellation/disqualification is part of a punitive sentence. Mandatory for serious motor vehicle offences (listed), with minimums: dangerous driving causing death or serious injury 18 months; substance-influenced offences (other than aggravated carjacking) 12 months; other serious motor vehicle offences two years; dangerous or negligent driving while pursued by police 12 months; stealing a motor vehicle — default three months if unspecified (these last two follow conviction). No maximum. Serious motor vehicle offences attract the mandatory order on a finding of guilt or conviction (16.1; 2.4.3 says “found guilty and convicted”: flag.licence_guilty_or_convicted). The form of the order depends on the licence held (licence.form_by_licence_status). Discretionary disqualification is available for other offences (default three months) and under the RSA. A finding of drug/alcohol contribution must be made for culpable driving by being under the influence (taken to be made if not expressly made). The period is fixed like a sentence (licence.period_principles).

title: Children: offences that must be uplifted; the Children’s Court must otherwise hear indictable charges summarily
statement: Charges against a child of murder, attempted murder, manslaughter, child homicide, arson causing death or culpable driving causing death are outside the Children’s Court’s jurisdiction and must be uplifted to the higher courts (Category A serious youth offences have their own presumptive uplift: order.youth.scope_and_jurisdiction). For other offences the Court of Appeal has said the CYFA policy is that the Children’s Court has jurisdiction to hear and determine summarily all indictable charges against children (other than the few excluded “death-related” offences) and must do so unless the child objects or there are “exceptional circumstances” justifying uplift. (Children’s Court sentencing is outside the app’s scope; this explains why a child is before a higher court.)

title: Youth detention: report first; age bands; detention with imprisonment; suspension while at large; aggregate; custody declared
statement: A court considering a YJC or YRC order must first order a pre-sentence report. A YJC order cannot be made for an offender under 15 at sentence, and a YRC order cannot be made for one who is 15 or over. Youth detention may be served concurrently or cumulatively on imprisonment, but if a higher court imposes imprisonment exceeding the maximum possible YJC term it can be impracticable also to impose a YJC on any other charge. Time after a young offender is allowed to go free (for any reason) until their return to custody, and after an escape or failure to return until apprehension or surrender, does not count and the sentence is suspended. An aggregate detention order need not identify the separate events, the sentences that would have been imposed on each charge, or whether they would have been concurrent or cumulative. Custody referable to the proceedings must be declared as time served unless the court orders otherwise.

title: Children sentenced in the higher courts: CYFA considerations and policy objectives; no CCO with a YJC order
statement: In sentencing a child the court must, as far as practicable, consider the listed CYFA matters (youth.higher_courts_principles; including, if appropriate, the need to ensure the child is aware they must bear responsibility for any illegal action), and the sentence must, as far as practicable, achieve the policy objectives: strengthen and preserve the child’s relationship with their family; allow them to live at home; allow their education, training or employment to continue; minimise stigma. The normal sentencing considerations may be subordinate when the court first assesses whether a CYFA disposition is adequate, because the CYFA requires very different factors from the Sentencing Act. A CCO cannot be combined with a YJC order: although it would help rehabilitation, a legislative gap prevents that sentence (flag.yjc_combination_wording).

title: CCO: what the report may address; how a judge’s reservations are expressed; consent does not bar a later complaint
statement: Per Boulton, the pre-sentence report may include information, based on empirical research or experience, on the time needed to overcome or manage substance abuse. A judge may share reservations about the offender’s ability to comply, but care must be taken in how they are expressed: it is improper to state in absolute terms that the judge knows the offender will breach the CCO and that the breach will result in imprisonment. Informed consent to a CCO does not preclude a later complaint that the sentence was erroneous or excessive.

title: CCO length: rehabilitation material; best assessment of therapeutic time; matching lengths are not error
statement: In fixing a CCO’s period the court considers material directed to the offender’s rehabilitation (including expert reports, which should form part of the pre-sentence report) and makes its best assessment of how long the offender should “submit to therapeutic intervention” — but rehabilitation is not thereby the primary consideration in fixing the length. A term of imprisonment and a CCO of the same length do not by themselves show error. It is fruitless to compare a combination sentence’s duration with a possible head sentence (including a non-parole period) to show it is too long; such a comparison is not required by the instinctive synthesis.

title: Unpaid community work: presumption of concurrency; treatment hours counted as work
statement: Unless otherwise ordered, unpaid work hours under a fines order are concurrent with hours under a CCO (whether the CCO was made before or at the same time), and multiple orders to perform unpaid work are generally performed concurrently with hours under a new or existing CCO (the presumption also applies between standard CCOs). Where a CCO has both an unpaid community work condition and a treatment and rehabilitation condition, the court may determine that some or all treatment and rehabilitation hours count as unpaid work; if it so determines without specifying the number, all such hours satisfactorily undertaken count.

title: CCO conditions: justice plan; no restitution/compensation conditions; submissions; supervision; residence; curfew; bond; monitoring
statement: A justice plan condition requires compliance with a plan of services under Part 2 of the Disability Act 2006, and a copy of the CCO must then be supplied to the DHS Secretary. title: CCO variation and contravention: compliance assessed; notice; warrants; the same powers as on variation

title: Boulton in detail: suitability, parsimony, punishment, deterrence, rehabilitation, protection; the discretion; combinations
statement: Boulton appears to accept that suitability derives from the Act (the offender’s circumstances and capacity to comply, subject to proportionality); an offender is not unsuited merely because a disadvantage or disability makes compliance difficult. The Manual says it also appears the Court might be of the view that some incarceration is required for intentionally causing serious injury, reckless conduct causing injury (such as driving while intoxicated), or a series of linked domestic-violence incidents over some hours. The first question is whether any feature requires the conclusion that imprisonment is the only option — i.e. whether confinement is necessary and, if so, the minimum term. Although a CCO’s punitive effect never equals imprisonment, it is a “significant punishment”, not a “mere slap on the wrist”: its conditions are coercive and restrictive, an intensive compliance period increases the burden, and every CCO is punitive every day it is in force; after a term of imprisonment the punitive purpose should be progressive and supervision should reduce over time. In Dyason the argument that Boulton required reconsideration of the primacy of deterrence for white-collar offending was rejected. Most youthful offenders disengage from crime quickly, so a CCO should avoid alienating them; the circumstances always control. Community protection is not legislatively primary for a CCO but remains the ultimate purpose. Boulton does not fetter the discretion, is no “Get Out of Jail Free” card, and does not require a CCO that would not reflect the objective seriousness and the offender’s circumstances; current sentencing practice informs the first question. Reasonable minds differ on the longest term before a combination is more severe than necessary; a short term of imprisonment may be needed for purposes a CCO cannot serve. A CCO and a non-parole period should ordinarily be alternatives. The discretion to “otherwise order” on time served is not unfettered; the custodial period is fixed after deducting time served (even if concurrent with another offence).

title: Fines: capacity to pay; deterrence; no concurrency (totality must be applied); third-party payment
statement: A fine must be an appropriate punishment given the offender’s capacity to pay; the amount and method of payment take account of the offender’s financial resources and the burden; it must be sufficient to punish and to deter others; a fine totally beyond the offender’s means that will never be paid has no general deterrent effect. Fines cannot be ordered concurrent and must operate cumulatively, so totality must be applied to avoid a disproportionate total; the concerns about moderating individual sentences arose where concurrency is possible. A fine calculated on the assumption that the offender’s employer would probably pay it may involve an irregularity, but each case turns on its facts.

title: RTOs: eligible charges are not a gateway for other charges; leave; variation and cancellation
statement: Where only some charges are RTO-eligible, the eligible offences cannot be used as a gateway to impose an RTO on all offences on the indictment. A copy of an RTO goes to the DHS Secretary. Leave may be granted only if the court is satisfied on reasonable grounds that the safety of the offender or the public will not be seriously endangered (up to 12 months each, more than once, on conditions). On application, the court that made an RTO may confirm, vary or cancel it if satisfied that the offender is not complying, the offender’s needs are not being met, or the order is no longer appropriate (a more restrictive environment such as prison may be more effective; staff and residents must be protected); on cancellation the court considers compliance, including whether non-compliance was wilful or due to complex needs.

title: Court assessment orders and CSTOs: form and notification; CSTO criteria; effect as imprisonment
statement: A court assessment order states whether it is a community or an inpatient order; the authorised psychiatrist is notified and given a copy, and an inpatient is taken to a designated mental health service as soon as practicable. A CSTO may be made for a person found guilty or pleading guilty, subject to mandatory considerations; it requires that the person “has a mental illness”, unlike a hospital security order (“appears to be mentally ill”). A person on a CSTO may serve some, or virtually all, of the period in prison.

title: DATOs in detail: transfer; the custodial part and activation limits; sanctions; graduation; cancellation; reports; subsequent charges
statement: Before transfer the Magistrates’ Court must be satisfied the accused may be eligible, without assessing sentence. The court must impose a term of imprisonment as the custodial part, which is not served unless activated; activation is not a fresh sentence (no occasion for a s 18 declaration). The maximum activatable custody excludes declared pre-sentence detention and sanction time, (with a worked example) and in some cases is reduced by the excess days of operation of the treatment part; a shorter activation involves listed factors, and compliance is assessed by effort. Conditions run for the treatment and supervision part unless cancelled; core conditions include attending the Drug Court. A sanction may activate the custodial part for 1–7 days (if satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of non-compliance; after notice; in a specified kind of facility), served only if the period or total of unserved activated periods is at least seven days. Graduation cannot be granted once the program conditions have ceased. Cancellation under s 18ZP requires a listed ground on the balance of probabilities (cancellation for reoffending under s 18ZN requires satisfaction beyond reasonable doubt: order.dato.activation_and_cancellation); compliance is not measured by duration; unwillingness and non-compliance are not to be conflated; the remaining custodial part is calculated first and compliance taken into account; notice is required, and the parties must have an adequate opportunity to call evidence and make submissions on both the decision to cancel and its consequence (not necessarily in separate stages, though a two-step process is preferable). Assessment reports are filed and served, and disputed parts are tested before use. If no DATO is imposed the court must take one of the listed courses. On a new offence, an immediate term may be subsumed within the remaining custodial part, failing which the treatment part is cancelled; a Magistrates’ Court has no jurisdiction over a summary or triable-summarily charge against a County Court participant and must transfer it to the County Court Drug Court for sentencing (for a not-guilty plea see flag.dato_county_court_subsequent_charge).

title: Children and young offenders: the Manual’s scope, and which court sentences
statement: Sentencing children operates within a largely separate system (Children’s Court Bench Book); the Manual covers children and “young offenders” sentenced in the higher courts and youth detention as an alternative. Murder, attempted murder, manslaughter, child homicide, arson causing death and culpable driving causing death by a child must be heard in the Supreme or County Court. Category A serious youth offences must be uplifted unless a party requests summary hearing, the Children’s Court’s options are adequate, and a listed reason applies. Otherwise the Children’s Court hears indictable charges against children summarily unless the child objects or exceptional circumstances justify uplift. The app should flag that sentencing of a child in the Children’s Court is outside the Manual’s coverage.

statement: Except for a CCO limited to 300 hours or less of community work (11.4.2.1 says “less than 300 hours”: flag.cco_work_only_300_hours), a pre-sentence report must establish suitability, available facilities and appropriate conditions; it should cover treatment and programs and how long support and monitoring are likely to be needed. title: CCO mandatory conditions
statement: Every CCO requires the offender not to commit an imprisonable offence during the order; comply with the regulations; report to and receive visits from the Secretary; report to the specified community corrections centre within two clear working days; notify changes of address or employment within two clear working days; not leave Victoria without permission; and comply with the Secretary’s directions.

title: CCO treatment and rehabilitation condition
statement: The court must specify one or more types (drug/alcohol assessment and treatment including testing, residential withdrawal or rehabilitation, medical, mental health, offending-behaviour programs, other programs including employment, educational, cultural and personal development). It must address the underlying causes of offending and the pre-sentence report’s recommendations. Completion of programs may reduce unpaid work hours. Compliance is generally assumed, though a CCO may be inappropriate if there is no realistic prospect of compliance.

title: CCO supervision and non-association conditions

In imposing either, the court must have regard to the recommendations, information and matters in the pre-sentence report (for non-association, in relation to treatment and rehabilitation); for non-association it may also consider employment effects.

title: CCO residence restriction/exclusion, place/area exclusion and curfew: consistency with intervention orders
statement: A residence restriction or exclusion condition must not be imposed if inconsistent with a family violence intervention order, personal safety intervention order or child protection order; a place or area exclusion condition, and a curfew condition, must not be imposed if inconsistent with a family violence or personal safety intervention order. Safety of co-residents and employment effects may be considered. With a residence condition the offender may not move unless the court first varies the CCO. Whether a condition is inconsistent with an order is a judgement on the orders’ terms, so the auditor applies it (caution where the intake records an existing FVIO, PSIO or child protection order affecting the offender and the conditions may conflict).

title: CCO alcohol exclusion condition: content, purpose, and when it may moderate sentence
statement: Excludes the offender from nightclubs, bars, restaurants, cafés, reception or function centres, major events and bar areas, and from drinking in other licensed premises (exemptions and hours may be specified). Primary purpose is community protection; it may aid rehabilitation and can be punitive. An offender contending it has additional punitive impact must say so expressly, with evidence, and address the s 89DE(5) exemption; the court should then make a finding on its punitive extent and explain its effect on sentence. title: CCO bond condition
statement: A bond secures compliance and may be forfeited on non-compliance; the court must consider whether the offender’s financial circumstances (per the pre-sentence report) support it and fix a time to pay. Repayment rules apply on cancellation, variation or expiry: within seven days (unless a longer period is ordered) if the CCO or bond is cancelled, varied or otherwise dealt with; otherwise, where the money is not liable to be forfeited, on the later of the listed events (one of which is three months after the CCO expires) — post-sentence administration, not a sentencing limit.

title: CCO judicial monitoring condition
statement: If the court is satisfied it is necessary to review compliance, it may direct court monitoring with review hearings (information, reports or tests may be required; no medical testing without consent); it may then cancel, vary or keep the condition; failure to re-appear may lead to an arrest warrant.

title: CCO justice plan condition (offenders with an intellectual disability)
statement: For an intellectually disabled offender the court may attach a justice plan condition directing participation in a plan of services. Before imposing it the court must consider a pre-sentence report, a statement from the DHS Secretary that the person has an intellectual disability, and a plan of available services; the Manual says both that the court “must request” the plan and that it “may request, and must consider” these materials (flag.justice_plan_request). The condition lasts for a specified period of less than two years or the period of the sentence, whichever is shorter. The court may direct a review at a specified time; if it does not, the Secretary must review the plan within a year and then at intervals of no more than a year. On application the court may confirm, vary or cancel the condition if the offender is no longer willing to comply, their needs are not being met, they have failed without reasonable excuse to comply, or the condition is no longer appropriate; on cancellation it may cancel the sentence and re-sentence, considering prior compliance.

title: CCO variation
statement: On application, the court may act if circumstances have materially altered so the offender cannot comply; circumstances were wrongly stated; consent is withdrawn; rehabilitation would be advanced; or continuation is unnecessary. It may confirm, cancel and re-sentence as if just found guilty, cancel with no further order, vary, alter conditions or programs. It must first assess the extent of compliance.

CCO variation
On application, the court may act if circumstances have materially altered so the offender cannot comply; circumstances were wrongly stated; consent is withdrawn; rehabilitation would be advanced; or continuation is unnecessary. It may confirm, cancel and re-sentence as if just found guilty, cancel with no further order, vary, alter conditions or programs. It must first assess the extent of compliance.

title: Sentencing on contravention of a CCO
statement: Contravention is a State offence; the court has the variation powers. Bond forfeiture may be ordered on variation or confirmation and must be ordered on cancellation. Account must be taken of compliance; non-compliance diminishes rehabilitation prospects and is relevant to specific deterrence. On cancellation the better course is to set aside the whole sentence and sentence afresh, declaring pre-sentence detention including time served; a custodial term longer than the original combination sentence would be a “very unusual case”. The Manual describes the breach offence only as one that “may attract a three-month term of imprisonment” (11.7.3); the offence register has no CCO-contravention row, so for a contravention charge the app asks the user to confirm the maximum.

title: CCO and the purposes: all purposes achievable; community protection
statement: A CCO may achieve all the s 5(1) purposes (Boulton). It provides both specific and general deterrence; its effect as a general deterrent depends on how far it is perceived as punitive and communicated. As a specific deterrent, breach of the mandatory no-reoffending condition attracts three separate penalties (for the offence, for the breach, and resentencing for the original offending). Community-protection primacy for serious offenders does not apply to non-custodial CCOs but may bear on combining a CCO with imprisonment; protection is served by treatment conditions, but conditions cannot run longer than necessary merely to protect the community.

title: Combination sentences and parsimony
statement: Parsimony applies to combination sentences but there is no single term above which it is infringed; it is infringed only where the custodial term falls clearly beyond the range open; a short term may be needed where a CCO cannot serve some purposes. The question is whether the total sentence was wholly outside the range open.

title: Combination sentences: pre-sentence detention and the one-year ceiling
statement: Pre-sentence imprisonment must be deducted from the custodial component unless the court otherwise orders: not giving credit needs a compelling reason (e.g. the offender’s own conduct caused extra detention) and is not encouraged (compare psd.declare: the court may not “otherwise order” merely to make a combination sentence available). Time served does not affect the length of the custodial component; the custodial period is determined after deduction. Except for arson, the sum of all terms cannot exceed one year after deducting pre-sentence detention — the ceiling is enforced once, in cco.combination_one_year (with its arson rules and flag).

title: Directors’ liability for a body corporate’s fine
statement: On application, a director may be declared liable to pay a body corporate’s fine if the body cannot pay an appropriate fine and there were reasonable grounds to believe it could not meet its liabilities; a director who proves reasonable belief and reasonable steps is protected.

title: Fines likely to be paid by others
statement: The court cannot direct personal payment. Whether the offender will pay personally affects punitive and deterrent value and whether to fine; family payment may still punish if it creates a substantial obligation; the quantum should not be fixed by reference to an alternative source of payment.

title: Instalment and time-to-pay orders
statement: A fine is ordinarily payable immediately; the court may allow instalments or time to pay, and may later vary or cancel on listed grounds (re-sentencing as if just found guilty, considering compliance).
