title: Fine work orders (fine conversion; fine default unpaid community work)
statement: Unpaid fines may be converted to unpaid community work: a fine conversion order (not in default; before an enforcement hearing; the fine does not exceed 100 penalty units, or the application relates to a part of the fine up to 100 penalty units) or a fine default order (the unpaid fine does not exceed 100 penalty units). One hour per 0.2 penalty unit; at least eight hours; aggregate between eight and 500 hours; maximum completion periods by hours; no more than 20 hours in seven days (up to 40 on written request). Hours are cumulative unless directed otherwise; the order commences within three months (a later cumulative order commences once the earlier is completed: flag.fine_work_order_commencement). Mandatory terms mirror the CCO terms. Variation and contravention follow listed rules (on contravention, where circumstances materially altered or were wrongly stated: discharge the outstanding fines in full, discharge up to two-thirds (with or without imprisonment of one day per outstanding penalty unit), or adjourn for up to six months; imprisonment of one day per unpaid penalty unit up to two years where the court considers the other orders inadequate because of the nature of the offence and the offender’s characteristics, and the offender has refused to pay the fine and to perform unpaid community work). Manual issues: the completion-period table overlaps at 375 hours (both “375-500 → 24 months” and “251-375 → 18 months”), and the community-work threshold is stated as “does not exceed 100 penalty units” (12.9) but “less than 100 penalty units” at an enforcement hearing (12.10) (flag.fine_work_order_thresholds).

title: Adjourned undertakings: special conditions
statement: Special conditions are not defined, so any fit condition may be imposed (e.g. psychiatric care, firearm prohibition, non-contact, a drug education program, driver education or behaviour change programs). Be cautious about conditions on leaving or residing outside Victoria or amounting to an unauthorised deportation order, and about combining special conditions with parole.

title: Adjourned undertakings: variation, cancellation and contravention
statement: Variation or cancellation on application where circumstances materially altered, were wrongly stated, or the offender is unwilling to comply, considering compliance; the court may re-sentence for the original offences or impose a new unconditional undertaking. Contravention without reasonable excuse: maximum level 10 fine plus variation, confirmation, cancellation and re-sentence, or no further order, considering compliance and ability to comply. Time limits: within six months of the later conviction and no more than two years after the order ends (imprisonable reoffending); otherwise within one year after the order ends.

title: Purposes of dismissals, discharges and adjournments (release orders)
statement: For Victorian offences a court may, where a charge is proved, dismiss without conviction, discharge on conviction, or release on adjournment with or without conviction on an undertaking with conditions. These orders may be made to: provide for rehabilitation by serving the sentence in the community; take account of the trivial, technical or minor nature of the offence; allow the offender to demonstrate remorse as agreed with the court; allow for cases where recording a conviction, or more than nominal punishment, is not appropriate; or allow for other extenuating or exceptional circumstances justifying mercy. (app policy) A reasoning that proposes one of these orders should identify which purpose it serves.

title: Court assessment orders (community or inpatient)
statement: Available where the person is found or pleads guilty, is not in custody pending sentence, appears to have a mental illness needing immediate treatment to prevent serious deterioration or serious harm, can be assessed, no less restrictive means are reasonably available, an authorised psychiatrist reports facilities are available, and (inpatient) assessment cannot occur in the community. Its purpose is to determine whether a temporary treatment order or court secure treatment order should be made. A community assessment order is in force for seven days from when it is made; an inpatient order expires seven days after the person is received at a designated mental health service. Afterwards the court may make a court secure treatment order or sentence, deducting detention under the assessment order. Examination and treatment occur at a designated mental health service. (The intake must record whether the offender is in custody pending sentence, which excludes the order.)

title: Court secure treatment orders: a distinct sentencing option; single orders for multiple offences
statement: Imposed on conviction; a distinct option — custody in a mental health service requires a court secure treatment order, not imprisonment with a direction on how it is served. A single order may cover multiple offences (a power that does not depend on the aggregate-sentence power); it must not be longer than the appropriate period of imprisonment, and the judge must consider the otherwise appropriate dispositions for the individual offences and any cumulation orders. The court must notify the authorised psychiatrist. Of the predecessor hospital security order (whose analyses likely still largely apply): the person was not excused from responsibility — detained because of a serious offence, not because of the illness. (Reasons and practice points: order.csto.aggregate_reasons.)

title: Court secure treatment orders for multiple offences: totality, reasons and multiple orders
statement: Totality applies to both the operational period and the non-parole period of a CSTO. The court should specify the individual sentences underlying a single CSTO (part of the duty to give adequate reasons; the statutory limits on reasons for aggregate imprisonment do not apply to CSTOs). Multiple CSTOs may be inappropriate. Different penalties may be imposed for different offences, provided all orders can be given effect.

title: DATO treatment and supervision part: core and program conditions
statement: Mandatory core conditions (no imprisonable reoffending, attend Drug Court, report within two clear working days, treatment, supervision, notice of address change, not leave Victoria, obey directions) operate for two years or the custodial part, whichever is longer; at least one program condition is required (no more than necessary), operating for two years.

title: DATO management: case conferences, variation, sanctions and rewards
statement: Breach is not an offence; where satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the offender has, without reasonable excuse, failed to comply (other than by an offence punishable by more than 12 months’ imprisonment), the Drug Court must consider the sanctions in order and take only the first it deems appropriate (confirm; vary; curfew; up to 20 hours work; remain at a place up to 14 days; activate one to seven days of custody if proved beyond reasonable doubt). Reoffending punishable by more than 12 months (15A.2.2; fn 2796) allows sanctions or cancellation — 15A.2.4.2 says “at least 12 months” for cancellation under s 18ZN(1) (flag.dato_cancellation_threshold). Compliance may be rewarded, including “graduation” (cancelling the remainder).

title: DATO activation and cancellation
statement: Activation only in the circumstances listed (s 18ZL(1)(f) sanction; cancellation for reoffending; s 18ZP(1)). The court first calculates the remaining custodial part and may order less but never more. The maximum remaining custodial part (both courts) is two years less the time the treatment and supervision part has operated if the original custodial part was no more than two years, otherwise the original custodial part less that time; within that maximum, declared custody and secure-custody sanction periods are deducted. The court weighs compliance (efforts, not mere time), the punitive aspects of compliance and earlier sanctions, and all the circumstances. An activation of one year or more may attract a non-parole period. Cancellation under s 18ZN(1) follows reoffending punishable by “at least 12 months” imprisonment (compare “more than 12 months” in 15A.2.2: flag.dato_cancellation_threshold). Cancellation under s 18ZP is a two-step discretionary process focused on events during the order; unwillingness to comply is distinct from a dependency-affected capacity to comply; it would be erroneous to treat s 18ZP(1)(c) as a power to sanction serious non-compliance, but repeated non-compliance may show that the order is not likely to achieve its purposes and so engage the power to cancel under s 18ZP(1)(d); re-sentencing after cancellation cannot be imprisonment; reasons are required for a decision that adversely affects the offender.

title: DATO assessment report and consent; examples of refusal
statement: Before making a DATO the Drug Court must order an assessment report on suitability (contestable) and adjourn; informed written consent is required. If no DATO is made, the court sentences with consent or adjourns to the non-Drug Court jurisdiction. DATOs have been refused for repeated non-attendance and threats, inability to meet requirements, residence outside the gazetted area, past non-compliance with an otherwise appropriate sentence over four years, and “overservicing”.

title: DATOs and subsequent charges (four-stage process)
statement: The Drug Court that made the DATO may hear a further charge; if it imposes immediate imprisonment it decides whether the sentence is subsumed within the remaining custodial part, otherwise it cancels the treatment and supervision part and activates or re-sentences non-custodially. The Manual says it is not clear what happens when an offender on a County Court DATO is charged with an offence within the Magistrates’ Court’s jurisdiction and pleads not guilty (flag.dato_county_court_subsequent_charge).

title: Discretionary licence suspension, cancellation and disqualification (s 89A; RSA)
statement: Under s 89A of the Act, for any offence other than the mandatory offences or RSA offences (default three months; record the section and offences). Under the RSA, for RSA offences (not the RSA’s other mandatory disqualification offences, nor obstructing the taking of blood samples unless the offender was in charge of a motor vehicle less than 3 hours before: fn 2911) or any offence “in connection with the driving of a motor vehicle” (a substantial relation to driving, not its manner); the period must be specified; disqualification without express cancellation cancels the licence; it may be limited to categories.

title: Licence suspensions: presumption of concurrency; RSA Part 6B suspension taken into account
statement: A later suspension under the same specified provisions is presumed concurrent unless the court orders otherwise or the RSA requires consecutive periods; a Part 6B RSA suspension must be taken into account in fixing the period. (A presumption the court may displace and a matter to take into account: the auditor checks the reasoning addresses any current or Part 6B suspension recorded in intake.driving.)

title: Generic and specific gravity of the offending
statement: Generic gravity is reflected in the maximum penalty and the elements of the offence. The court must also assess the gravity of the specific offending relative to other examples of the offence, by identifying its particulars (e.g. planning, method, abuse of trust), its explanation (mitigatory factors that reduce moral culpability but not offence gravity) and its consequences (for the victim, the community or society).

title: The maximum penalty: absolute limit, Parliament’s view, mandatory consideration
statement: Unless an indefinite sentence is available, the maximum is the absolute highest term, indicates Parliament’s view of the gravity of the offence and is a mandatory consideration. It is a navigational aid (the court steers by it, not towards it) that always requires careful attention. The court must place the offence and offender on a spectrum from the least serious instance of the offence to the worst.

title: Where maximum penalties are found
statement: Maximum penalties are found at the foot of the section for statutory indictable offences and in the offence-specific chapters of the Manual (offences.json in this knowledge base). In Victoria the maximum is often expressed as a “level” or “unit” (the penalty scale), but some legislation still states it in years or months (where the two are inconsistent the level prevails unless there is a contrary intention: audit.level_term_mismatch).

title: “Worst category” is reserved for cases warranting the maximum
statement: Offending that does not warrant the maximum should not be described as “within the worst category”; the phrase is reserved for cases where the maximum is warranted and should not be used as shorthand. It is better to say whether the offending is so grave as to warrant the maximum or not.

title: Factors relevant to whether the maximum penalty is called for
statement: Factors relevant to whether the maximum is called for include role, drug quantity/value/sophistication/international scope, relevant prior history, the stage of any plea, genuine remorse, commercial motive, delay, and (for child sexual offending and for rape and other sexual offences) the specific features listed.

title: Indictable offence that could have been tried summarily
statement: If an indictable offence might have been tried summarily but was not, the court may consider that fact, but it is not limited to the maximum available in the summary jurisdiction.

title: Misidentifying the maximum is appealable error unless immaterial
statement: Misidentifying the applicable maximum is an appealable error unless shown to be immaterial. Indicators of material effect: the sentence is a high percentage of the wrongly believed maximum; the affected charges are a large part of the total effective sentence; the court appeared influenced by the wrong maximum; or the error cannot be disregarded (e.g. imprisonment imposed where the maximum is a fine).

title: Changes to the maximum penalty between offence and sentence
statement: For offences before a change: apply any reduction, never an increase. If the maximum was reduced then increased between offence and sentence, the court need not apply the temporarily reduced maximum and may use the original if the current penalty is of the same magnitude or higher. For offences after a change: the change reflects Parliament’s new assessment; an increase signals existing sentences were insufficient and should increase. A repealed offence keeps its maximum for conduct under it; a new similar offence does not affect it.

title: Statutory factors bearing on gravity (s 5(2))
statement: The Act lists non-exclusive circumstances: nature and gravity; culpability and degree of responsibility; hatred or prejudice motive; impact on the victim; circumstances of the victim; injury, loss or damage resulting directly; aggravating or mitigating circumstances; any other relevant circumstances. Generally, gravity is informed by the degree of risk of harm and the extent of potential harm, assessed on the individual circumstances; the factors overlap with the offender’s circumstances and the purposes and principles.

title: Planning, duration, scale and sophistication
statement: Premeditated or planned offending (even if inept or unsuccessful) is usually more serious than spontaneous, opportunistic or unplanned offending; generally the greater the planning, duration, scale and sophistication, the graver the offending, and it also invokes general deterrence and community protection. But the Court of Appeal has also said there may often be little to distinguish a premeditated attack from a random one of sustained violence; the Manual suggests (“it seems”) the Court was reinforcing the need to condemn public and family violence regardless of planning. In quantity-based offending (drug trafficking/importation) quantity is more significant than duration or number of transactions and is a key indicator of gravity.

title: Intent, recklessness and knowledge of risk
statement: All things being equal, intentional offending attracts a higher sentence than reckless offending. Acting with knowledge of a possible risk increases culpability, particularly knowledge of a large-scale risk or separate attacks of escalating violence. Impaired decision-making may reduce the level of recklessness depending on the impairment. Knowledge of risk must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

title: Repetitive or persistent (versus intermittent) offending
statement: Repetitive or persistent offending increases culpability (knowledge of unlawfulness, failure to take the opportunity to cease, fear engendered in victims and community); intermittent offending is less serious.
embed_text:
Repetitive or persistent (versus intermittent) offending
Repetitive or persistent offending increases culpability (knowledge of unlawfulness, failure to take the opportunity to cease, fear engendered in victims and community); intermittent offending is less serious.

title: Role in offending with co-offenders
statement: Each participant’s role must generally be assessed: a subordinate or non-consequential role generally reduces culpability; a substantial or leading role may increase it. For offences of great magnitude (terrorism, drug trafficking) any involvement indicates high moral culpability. Never lose sight of the offence charged and what the offender actually did. Do not place excessive weight on positioning the offender in a notional hierarchy (e.g. drug roles). Without evidence the court need not make a favourable finding; distinctions between co-offenders (important for parity) need an evidentiary basis.

title: Principal and accessory but unknown which is which
statement: Where the evidence shows one joint offender was a principal and another an accessory but not which was which, both are treated as no more culpable than an accessory. This does not apply where there is no evidence of a distinction, and an accessory’s culpability is not presumptively lower than a principal’s.

title: Abuse of status or position; breach of trust
statement: Abuse or misuse of status or position, particularly a breach of trust, may aggravate objective seriousness — e.g. offending by those in the justice system, public officials, a parent or carer against a child, a family friend sexually offending against a child, and persons in positions of trust (teachers, doctors, employees, others).

title: Provocation
statement: Provocation by the victim may lessen culpability but not the significance of the harm. Its weight is a matter of degree and circumstance: a sudden or spontaneous loss of control (particularly from fear rather than anger) may reduce culpability; mitigation is limited where the response reflects an inability to control anger or is wholly disproportionate; time elapsed does not of itself remove it. In a family relationship, provocation or emotional stress is subordinate to general deterrence, denunciation and just punishment unless the offending stems from fear rather than anger.

title: Hatred or prejudice motive (s 5(2)(daaa))
statement: If the offending was wholly or partly motivated by hatred for or prejudice against a group of people with common characteristics, that aggravates gravity and moral culpability. Groups are not limited by the Act (the second reading speech identified religious affiliation, racial or cultural origin, sexual orientation, sex, gender identity, age, impairment and homelessness) and are determined case by case. The victim may be a member of the group, a “Good Samaritan”, an advocate, someone employed in relation to the group, or an acquaintance or family member. There has been little judicial consideration of the provision: one case held the motive must be proved beyond reasonable doubt (consistent with findings.formosa); in another, intoxication and a drug-induced psychosis did not obviate the stated motivation, though such matters may reduce its aggravating force.

title: Circumstances of the victim (general)
statement: The victim’s circumstances are highly significant to gravity; harm is usually the most important, with vulnerability, protected class, conduct, relationship to the offender and sometimes attitude to sentence. Where harm is an element of the offence, Parliament has already taken it into account in the maximum, so it must not be doubly weighed. “Victim” is construed broadly (direct victim, family, secondary victims such as witnesses, society or the community; there may be several victims).

title: Vulnerable victims
statement: Offending against vulnerable victims is particularly grave: elderly people; younger people, children and infants (significant age disparity tends to increase gravity where an adult sexually exploits a child); sleeping or unconscious people; sex workers; pregnant people; intoxicated people; physically or intellectually disabled people; small businesses; women going about their business in a public place at night. Where a victim characteristic (e.g. a child’s age) is an element of the offence charged, it cannot also be counted as aggravating, although conduct that exceeds the minimum needed to satisfy an element can indicate a more serious example of the offence (factor.element_not_aggravating).

title: Protected persons as victims
statement: Offending against protected persons — law enforcement officers (including police, corrections and youth justice custodial officers), emergency service workers and prisoners — is especially serious. (See also the mandatory minimum regimes for offences against protected officials in rules.json.)

title: Relationship between offender and victim (domestic context; innocent stranger)
statement: A relationship may be relevant to gravity. Offending in a domestic context can never be mitigating and may be aggravating, particularly family violence, rape or other sexual offending. The absence of any relationship may also be significant: offending against an “innocent stranger” is serious.

title: Victim’s conduct
statement: A victim’s conduct, if established on the balance of probabilities, may bear on sentence even if it does not lessen moral culpability or gravity. It is unhelpful to label it mitigating or otherwise, or to call the victim “complicit”. Weight is a matter for the court in the circumstances.

title: Victim’s attitude to sentence; forgiveness; no victim impact statement
statement: Generally a victim’s attitude to sentence is irrelevant, but forgiveness may indicate the effects were not long lasting and suffering is lessened; it is of greater relevance for negligence offences. Treat forgiveness cautiously, and with extreme caution in family violence. A victim’s failure to make a victim impact statement or take part is not mitigating.

title: Harm: injury, loss or damage resulting directly from the offence
statement: The nature and degree of harm is highly relevant to gravity (physical/psychological; transient to permanent; for endangerment offences the risk created; for dishonesty offences financial loss). The Act requires consideration of impact on the victim and injury, loss or damage resulting directly, whether or not reasonably foreseeable or intended. The prosecution must show a temporal or other connection establishing the harm was the direct result of the offending. Evidence of harm is normally led at trial or, on a plea, in the depositions; where the court must look beyond these, most often through victim impact statements; absent those, the court may draw reasonable inferences (particularly in sexual offending).

title: Aggravating circumstances need not be strictly contemporaneous
statement: Aggravating circumstances are not limited to those strictly contemporaneous with the offending; the court may consider surrounding circumstances directly related to the offence — this may be a question of degree best left to the sentencing court.

title: An element of the offence cannot be counted as aggravating or mitigating
statement: A factor that is an element of the offence cannot be counted as aggravating or mitigating; it is part of the inherent gravity. But conduct exceeding the minimum needed to satisfy an element can indicate a more serious example of the offence.

title: Use of a weapon
statement: Use of a weapon is relevant to gravity: the more dangerous the item and the greater its capacity to invoke fear, the more serious. The use made of it matters — more serious when used to overcome resistance, obtain submission in sexual offences, instil fear and enforce demands, attack or harm the victim, in a public place or at a busy time, or against vulnerable victims or those protected by law. Little or no distinction is generally drawn between imitation and real weapons, though some authority treats an imitation or unloaded weapon as less serious.

title: Benefit to the offender and loss to the victim
statement: Benefit gained and loss caused help assess gravity (property offences; offending for reward such as trafficking). Make reasonable efforts to value property, though quantum errors may be immaterial and value is one guide only. Broad regard may be had to profit if reliable information is available, without detailed examination of illegal dealings; co-offenders may be assumed to share equally absent contrary evidence. Actual enrichment may significantly aggravate; benefit includes benefit to dependants; lack of actual enrichment (e.g. failed offending) is not necessarily mitigating. Lower-level participants who benefit less are less culpable. Failure to quantify loss may limit the available range. Recoupment by insurer or indemnity fund carries little or no mitigating weight if it merely shifts the loss (compare 6.3.4.2 on restitution by third parties: flag.third_party_restitution_weight).

title: Family violence
statement: Victorian courts repeatedly emphasise the need to strongly condemn family violence (breach of trust, gravity of harm, vulnerability of victims); denunciation, just punishment and general deterrence have primacy. Gravity increases if the offending breaches a family violence intervention order or is committed in front of children. Family violence includes physically, sexually, emotionally, psychologically and economically abusive, threatening or coercive behaviour; the surrounding behaviours must be considered to assess true gravity, which is not measured solely by physical consequences, and individual charges are not divorced from the context of control and fear. The community abhors such conduct. Related rules: provocation or emotional stress in a family relationship is subordinate to general deterrence, denunciation and just punishment unless the offending stems from fear rather than anger (factor.provocation); forgiveness is treated with extreme caution; childhood disadvantage cannot reduce the protection due to victims of domestic violence; where the charge is itself a breach of a family violence intervention order, that breach is an element (factor.element_not_aggravating).

title: Entrapment by police
statement: Entrapment is not a defence but police entrapping conduct may mitigate. A real possibility that the offending would not have occurred but for police involvement may carry some weight; the focus is its bearing on culpability (from very little to substantial). Relevant: how police contributed, any coercion/pressure/inducement and its degree, whether direct or through an intermediary (more remote, less weight); little weight if the offender instigated, more if their will was overborne.

title: Uncharged conduct and surrounding facts (no punishment for a more serious uncharged offence)
statement: Uncharged or discreditable conduct may aggravate and indicate increased culpability, but not where it constitutes an aggravated version of the offence, should have been a separate charge, or would warrant conviction for a more serious offence. Considering a victim’s injury when sentencing for recklessly exposing an emergency worker to risk, where no separate charge was brought for the injury, does not infringe that principle; but conduct separately sentenced cannot also be used (double punishment). The Manual notes contrary authority for the conditional-liberty and enlisting-others-to-lie examples (fns 1006, 1007). The line is a matter of degree (“fine line”), depending on contemporaneity and the disparity in seriousness. Permissible examples: concealment (disposing of a body, denying knowledge of whereabouts); delaying or preventing medical assistance; lying or enlisting others to lie; offending while on conditional liberty or in contravention of court orders. Highly fact-dependent; the court may decline a negative inference where there is another explanation.

title: Current sentencing practices: mandatory but only one factor
statement: The court must have regard to current sentencing practices (“the approach currently adopted by sentencing judges when sentencing for the particular offence”), but it is one factor among many. The aim is consistency in applying legal principle (like cases alike, different cases differently) — consistency is described as an aspect of the rule of law (the footnote for that statement is unreliable: flag.fn1012_ibid_pinpoint). A range contrary to principle (e.g. insufficient regard to the maximum or the seriousness of the offence) should not be followed, and a court should not consider cases having idiosyncratic features (they are unlikely to be useful comparators).

title: After Dalgliesh: practices are one consideration; appellate calls for change apply immediately
statement: Before Dalgliesh (HCA), current sentencing practices were treated as a primary consideration and the Court of Appeal would on occasion declare practices for an offence inadequate — where the maximum had been increased and practices did not reflect it; the offence had become more prevalent; community attitudes to its gravity had changed or concern had been expressed; its impact on victims was better understood; a category of offenders had persistently been given too much weight for mitigation (e.g. good character in white-collar crime or culpable driving); or the seriousness of conduct had been wrongly categorised or a disposition was not ordinarily appropriate. Such statements were applied incrementally. That approach is no longer followed: practices are merely one consideration and, where an appellate court indicates practices must change, sentencing courts give effect to it immediately.

statement: “Current sentencing practices” are those at the time of sentencing (including the weight given to particular considerations), used alongside awareness of the maximum at the time of offending — with caution where the maximum is now higher. Equal justice may require regard to historical practices so far as they can be established and show a materially lesser sanction, if reasonably practicable; it is not an inflexible rule.

title: Comparable cases: “relevantly comparable or instructively different”
statement: Case comparisons are an important primary resource but help only if relevantly comparable or instructively different. Comparability depends on the circumstances of the offender and the offending (generally the same category of seriousness), not merely the same physical conduct. A party relying on cases must identify them and spell out what makes them comparable; a bare list or table of sentences is not enough — tables must explain each case’s key features; references are useful only if they articulate unifying principles. title: Limitations of case comparisons
statement: Use comparisons cautiously: a past range does not set the outer limits of the discretion or confirm the range is correct; a range should not be defined by a few cases (at most they are points on a spectrum); truly comparable cases are hard to find, especially for extremely serious offending with limited mitigation; do not analyse similar cases in detail to find the “right” sentence or a confined range — they are not binding precedent. Comparisons are of particularly limited use where circumstances vary greatly (manslaughter, intentionally causing serious injury, assault with intent to commit a sexual offence). Great caution with cases predating an appellate declaration of inadequacy. Victorian courts rarely look to other States’ practices.

title: Sentencing statistics and medians
statement: Statistics are a primary resource and, used correctly, a valuable yardstick, but alone they cannot establish a practice. Shortcomings: they do not identify the appropriate range; may distract from the circumstances; cannot substitute for the instinctive synthesis; alone cannot show manifest excess; cannot analyse wide-ranging offences; say nothing about why sentences were fixed. A median is an accidental or contingent statistic, not a measure of seriousness, and cannot represent the sentence for mid-range offending; selecting a median and asking whether the offending is above or below it risks an improper two-stage approach. Permitted uses: courts have used statistics to help check whether a sentence accords with current practices, and appellate courts to check whether a consideration (e.g. youth) was given too little or too much weight.

title: Distinguishing co-offenders’ roles needs an evidentiary basis

title: Surrounding circumstances; elements inform seriousness; uncharged injury in exposure offences
statement: The circumstances of an offence are not marked by neat lines at its technical beginning and end; surrounding circumstances directly related to it may be considered (it may be a question of degree). title: Family violence: stern punishment; context of control is not “merely background”

The offending as a whole cannot be deconstructed to divorce individual charges from a context of degradation, control, threats and fear; conduct in an atmosphere of vitriol after a relationship breakdown is not merely background.

title: Verdins evidence: impact, not labels; proper expert opinion; rigorous assessment
statement: Verdins does not depend on diagnostic labels but on the impact of the impairment on the offender and their behaviour; it is generally not enough for an expert simply to describe the impairment. The court’s assessment must be rigorous and careful; the prosecution has an important part in identifying and challenging inadequacies.

title: Prior and subsequent convictions: scope and proof

title: Why the offender’s circumstances matter
statement: Personal circumstances are a fundamental consideration that overlap with the offence. title: Advanced age (mature or elderly offenders)
statement: Age may mitigate where imprisonment may adversely affect an elderly offender’s health, the offender is less likely to be dangerous, more likely to die in prison (a larger proportion of remaining life), or imprisonment is more burdensome. Age is assessed at sentence (delay may make the offender older), but the effect of delay on the victim must be considered and a sentence is not moderated purely because delay made the offender older. Age is relevant to setting a minimum term and fixing the non-parole period. Weight depends on the circumstances; age never by itself excuses punishment; significant imprisonment may be appropriate for serious offences; just punishment, proportionality and deterrence remain primary. (Youth is dealt with by special statutory considerations: see purposes and youth orders.)

title: Ethnicity, culture and race (no differential sentencing in themselves)
statement: Ethnicity, culture and race are not in themselves bases for differential sentencing, but associated considerations may be taken into account depending on their connection with the offence. Treating Aboriginal offenders as generally less culpable because of deprived background is racial stereotyping; an Aboriginal offender’s deprived background may mitigate to the same extent as a non-Aboriginal offender’s.

title: Participation in a Koori Court sentencing conversation

title: Cultural norms
statement: The weight of a cultural norm is discretionary: if it obliged the offender or confined their choices (little or no choice), culpability may be diminished and rehabilitation viewed positively; if merely a justification, it does not. A norm may not outweigh the seriousness of the offending or the principles (so-called “honour killings” call for the strongest denunciation and increased general and specific deterrence); it cannot create a different range for a cultural group; and a bare assertion is not enough — it must be established by evidence relevant to the offender.

title: Physical health or disability
statement: Relevant where imprisonment will be a greater (6.2.1.1: “significantly more”) burden because of the offender’s health (ask whether ill health makes imprisonment more burdensome, not vice versa — e.g. dietary management, therapies, treatment), or there is a serious risk of imprisonment having a grave (6.2.1.2: “materially adverse”) effect on health; the Manual words the thresholds differently and the app applies neither as stricter (flag.physical_health_thresholds). Weight depends on the circumstances. Likely death within the sentence goes to burden but can never justify a manifestly inadequate sentence. No special rules for particular conditions; a condition alone is not mitigating — evidence must establish hardship in prison (prison may even improve health); without evidence the court may decline to discount. Lowered life expectancy may reduce the need for specific deterrence.

title: Impaired mental functioning (Verdins): the six ways it is relevant
statement: The court must take into account impaired mental or intellectual functioning of any cause, permanence, severity or duration, existing at offending or sentence. Labels do not matter: what matters is the evidence of the nature, extent and effect of the impairment at the relevant time. Six (non-exhaustive) ways it may be relevant (limbs below); the nature and degree of a relevant impairment may differ from one aspect to another, so it is assessed limb by limb. The considerations may moderate both head sentence and minimum term, but are exceptional, should not be invoked in routine cases, and need not be recited as a checklist.

title: Verdins limb 1: moral culpability
statement: Culpability may be reduced if, at the time of the offence, the impairment reduced the ability to exercise judgment, make calm and rational choices, think clearly or appreciate wrongfulness; disinhibited the offender; obscured intent; or contributed causally (a descriptive, non-exhaustive list). It is a matter of degree assessed with expert evidence and the offender’s conduct before, during and after: did the impairment make the offender less blameworthy? A causal connection is not required but some connection is: a “realistic connection”, or the impairment “caused or contributed to” or was “causally linked” to the offending (flag.verdins_connection_test). For serious offences, or where the offender knew the nature, gravity and wrongfulness of the conduct (indicated by planning and avoiding detection), the reduction may be minor or limited (the Manual notes contrary authority on the latter: fn 1151). Both Verdins and Bugmy allow culpability to be viewed as reduced; expert evidence is required to show how the two are connected and, where they converge, inappropriate double counting is avoided, but Bugmy is considered in its own right.

statement: Impairment may make some sanctions (e.g. imprisonment where the impairment is significantly impacted or treatment is unavailable) inappropriate; specific statutory sanctions and custodial alternatives exist for impaired offenders. But limb 2 does not mean imprisonment cannot be imposed; the court considers the possibility on the facts.

title: Verdins limb 3: general deterrence
statement: General deterrence may be moderated or eliminated, but not automatically: it depends on the severity and nature of the condition and its effect on mental capacity at offending, sentence or both, and generally some (possibly causal) connection with the offending. There must be an evidentiary basis and “proper and informed” consideration of how the impairment materially diminished the capacity to reason about wrongfulness, or why full general deterrence would be repugnant to humanitarian considerations. An offender may not be an “appropriate vehicle” (a causal relationship is usually sufficient, although this may not apply if the offender acted knowing the conduct was wrong). Extent depends on symptoms, effect on capacity, and the nature and gravity of the offence. It is relatively clear that general deterrence will be wholly eliminated in the most extreme cases (where a mental impairment defence might have been established); it is not moderated where the impairment arose as a reaction to discovery or the prospect of prison; each case is decided on its facts.

title: Verdins limbs 5 and 6: heavier burden; serious risk to mental health
statement: Limb 5: a significant additional burden must be shown, considering the nature of custody (isolation, protection, circumscribed conditions, unavailable treatment). Limb 6: a serious risk of a significantly adverse effect on mental health beyond the deterioration imprisonment causes anyone, assessed by illness history, likely conditions, management difficulties and likelihood and effectiveness of treatment. For these limbs it does not matter that the impairment arose on discovery or because of the prospect of prison. Impairment alone, or stress at the prospect of prison, is not enough; the defence must establish the likely effect; without evidence no moderation is needed, though the court may infer greater burden for a severe condition depending on the totality of the evidence (flag.verdins_expert_evidence_normally_vs_required). Weight varies and does not displace the other purposes.

title: Self-induced impairment, substance abuse and relapse
statement: Mitigation may be reduced where the condition is self-induced (drugs, alcohol): the key is foreknowledge that the substance was likely to produce a delusional state. A history of using substances known to cause hallucinations and violence means culpability is unlikely to be reduced and use may aggravate. If impairment and substance abuse are independent, Verdins applies with full force. If the impairment caused the substance abuse, culpability and deterrence may be moderated, but the defence must still prove a connection between impairment and offending (drug quantity may be considered). A relapse caused by not taking medication or by illegal drugs is not mitigating, although moral culpability may still be reduced if another factor beyond the offender’s control (e.g. significant stress from a relationship breakdown or personal loss) also played some part.

Self-induced impairment, substance abuse and relapse
Mitigation may be reduced where the condition is self-induced (drugs, alcohol): the key is foreknowledge that the substance was likely to produce a delusional state. A history of using substances known to cause hallucinations and violence means culpability is unlikely to be reduced and use may aggravate. If impairment and substance abuse are independent, Verdins applies with full force. If the impairment caused the substance abuse, culpability and deterrence may be moderated, but the defence must still prove a connection between impairment and offending (drug quantity may be considered). A relapse caused by not taking medication or by illegal drugs is not mitigating, although moral culpability may still be reduced if another factor beyond the offender’s control (e.g. significant stress from a relationship breakdown or personal loss) also played some part.

title: Personality disorders under Verdins
statement: Verdins applies to personality disorders like any other condition (no blanket exclusion), but a disorder does not necessarily show impaired functioning; what matters is what the expert evidence shows about its effect on mental functioning at the offending or in future. Contrary statements in DPP v O’Neill should not be followed.

title: Verdins: raising it, evidence and reasons
statement: Generally, Verdins need only be considered if clearly raised and supported by sufficient evidence; the defence must adduce it and the court need not inquire (save where a link is shown and the inference is the only one reasonably open). It is wrong to assume Verdins applies because an impairment exists: rigorous consideration of which limbs apply is required. Cogent, normally expert, evidence must establish on the balance of probabilities the impairment at the relevant time and its nature, extent and effect, assessed against the offence facts (the Manual also says expert evidence “is required” but not determinative: flag.verdins_expert_evidence_normally_vs_required). Experts must not opine on whether the principles apply — that is for the court. Be cautious; imprecise opinions make firm findings difficult; self-reported and uncorroborated reports may be rejected. If not accepting uncontested expert evidence, give notice and an opportunity to be heard. Reasons must explain how the impairment was taken into account (or why Verdins was rejected).

title: Addiction (gambling, drugs, alcohol)
statement: Addiction may bear on culpability (e.g. trafficking to feed one’s own addiction rather than greed), but that weight is greatly diminished, often to nothing, above street level; advantaged background, manner of involvement and intended use may lessen mitigation. Importation is inferred to be for profit absent evidence; needing money for a debt does not affect culpability; good character carries less weight in importation. Addiction is relevant to rehabilitation, deterrence and community protection, but someone with repeated opportunities for reform should not expect to rely on it. It may bear on choice of sanction (tailored or rehabilitative sanctions). Addiction does not require a conclusion that culpability is lessened.

title: Intoxication (rarely mitigating; may aggravate)
statement: Intoxication rarely mitigates and may aggravate; to reduce culpability the circumstances must be “quite exceptional”. The key is foreknowledge: knowing the likely consequences increases culpability. A long history of drinking without any indication of violence may make the circumstances exceptional enough to mitigate. Intoxication may also be relevant to remorse and rehabilitation.

title: Character, past history and antecedents
statement: Character (synonymous with past history and antecedents) includes at least prior criminal history. title: Good character
statement: Good character is an established mitigating factor assessed apart from the current offending (“otherwise of good character”) and, subject to a statutory exception, must be taken into account; weight varies and the court may consider the nature of the offending when weighing it. A lack of similar priors is significant mitigation; good character always earns some (possibly minimal) leniency, balanced against the offence and purposes, depending on seriousness and whether isolated or a course of conduct (less weight for multiple offences). Significant for first offenders (especially mature ones or those under extraordinary external pressure), qualified by gravity, and relevant to rehabilitation. Reduced significance for offences commonly committed by people of good character or where respectability was exploited.

title: Bad character: prior and subsequent convictions cannot increase the sentence
statement: Prior criminality is relevant but cannot be used in aggravation to increase a sentence or to doubly punish; it may indicate moral culpability, persistent lawlessness or propensity and so inhibit mitigation such as rehabilitation. Subsequent convictions likewise cannot increase the head sentence or aggravate; they may only rebut claimed mitigation. The defence need not disclose subsequent convictions unless relying on good character; the prosecution must prove later convictions and relevant subsequent conduct whenever a non-parole period may be fixed. Rehabilitation between offending and sentence may reduce the negative impact of bad character.

title: Motive
statement: Motive may aggravate or mitigate depending on the circumstances. Lessening: genuine (not false) altruism; addiction without profit motive; personal or financial pressure or need; threats short of duress. Aggravating: misguided loyalty; greed or profit; status, self-aggrandisement or a lavish lifestyle; vigilantism; revenge, spite or dislike.

title: Childhood deprivation and disadvantage (Bugmy)
statement: Childhood deprivation or violence must be considered: its effects do not diminish with time and can explain but not excuse offending. Significant circumstances include family violence or abuse, addicted or alcoholic carers, educational disadvantage, sexual abuse, separation from natural parents, and severe persecution or refugee experience. It is an error to require the offender to demonstrate “significant childhood deprivation”, and it need not be “profound”; the Manual elsewhere speaks of “extreme disadvantage” (6.3.3) and of “significant deprivation” in the general expression’s rationale, so no threshold label is applied (flag.bugmy_degree_of_deprivation). It is also relevant in applying the fundamental principles and purposes. The court should make clear how the background moderated the weight given to purposes or principles and evaluate its extent. Mitigation must at some point yield to serious violent offending and community protection, particularly domestic violence. A disadvantaged upbringing may elevate rehabilitation and the need to avoid or minimise incarceration.

title: Bugmy: general expression (inferred) versus specific expression (nexus by evidence)
statement: General expression: childhood deprivation may reduce culpability and can be inferred from the simple fact of deprivation, with no causal connection required. Specific expression: extreme deprivation explaining recourse to violence when frustrated may substantially reduce culpability, but requires a nexus between the deprivation and the inability to control the relevant impulse, a causal connection established by an appropriate evidentiary foundation and rigorous evaluation (not a diagnostic label). The nexus cannot be inferred from judicial experience or common sense; it is difficult to envisage sufficient evidence without a professional reasoned opinion.

title: Remorse (repentance, contrition)
statement: Remorse is relevant at common law and implicitly under the Act (forfeiture effects and conduct at trial as indicators). Genuine remorse is extremely rare and very important: it enhances rehabilitation prospects and reduces specific deterrence and community protection. A plea made appreciating wrongfulness and impact and wishing to make amends calls for a significant reduction beyond the utilitarian discount. Even genuine remorse does not displace the need to reflect gravity. Genuine remorse differs from feigned remorse, self-pity, depression or anguish at being caught; determination to change and make amends is the indicator. It must be proved on the balance of probabilities on proper evidence (the offender’s own testimony is the most compelling; words and deeds over time are more informative); be cautious before treating a plea as showing more than utilitarian value; long delay before the plea may detract. A victim impact statement cannot disprove remorse. (Footnote 1334’s “Ibid” is resolved to BarbaroVIC by its pinpoint: flag.fn1334_ibid_after_see_also.)

statement: Absence of remorse cannot aggravate, but may indicate a need for specific deterrence; if it reveals contempt for the victim or the law it may be relevant to culpability and rehabilitation prospects, depending on the case.

title: Doran discount: admissions to conduct otherwise difficult to prove
statement: Admissions to conduct otherwise difficult to prove, or that supply evidence needed for conviction, warrant a “demonstrable discount” to encourage others (the Doran discount), including admissions leading to more or more serious charges. Not confined to unknown crimes or incapable complainants; may apply to a confession after being confronted with evidence if it affected the form of the charge. Depending on the admissions, 30% to 50% may be appropriate — generally more for confession to an unknown crime, less where it adds detail to existing allegations; leniency is called for where proof depends entirely on the confession. A matter of degree and fact.

title: Restitution and reparation
statement: Restitution is a common law factor allowing a reduced sentence or shorter non-parole period, but even full reparation does not avoid all punishment. It is always relevant and mitigating and should be encouraged (reparation, remorse, no profit); hardship and willingness to assume burdens get great weight; mitigation is not removed but may be lessened when made by third parties or court order (compare 5.2.8.2 on loss recouped from an insurer: flag.third_party_restitution_weight); an offender must not buy, or appear to buy, a lower or suspended sentence; first-time offers on the plea are viewed cautiously; deferral to allow restitution is rare and viewed cautiously; differences in restitution may explain disparity; failure to make restitution is not aggravating.

title: Guilty plea: statutory consideration and why it is rewarded
statement: The Act requires the court to consider whether the offender pleaded guilty and at what stage any plea or intention to plead occurred. A plea saves the State and victims the cost and trauma of a trial, spares witnesses (especially in homicide and sexual cases) the ordeal of giving evidence, and abandons any chance of acquittal; it is publicly rewarded to encourage pleas because of the public good that follows.

title: Pleas during the COVID-19 pandemic (and its subsiding)
statement: A plea entered during the currency of the pandemic (while courts worked under its adverse effects) carried greater utilitarian benefit and attracts augmented weight: a significant discount that the court need not quantify, applied consistently and not dependent on venue. The Manual notes that as at the end of 2023 the effects had subsided, but fixes no end date.

title: Weight of a guilty plea
statement: Every plea must be considered, with weight depending on the circumstances after specific and sound consideration. A plea need not always produce a discount, and the court is not bound by a Crown concession that it should.

title: Utilitarian value of the plea
statement: In all but exceptional cases the utilitarian value must be acknowledged by a reduction, regardless of remorse (even a self-interested plea has utilitarian value). The strength of the Crown case is irrelevant to utilitarian value, but the length and complexity of the trial avoided is relevant (the benefit might be considered great where an overwhelmingly complex, lengthy circumstantial case is avoided). Contesting other charges does not diminish the utilitarian value of the pleas entered.

title: A plea of not guilty is never aggravating
statement: A not guilty plea is never aggravating: an accused cannot be penalised for insisting on trial, and the court may not increase a proper sentence to mark disapproval of putting the Crown to proof or of a time-wasting or scurrilous defence.

title: The plea as an indicator of remorse; strength of the Crown case
statement: A plea showing genuine remorse, entered at the earliest practical opportunity and saving a trial and witness trauma normally deserves a substantial discount. The strength of the Crown case may bear on whether the plea reflects remorse (a strong case may mean recognition of the inevitable), but care is needed because an offender may be genuinely remorseful whatever the strength; a plea to a weak case generally warrants an additional discount (this additional discount goes to remorse and willingness to facilitate justice, not utilitarian value, on which the strength of the case has no bearing: 7.1.2.1). Where remorse is inferred from the plea, the court should identify its weight and how it was taken into account.

title: Timing of the plea (early, late, and pleas that are not late)
statement: An early, unconditional plea ordinarily attracts a substantial discount (normally high if it also evidences remorse and rehabilitation; usually still significant if it only saves costs). A late plea attracts a lower discount. Timing is characterised by when it was first reasonably open to plead guilty. Pleas that are not late are listed below. Where a statutory alternative was available earlier, a later plea is not necessarily “early”. Where a plea is late and the accused caused lengthy, expensive extradition proceedings, the discount may be small. Where the conviction reflects a rejected plea offer, the offender gets the discount that acceptance would have attracted.

title: Applying the plea discount (head sentence, then non-parole period; mandatory minimums)
statement: The discount is applied consistently with the form of sentence and may change that form. For imprisonment it is applied first to the head sentence, then to the non-parole period (possibly with an additional discount there if the plea evidences rehabilitative prospects). Mandatory minimum regimes do not oust common law principles but modify them (little authority). For suspended sentences (where available) the discount applies to the sentence, then to the part served immediately. (The authority for the suspended-sentence rule is fn 1420, “Ibid.” after a Western Australian mandatory-sentencing case: cite it by section and footnote only — flag.ibid_1420_suspended_sentence_attribution.)

title: Pleas to the gravest offending (competing authority); worst murders
statement: Authorities compete: one line gives more weight to a plea the more serious the crime (utilitarian value and sparing victims); more recent authority asks whether the enormity of the criminality means utilitarian benefit must yield to public protection and the rule of law. For the worst murders a plea is generally a necessary condition for fixing a non-parole period, but a plea will not necessarily save a murderer from life imprisonment. (Competing authority: flag.worst_category_plea_competing_authority.)

title: Section 6AAA: stating the notional sentence but for the plea
statement: When the sentence involves a custodial order, an order to serve imprisonment, a CCO of two years or more, a fine over 10 penalty units or an aggregate fine over 20 penalty units, and the plea produced a less severe sentence, the court must state the notional sentence it would have imposed after trial — for the overall sentence (total effective sentence and single non-parole period; an aggregate sentence is a single sentence), including the notional non-parole period — and record it. Where the offender pleaded to only some charges, the Court of Appeal has suggested the statement concern the total effective sentence (the Manual says the position is unclear: flag.s6aaa_mixed_pleas → caution, not error). Where not required, the court may still state it (7.1.4; 2.4.9 fn 361 says “must”: flag.s6aaa_scope_2_4_9_vs_7_1_4). Always state the notional (undiscounted) figures. The plea may change the form of sentence, so the notional sentence may be of a different (more severe) type. Failure to make the statement likely does not invalidate the sentence (7.1.4.6; s 103) — report it as a missing statutory statement, not an unlawful sentence.

title: Section 6AAA: what is quantified and how (no two-tier sentencing)
statement: The court (at least privately) isolates the plea considerations but need not explain the allocation, though where remorse has an important impact it may indicate whether it was treated in the general synthesis or as part of the plea. The notional sentence is a hypothetical post-trial sentence. The preferred Victorian approach is to take each aspect of the plea (utilitarian value, remorse, admissions, offered assistance) together for the reduction, and remorse and contrition keep independent force. Endorsed method: fix the sentence by instinctive synthesis, then estimate how much longer it would have been without the plea (or fix the notional first and subtract); the method is discretionary but must not become two-tier sentencing.

title: Section 6AAA: cooperation undertakings and hypothetical difficulties
statement: Past cooperation is taken into account in the notional sentence; different approaches have been taken for undertakings of future cooperation (unresolved in the Manual: flag.s6aaa_future_cooperation_approaches). Where cooperation and plea are dealt with compendiously, resentencing for failure to cooperate should not increase the sentence by more than part of the discount. The hypothetical is artificial (e.g. sentencing facts may not match a hypothetical trial). Where both s 6AAA and the Commonwealth s 16AC apply, it is not desirable to aggregate the discounts: the processes are better kept separate — the judge assesses what they would have done without the undertaking (the s 16AC specification) and separately identifies the sentence but for the plea. The Court did not say whether the s 16AC specification assumes a plea of guilty or not guilty; the Manual says the disapproval of the aggregate practice suggests the judge should assume a plea of not guilty (Commonwealth; outside the app’s Victorian scope).

title: Section 6AAA: status of the notional sentence on appeal
statement: The notional sentence is not part of the sentence and errors in it are not in themselves appealable. Section 6AAA states no consequence for failing to specify the discount, and the Act’s general rule that a failure to give reasons or comply with another procedural requirement does not invalidate a sentence likely applies; failure to make the declaration is an irregularity that will rarely, if ever, justify interference where sufficient weight was given to the plea. title: Sentence indications (Criminal Procedure Act 2009)
statement: Sentence indications help accused decide early whether to plead guilty. Magistrates’ Court: on its own initiative, once summary jurisdiction is invoked, the magistrate may indicate imprisonment to be served immediately or a sentence of a specified type (type only, not quantum); must not impose a more severe type; another magistrate hears the matter if no plea at the first opportunity (unless parties agree); the application cannot be evidence against the accused. Higher courts: after the indictment is filed, only on the accused’s application with prosecution consent (informal indications are discouraged); a specified type or a specified maximum total effective sentence; no more severe sentence may be imposed. An indication binds only the judicial officer who gave it. Discretion to give one is final (judicial review only); the court may decline for insufficient information on the effect on any victim. A plea after an indication is not necessarily inconsistent with remorse (a question of fact; in NSW such a plea has been given less weight than a plea expressing remorse). For an applicant already in custody, an indication of immediate imprisonment means actual imprisonment from sentence. The binding effect is hard-checked by audit.sentence_indication (intake records the indication and whether the plea was entered on it).

title: Cooperation with authorities: policy and statutory announcement (s 5(2AB))
statement: Encouraging offenders to inform on co-offenders is very much in the public interest. Assistance is considered in mitigation and can produce sentences much lower than otherwise expected — a price society must pay. The discount varies with the level of cooperation, its subjective significance and its actual or potential utility. Section 5(2AB) requires the court to announce that it is imposing a less severe sentence and to have the undertaking and its details noted in the record.

title: Levels of cooperation and the size of the discount (no tariff)
statement: The discount rises or falls with objective and subjective factors: lowest — admissions and a plea; higher — implicating co-offenders, providing information and giving evidence; highest — “true informers” who proactively assist, often undercover and at great risk. Labels matter less than the nature of the assistance and its consequences for the offender. There is no mathematical process, tariff or standard discount; factors include the nature and extent of cooperation, willingness to testify against co-offenders and danger. The Court of Appeal has said the highest level could attract 50% to 66% for a true informer, but each discount must be assessed in context, not mathematically.

title: Assessing the value of cooperation
statement: Assistance is rewarded regardless of motive, though willingness matters (sometimes only voluntary cooperation counts; genuine remorse warrants more). No discount if the offender tailors information to what they know police already have, but not lost if they did not know, if the information proves ineffective, or if authorities do not act on it. The discount is rarely substantial without full disclosure; what matters is the potential to assist as comprehended by the offender. False information earns nothing. Not lost if the person informed on pleads guilty or is acquitted for unrelated reasons. The court does not assess whether the offender will comply with the undertaking.

title: Assistance on other offences or in other jurisdictions (no double counting)
statement: Assistance on other offences may be considered (but earlier informing gives no immunity for later offending); assistance to interstate or international agencies may be reflected, but must not be double counted — if already rewarded elsewhere the discount is exhausted.

title: Risk of reprisal; victims who give evidence
statement: Exposure to retributive violence is a significant component of the discount; it cannot be calibrated precisely but is generally found substantial; whether the cooperation is known or likely to become known may affect the quantum. A victim who gives evidence as a victim earns no discount for separate offending, unless that assistance causes them to serve imprisonment in protective custody. Protective custody because of cooperation also attracts greater leniency as a hardship (hardship.protection_prisoner); the Manual does not address the overlap — (app policy) do not count the same risk or burden twice, and say how each was weighed.

title: Cooperation must be proved (not asserted from the Bar table)
statement: Assistance must appear from or be proved in evidence; Bar-table assertions are not enough even with Crown consent. The offender must establish on the balance of probabilities that assistance was given and its nature and value.

title: Combined plea and cooperation discounts must not produce an inadequate sentence

title: Victorian scheme: announce the reduction for an undertaking to assist; record it
statement: If a less severe sentence is imposed because the offender undertook to assist, the court must announce this and have the undertaking details recorded; non-compliance does not automatically vitiate the sentence but compliance is important. Whether the announcement also extends to past cooperation is unclear in the Manual (7.3.3.1 speaks of an undertaking; 2.4.9 and 7.3.1 of cooperation generally): announce whenever cooperation (past or promised) produced a less severe sentence; error only where an undertaking-based reduction is not announced (flag.s5_2AB_past_vs_future_cooperation; hard-checked by audit.cooperation_statement). The sentence that would otherwise have been imposed need not be stated, and stating it is undesirable except in the simplest cases.

title: Failure to fulfil an undertaking: Crown appeal and resentencing
statement: Failure to fulfil an undertaking that produced a benefit can ground a Crown appeal; in Victoria the appellate court may impose the sentence it considers appropriate. Resentencing does not punish the failure but imposes the sentence that would have been imposed without the offer to cooperate (and may restore the original value of other considerations that were reduced).

title: Prevalence (a circumstance of other offences)
statement: Prevalence is neither a circumstance of the offence nor of the offender. It need not be proved beyond reasonable doubt, but the court should be sure of it before weighting the synthesis toward general deterrence and giving less weight to mitigation; even then an increase is not inevitable. The court may use general knowledge, but special knowledge must be disclosed with an opportunity to address it; the better view is that any reliance requires procedural fairness and disclosure of the source. Prevalence principles are engaged only if it is used to aggravate. Recent cases focus on the content of the offending (examples below) rather than locality or ethnic community (an exception: more current references to young people committing high volumes of violent crimes, fn 1561). It operates alongside seriousness to increase the importance of general deterrence. The Manual says the material or evidentiary foundation sufficient for a finding of prevalence remains unresolved (evidence or official statistics may be tendered; earlier cases treated some offences as so notoriously prevalent that no proof or prior canvassing was needed): flag.prevalence_evidentiary_foundation. (app policy) Do not aggravate for prevalence without a disclosed source and an opportunity to be heard. The standard is that the court be “sure” (not proof beyond reasonable doubt). The authority for “a circumstance of other offences” (fn 1551, “Ibid.”) is cited by section and footnote only (flag.ibid_1551_prevalence_attribution).

title: Delay: the unfairness limb and the rehabilitation limb
statement: Significant delay (interview to charge; charge to trial) can be a powerful mitigating factor, but there is no automatic discount; undue prosecution delay makes a discount much more likely. Two limbs: unfairness (anxiety of a charge hanging over the offender — not eliminated by failure to confess undisclosed offences) and rehabilitation (progress during the delay and good prospects). Their operation depends on cause, length and consequences, with understanding and flexibility. Some evidence is required for either limb (a psychological report may support anxiety, though anxiety may sometimes be accepted without it); full weight on the rehabilitation limb requires both remorse and rehabilitation — mere non-offending is relevant but not in itself sufficient (it attracts less than full weight). Delay affects both head sentence and non-parole period (not as an application of totality). Reasons should refer to delay, and mentioning only one limb may suggest the other was ignored.

title: Delay: when it is “undue” and who is responsible
statement: Delay need not be inordinate; if unduly long it may and often will mitigate. Whether undue depends on elapsed time, the nature/complexity/sophistication of the offence, the investigation required, the period of a series of offences and the offender’s cooperation or obstruction — a matter of degree and common sense. In sexual abuse cases delay in detection or complaint is common and often cannot be relied on. Delay mitigates most where the offender is not responsible: contesting charges is never the offender’s fault, but a late plea after asserting a trial against an overwhelming case cannot be used to claim delay; delay attributable to the offender (absconding, non-cooperation, inaction) gets less significance (an absconder’s rehabilitation may still be reflected in a shorter non-parole period). Witness fear of the accused may make delay not undue (the court may still take rehabilitation into account). Plea negotiations do not necessarily disentitle the offender unless used as a deliberate delaying tactic (such cases are likely rare; but see Ververis, fn 1599); challenging the validity of legislation does not reduce it. Delay caused by prosecution or system is more likely to be major (authorities must act promptly); where delay is relied on as unfairness rather than as harm to the offender, prosecution or investigator responsibility assumes greater significance. Where offending over a long period required long and complex investigations, the weight of delay may be reduced (fn 1586). Trial length generally does not mitigate unless extraordinary. Lack of explanation does not of itself justify a greater reduction.

title: Delay: consequences (additional punishment, rehabilitation, change of regime)
statement: Unfairness limb: delay may be additional punishment or unfairness requiring compensation (natural anxiety until arraignment; ordinarily mitigating if unduly long), including a life put “on hold” after an early plea where imprisonment is likely, or strict bail conditions (curfew) during lengthy delay. Rehabilitation limb: full weight requires both remorse and reformation (less for mere non-offending); delay mitigates where there has been a substantial positive change; where rehabilitation is achieved, the focus may move to preserving progress; prospective rehabilitation may authorise a merciful approach and point to a rehabilitative disposition or earlier return to the community; the longer the non-offending, the better the prospects; ageing, onerousness of prison and genuine remorse may also arise. Structural: delay that makes a person who offended as a child liable to the adult regime may mitigate where there is a significant degree of rehabilitation and no further offending; similarly, delay that precludes the youth justice system may mitigate (less weight if a youth sentence would not have been open given gravity).

title: Hardship of sanction: three limbs; exceptionality only for hardship to family
statement: Hardship measures the consequence of the sanction on the offender given their circumstances. It may be experienced by (1) the offender personally, (2) the offender’s family or associates, (3) the offender through responsibility for family hardship. Limbs 1 and 3 need no exceptional hardship; limb 2 requires exceptional circumstances (7.6) — but see 7.6.4: for Victorian offences the test now appears to be hardship rising above the general hardship suffered by prisoners’ families and so significant that it will weigh heavily (flag.third_party_hardship_exceptionality: where mitigation rests on that formulation with cogent evidence, caution rather than fail). The Act provides for hardship in recording a conviction; other hardship is a common law consideration.

title: Protective custody
statement: Protective custody (informers, child sex offenders, former police) is relevant; weight depends on why protection is needed, the circumstances, likely duration and the actual effect (regimes vary from near-solitary to little hardship). Both counsel should provide information on the true conditions. Informers get more leniency than other protection prisoners. A real risk that threats will be carried out requires adjustment, assessed within the instinctive synthesis (not as a departure from an otherwise appropriate sanction). No significance if placement within the system results from the offender’s own past conduct (e.g. violence towards others, drug use, refusing to comply with the ordinary standards needed to keep prison safe). Where protection results from cooperation, see also coop.risk_to_offender (do not count the same risk twice).

title: Separation from family (offender’s own anguish)
statement: Anguish at being unable to care for a family member may mitigate if it makes imprisonment more burdensome or materially affects specific deterrence or rehabilitation; weight depends on the circumstances and can never produce a sentence inappropriate to the gravity. Incarceration commonly involves some separation from family, so this hardship is relevant only in limited circumstances. The Corrections Act allows the Secretary to let a parent have a child live with them in prison.

title: Hardship of imprisonment from age or ill health
statement: If age directly affects the hardship of imprisonment it may mitigate; deal with old age and ill health separately, as age alone is not mitigating in this sense; an elderly adult may not be a suitable subject for parole. Ill health counts where it directly increases hardship (examples include lung cancer with a short prognosis allowing a non-parole adjustment for immediate release); custodial disruptions for health care and a brain injury have been held insufficient. Mental illness or impairment and poor physical health are among the most significant causes of an increased burden of imprisonment; the main treatment is in 6.2 (factor.physical_health; the Verdins items).

title: Foreign nationals; religion
statement: A foreign national far from family support finds prison more burdensome — always relevant, weight varying with language and cultural differences, the offending and family ties. Ordinarily little weight if the offender came to Australia intending to offend, and it may also be given little weight if they opportunistically offended while visiting for an innocent purpose; a court may give it greater weight for a lawful visitor who offends through gross negligence (e.g. culpable driving); hardship is generally greater for offenders from vastly different countries (isolation). Religious practices likely to make the offender a target may be considered.

title: Pregnancy; transgender prisoners
statement: Gender alone is no basis for differential treatment, but pregnancy may make custody more onerous and should be considered (it may not avoid custody or shorten a sentence justice requires). A shorter term may be necessary for a transgender woman at risk and under protection in a men’s prison; prison is generally more onerous for transgender prisoners.

title: Prospect of deportation
statement: Likely deportation is relevant if it makes imprisonment more onerous or loses the chance to settle permanently, depending on personal circumstances and actual hardship; limited weight for particularly serious offending; visa cancellation and deportation are not extra-curial punishment. Evidence of both the likely risk and its impact is required, sufficient for sensible quantification; a reduction is appropriate if certain, and may be if probable. Without evidence or a concession the court need not consider it, but mandatory cancellation triggered by the sentence (the Migration Act does so for a sentence of one year or more, subject to revocation) lifts it above speculation. Unusual connections to Australia should be considered. It is error to artificially lower a sentence to avoid the Migration Act. Offence-specific mandatory cancellation (e.g. child sex offences) does not remove deportation as a consideration.

title: Fresh evidence of hardship in custody (appeals)
statement: New evidence may be admitted on appeal if it relates to events since sentence and shows the true significance of facts existing at sentence, but not if it only shows the sentence turned out to be excessive.
