title: Hardship to family or third parties (exceptional circumstances)
statement: Third-party hardship is not normally mitigating, but the court may mitigate if satisfied there are exceptional circumstances. The Court of Appeal previously described the Victorian test as “highly exceptional” or where mercy is irresistible; it appears now that for Victorian offences the circumstances must rise above the general (sometimes tragic) hardship commonly suffered by prisoners’ families and be so significant they will weigh heavily (flag.third_party_hardship_exceptionality). Generally only for especially vulnerable dependants (or several). Requires cogent evidence (possibly a combination of lesser hardships); rare; a question of fact and degree. Not a “passport to freedom”; may affect type and quantum of sentence and ameliorative orders; a reduction must be capable of ameliorating the hardship.

title: COVID-19 custodial conditions
statement: The Manual records that courts should be mindful, “in the present time”, that pandemic measures made custody significantly more restrictive, so time in custody has been and is likely to continue to be significantly more punitive than its numerical equivalent. (Elsewhere, in the guilty plea context, the Manual notes that as at the end of 2023 the pandemic’s effects on the Victorian criminal justice system had subsided.)

title: Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders as punishment (totality)
statement: Totality generally requires account of all punishment, including ancillary punishment, subject to legislative exceptions. Confiscation may be punitive and considered; compensation and restitution orders are not punitive and are not considered. Forfeiture that merely disgorges profit is not considered (the Act); forfeiture going further, or of previously owned property, may be. Proportionality requires the nature and extent of forfeiture to be considered, but it does not require mitigation: consider whether it has a disproportionate or exceptional effect and a substantial deterrent effect. Future forfeiture may be considered with sufficient evidence. The offender bears the onus: evidence enabling a positive finding on the balance of probabilities (direct evidence from the offender plus confirmation of the lawful source of funds; a solicitor relaying assertions is not enough). Totality generally requires account of all punishment, including ancillary punishment, subject to legislative exceptions. Confiscation may be punitive and considered; compensation and restitution orders are not punitive and are not considered. Forfeiture that merely disgorges profit is not considered (the Act); forfeiture going further, or of previously owned property, may be. Proportionality requires the nature and extent of forfeiture to be considered, but it does not require mitigation: consider whether it has a disproportionate or exceptional effect and a substantial deterrent effect. Future forfeiture may be considered with sufficient evidence. The offender bears the onus: evidence enabling a positive finding on the balance of probabilities (direct evidence from the offender plus confirmation of the lawful source of funds; a solicitor relaying assertions is not enough). title: Consequences under sex offender registration and working with children laws are not considered
statement: The court must not consider any consequence under the Sex Offenders Registration Act 2004 or the Working With Children Act 2005 arising from the sentence, whether automatic or by court order.

title: Continuing detention orders (Commonwealth terrorism regime)
statement: Commonwealth continuing detention orders (Criminal Code s 105A.3) may require an offender convicted of, generally speaking, terrorism-related offences to be detained after their sentence ends, if they are serving imprisonment and will be at least 18 when it ends, or are under a continuing or interim detention order; an order lasts at most three years, though successive orders may be made, and a court sentencing for a terrorism-related offence must warn the offender that an application may be made (s 105A.23). For sentencing they are of marginal relevance: they should not reduce the sentence through their effect on community protection; hardship should not be presumed from the prospect of an application; and they are an unavoidable consequence of imprisonment not given special mitigatory weight. (Commonwealth regime; outside the app’s Victorian scope.)

title: Public opprobrium and loss of career
statement: Loss of reputation may be punishment, but it is unclear whether opprobrium from conviction may be considered (tension with the offender’s position of privilege or power; flag.public_opprobrium_unclear → caution). title: Injury or loss suffered by the offender in the offending (extra-curial punishment)
statement: Injury or loss suffered in or as a direct consequence of the offending is generally taken into account (self-infliction is not a complete answer), but not in every case. It takes its place in the synthesis, bearing on just punishment, weight of remorse, and deterrence. To mitigate it must add to the burden of imprisonment and constitute extra-curial punishment (the test is framed for custody; for non-custodial outcomes its application is unclear — flag.extra_curial_test_scope: caution). Mental illness counts only in strictly limited circumstances: illness caused by the offender’s reaction to the consequences of offending (e.g. fear of prison) is not additional punishment. Counter-example: in R v Taylor a claimed sexually transmitted disease contracted in committing rape was not taken into account.

title: The plea: committal warning; encouragement; the “illogicality” with not-guilty pleas
statement: On committal for trial the magistrate must inform the accused that the sentencing court may consider any plea and its timing. The Manual notes a “certain illogicality” between the plea discount and the rule that a not guilty plea is never aggravating.

title: Plea and other mitigation under a mandatory minimum: little authority
statement: A mandatory minimum can complicate reductions for mitigating factors, including the plea: a minimum regime does not oust common law principles but modifies them, and there is little authority on mitigation in mandatory regimes. A plea cannot itself take the sentence below a statutory minimum: an early guilty plea may not be considered in deciding whether there are substantial and compelling reasons (the fourth special reason), and none of the other three special reasons concerns a plea (mm.special_reason). (app policy) How mitigation operates above the minimum is an evaluative matter: the reasoning should say how it applied it.

title: Section 6AAA: transparency, artificiality, and the effect of non-compliance
statement: The common law requires the justification for a sentence reduction to be transparent. Questions remain about which aspects of the plea are quantified (utilitarian value alone, or remorse and acceptance of responsibility too); in Victoria the preference is to take each aspect of the plea together (s6aaa.method). The Court of Appeal has noted the artificiality of the hypothetical post-trial sentence. Section 6AAA states no consequence for failing to specify the discount, and the Act provides that failing to give reasons or comply with another procedural requirement does not invalidate a sentence; but the Court of Appeal has used the s 6AAA statement, with other factors, to find error.

title: Sentence indications: when they can be given and whom they bind
statement: A magistrate’s power to indicate is engaged only once summary jurisdiction has been invoked. An indication binds only the judicial officer who gave it, not a hearing before a different judge or magistrate; the court may impose a less severe sentence type or total effective sentence than indicated. Courts generally decline to indicate where the decision turns on material not yet before them; the express reference to victim impact does not displace the other mandatory considerations.

title: Cooperation: known witnesses face greater risk; protection-prisoner classes differ
statement: It has been said that an offender who undertakes to give evidence becomes a known offender facing a notorious and grave risk of reprisal, unlike one whose assistance is unknown. Protection prisoners are not treated equally: more leniency is given to a prisoner in protection because of cooperation than to others (e.g. corrupt police officers, sex offenders). The risk to informers can never be accurately measured, but where there is a real risk the court must adjust the sentence (this is not bowing to criminals), within the instinctive synthesis — not by fixing a sentence and then departing from it.

title: Prevalence: procedural fairness has displaced the “notorious prevalence” cases
statement: Earlier cases said the prevalence of some offences was so notorious that no proof or prior canvassing was required; the better view now is that any reliance on prevalence requires procedural fairness and disclosure of the source of the reasoning.

title: Delay: the incongruity of systemic delay; prospective rehabilitation
statement: It is incongruous to say an offence is so serious that stern sentences are needed while sanctioning a leisurely progression of proceedings over years. Prospective rehabilitation during delay may warrant mitigation by a merciful approach and a disposition directed at rehabilitation or an earlier return to the community.

title: Fresh evidence of hardship on appeal: examples; family hardship cases
statement: Fresh evidence of hardship may be admitted on appeal where it shows the true significance of facts existing at sentence — e.g. an assault on an informer after incarceration showing the risk had eventuated, or a significant medical diagnosis that increases the burden of imprisonment and the risk of a gravely adverse effect on health. The decided third-party hardship cases concern mostly hardship to the offender’s family from imprisonment.

title: Forfeiture as punishment: proceeds vs punitive forfeiture; future forfeiture; tainted property
statement: Forfeiting proceeds of crime restores the offender’s prior position and is not punishment; an order going beyond that (or relating to previously owned property) may be punitive and considered — a “clear distinction”. Future forfeiture may be taken into account if there is enough evidence to assess its likelihood and effect; if not, there is no error in disregarding it. The offender bears the onus; for lawfully acquired “tainted” property the punitive element must be sufficiently identified.

title: Murder: the most serious offence
statement: Murder is the most serious offence: its deliberate taking of life is always a matter of the utmost seriousness, and anyone who contemplates an unlawful killing must anticipate that the penalty may be severe. (That passage is about murder; the other chapter-21 offences — notably infanticide, with its own regime and 5-year maximum — are assessed under their own items.) Chapter 21 covers murder (intentional and reckless), statutory murder, defensive homicide, infanticide, attempted murder and incitement to murder.

title: Murder: current sentencing practices
statement: Practices for murder have steadily increased. A guilty plea to murder is generally accepted to attract a non-parole period. Inciting the murder of a partner, former partner or family member is an extreme form of family violence whose gravity is not reflected in current practices, which should increase.

title: Murder: purposes
statement: The court must denounce and condemn the conduct, impose just punishment, vindicate the rights of the deceased and acknowledge the grief and trauma of those left behind; general deterrence is important. A murder to punish or take revenge on someone who assisted law enforcement calls for punishment and denunciation of a very high order.

title: Statutory murder (unintentional killing in furtherance of a crime of violence)
statement: Statutory murder is not inherently less serious than common law murder and may be more serious than some instances of it. It covers a wide range (from accidental death to intended death); the issue is the nature of the violent act and the offender’s state of mind when committing it. The characterisation of a type of murder is not determinative of objective gravity (fn 3320). The Manual adds that “It ‘has no bearing on the sentencing outcome’” without making clear what “It” refers to (presumably the statutory rather than common-law classification). (See csp.uplift_statutory_murder.)

title: Reckless murder
statement: Reckless murder may be regarded as seriously as intentional murder and is not necessarily of lesser seriousness or culpability.

title: Defensive homicide (abolished offence)
statement: Defensive homicide is serious (intentional taking of life; maximum 20 years). Seriousness is usually assessed by the disproportion between the perceived threat and the response. That is difficult in the family violence context, where the legislation allows reasonable grounds for believing the conduct necessary even if it involves excessive force or the victim is not the person posing the threat (and, e.g., a woman “invariably uses a weapon” and may strike multiple times); outside that context multiple strikes in response to a verbal or minor physical attack may make it a very serious example. The critical question is what inference to draw about state of mind. The authority for several of these propositions (fns 3329–3331) is uncertain (flag.ibid_chain_21_2_4).

title: Infanticide
statement: Infanticide requires that the balance of the woman’s mind was disturbed by a disorder consequent on giving birth within the preceding two years; sentence is fixed by reference to the five-year maximum and the nature and gravity of the disturbance. Acceptance of an infanticide plea does not affect sentences for other offences committed at the same time, which follow their own maxima and Verdins: although the same evidence will likely be considered, sentencing for the other offences is not informed by the unique infanticide regime. Labels like “very serious example” should not be applied simplistically.

title: Attempted murder
statement: Attempted murder requires a specific intent to kill; there is no specific practical ceiling below the maximum — each case turns on its facts, given the seriousness of the offence and the maximum penalty; gravity is assessed by reference to the murderous intent. Family violence, an informer victim, or catastrophic injuries can aggravate; those who attempt to kill a former partner, or those close to one, must expect very substantial sentences (Malovski, fn 3313).

title: Incitement to murder
statement: Seriousness depends on the crime incited; incitement to murder is a special, serious category that may call for more punishment than some murders; the circumstances giving rise to it must be considered. Inciting the murder of a partner is an extreme form of family violence: sentences must increase and culpability will typically be high.

title: Murder: aggravating circumstances (location, manner of death, post-offence conduct, domestic killings)
statement: These are possible aggravating circumstances that may lead to a more severe sentence. The location is frequently important: a killing in the victim’s home may aggravate; a stranger killing in a family home with children present is particularly serious; killings in public places endangering ordinary members of the community, or in remote locations, can aggravate. A more severe sentence usually follows a particularly painful or degrading death: prolonged and excruciating death, torture, a particularly callous or cold-blooded killing, sexual defilement of the body, mutilation or dismemberment; failing to reveal or hiding the remains may significantly aggravate. Domestic or relationship killings are particularly grave; breach of an intervention order is a serious aggravating feature.

title: Murder: life imprisonment without parole; fixing a non-parole period
statement: Life without parole is an exceptional step and a dreadful punishment, imposed in a handful of Victorian cases, typically for the most dreadful crimes given the offence and history; only three cases involved a guilty plea. Youth is not a bar, but life for a young offender is a grave step. Additional imprisonment for a person already sentenced to, or serving, life can only be concurrent (hard-checked: cum.life_parole). No type of murder automatically warrants life; the case usually must be in the worst category for that type of killing; those who kill a number of victims in horrendous circumstances, with no substantial factor of clemency, must in general expect to be seriously considered for the possible imposition of life without parole. Non-parole periods have generally been fixed on life sentences for murder (even with prior murder convictions); declining one removes a major incentive to rehabilitation.

title: Manslaughter, child homicide and homicide by firearm: scope
statement: Manslaughter comprises unlawful and dangerous act, criminal negligence and suicide pact manslaughter — three disparate offences involving a killing in circumstances not treated as murder. Child homicide (victim under six) and homicide by firearm (death caused by discharge of a firearm) are analogous statutory offences. Culpable and dangerous driving causing death are in ch 23; workplace manslaughter in ch 31. Schemes: common-law manslaughter (unlawful and dangerous act or criminal negligence) is not a “serious violent offence”, but it is a “serious offence” and may attract an indefinite sentence (22.1.1). Where the offender was 18 or older (Category 2), manslaughter and child homicide committed on or after 20 March 2017, and homicide by firearm committed on or after 1 July 2020, require a custodial sentence (other than imprisonment combined with a CCO) unless specified circumstances exist (offence register; cat2.custodial_unless; flag.suicide_pact_category2).

title: Manslaughter: current practices (increased maximum; limited use of comparisons and statistics)
statement: Generally, sentences for all forms of manslaughter have significantly increased since 2011, and on 1 July 2020 the maximum rose from 20 to 25 years, suggesting past sentences were inadequate. Current practice is hard to use given the vastly different circumstances and wide ranges; statistics are of little utility, especially where they do not distinguish intentional from negligent manslaughter or identify the bases of sentences.

title: Child homicide: current practices
statement: Circumstances and sentences vary, though probably less so because every victim is under six. When introducing it, the Attorney-General explained the offence responds to concerns about the perceived inadequacy of sentences for the manslaughter of young children, highlighting the victim’s age and vulnerability and freeing courts from past practices while generally being guided by them. The Court of Appeal (Woodford) held it does not require punishment closer to the maximum than past young-child manslaughter cases, but it uncoupled child homicide sentences from constraint by current manslaughter practices. Caveat (fn 3396): after Dalgliesh the limiting effect of past manslaughter practice is further reduced, and since Woodford Parliament has increased the child-homicide maximum, indicating a perceived insufficiency in existing sentences.

title: Manslaughter: gravity and culpability factors
statement: Manslaughter is extremely serious (unlawful taking of life, the key element), and sentencing is highly fact-specific along a spectrum. Unlawful and dangerous act manslaughter is generally more serious than negligent manslaughter, but not as a fixed rule. Factors listed below. “Failing to explain the killing or its circumstances” may bear on how the circumstances are assessed; (app policy, flag.failing_to_explain_killing) the offender’s silence is not treated as aggravating (where facts are disputed, 2.2.2.2.1 permits no adverse inference from a failure to give evidence on the plea save in rare and exceptional circumstances). Historically (before 23 November 2005), provocation manslaughter was regarded as generally more serious than unlawful and dangerous act manslaughter (fn 3403).

title: Unlawful and dangerous act manslaughter (including single-punch killings)
statement: Gravity also depends on the gravity of the underlying unlawful act, its dangerousness and the offender’s subjective awareness of the danger; the more dangerous the act, the more serious. A single-punch killing may be a serious example (knowledge that punching toward the head is inherently dangerous; see also the single-punch minimum, mmnpp.manslaughter_10y). Comparisons with the abolished defensive homicide offence require care: defensive homicide required an intent to kill or cause really serious injury (or recklessness), whereas this form of manslaughter requires neither intent.

Unlawful and dangerous act manslaughter (including single-punch killings)
Gravity also depends on the gravity of the underlying unlawful act, its dangerousness and the offender’s subjective awareness of the danger; the more dangerous the act, the more serious. A single-punch killing may be a serious example (knowledge that punching toward the head is inherently dangerous; see also the single-punch minimum, mmnpp.manslaughter_10y). Comparisons with the abolished defensive homicide offence require care: defensive homicide required an intent to kill or cause really serious injury (or recklessness), whereas this form of manslaughter requires neither intent.

title: Manslaughter by criminal negligence
statement: Relatively unusual; occurs where conduct falls so far short of the standard of care, with such high risk of death or serious injury, that criminal punishment is merited; failing to summon medical assistance may reach this standard where a duty of care is owed (e.g. parent to child; a person who caused the injury). Culpability rises with the degree of negligence and the length of inaction. Usually less culpable than unlawful and dangerous act manslaughter (the negligent offender will not have intended to kill or harm, whereas the other usually, but not always, intends at least harm), but not inflexibly. Child homicide and homicide by firearm committed by criminal negligence are linked here (link_conditions). The Manual notes contrary authority on when a duty is owed to an adult (fn 3432) and on the lower culpability of negligent killers (fn 3436): flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6.

title: Child homicide: gravity, purposes and burden of custody
statement: Child homicide has the elements of manslaughter with a victim under six; the age is central (a young and vulnerable victim has always been a significant aggravating factor in violent manslaughter). It is serious, more so where committed by someone entrusted with the child’s care. Where death results from excessive corporal punishment, the offender’s right to use such punishment may mitigate; excessive punishment by a person who knows they have no right is a more serious example. Anger and frustration may explain the context but do not mitigate (but see Vinaccia, fn 3445). Courts must send a strong message that significant deprivation of liberty will follow. Imprisonment may be more burdensome (likely protective custody); the weight depends on the actual conditions (hardship.protection_prisoner).

title: Homicide by firearm: gravity (standard sentence 13 years)
statement: A statutory offence created on 1 July 2020 with a standard sentence of 13 years; it has the elements of manslaughter except that death must be caused by the discharge of a firearm. The dangerousness of the use of the firearm is likely to be central. When introducing it, the Attorney-General indicated it is more serious where it would amount to murder but for the inability to prove intent due to lack of witnesses, or where death resulted from the dangerous handling of a firearm (extrinsic material, not a settled gravity rule).

title: Provocation and excessive self-defence in homicide sentencing
statement: Provocation can no longer reduce murder to manslaughter but remains a sentencing consideration (a person who forms an intention to kill or cause really serious injury after being provoked is sentenced for murder: fn 3453). Its relevance depends on its degree (low provocation increases gravity toward the confines of murder; great provocation reduces it; the court may look at an entire course of conduct, not just a “triggering event”: fn 3456) and the time to loss of control (if short, this may reduce gravity and culpability). As a sentencing factor it is not limited by the old common law test, though it appears that meeting that test gives it more weight. It is likely to be of limited relevance where the offender previously used domestic violence against the victim (deterrence, denunciation and just punishment remain primary), but likely relevant where the provocation was a further instance of domestic violence by the victim (but see Edwards, fn 3463: culpability is not lessened where the offender was equally or more abusive). Excessive self-defence remains relevant (in its own right or under cover of provocation); where there is a history of family violence it must be approached with caution, especially where the offender acted from anger rather than fear. Historically (before 23 November 2005) “provocation manslaughter” was usually seen as the most serious form of manslaughter. In causing-injury cases the Manual states provocation more narrowly (flag.provocation_injury_vs_homicide).

title: Manslaughter: purposes (and the suicide pact exception)
statement: Deterrence, denunciation and just punishment are the principal purposes, particularly for domestic or family violence, alcohol or drug fuelled public violence, one-punch attacks, weapon use (or use without proper safety), and child homicide; in those circumstances there is a particular need for the sentence to make clear that violence is intolerable (the strongest denunciation and stern punishment). Moral culpability is reduced where the offender was provoked against a history of domestic violence, but that does not remove the importance of general deterrence, just punishment and denunciation; even then a killing must be denounced and usually result in imprisonment (the Manual notes contrary authority: fn 3473, flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6). Suicide pact manslaughter is an exception: specific deterrence, denunciation and just punishment are lessened; general deterrence remains significant; mercy may permit a non-custodial sentence (Rolfe, 2008). Caution: for an adult offender and offending on or after 20 March 2017, whether suicide pact manslaughter is within Category 2 is unresolved in the Manual (flag.suicide_pact_category2).

title: Indictable driving offences: current practice
statement: Driving offences causing death or serious injury are very serious; absent exceptional circumstances a substantial custodial sentence is required for general and specific deterrence, community protection and just punishment. A non-custodial sentence may be available where moral culpability is exceptionally low; ten years for single-fatality culpable driving invites scrutiny though may be within range for very grave offending. Practices for dangerous driving causing death were held inadequate (2016) and the increase is not to be gradual.

title: Driving offences: aggravating features (Whyte and Victorian additions) — not a checklist
statement: Victorian courts apply R v Whyte (NSW guideline) to gravity of driving offences causing death or serious injury. The non-exhaustive features below may aggravate, but they are not a checklist: absence of some does not mean a case cannot be serious. Intoxication: alcohol or drug use may not be treated as aggravating culpable driving established under s 318(2)(c) or (d) (it is the basis of culpability), but may aggravate where culpability is under s 318(2)(b); the absence of alcohol or drugs may sometimes worsen the conduct (wilful disregard of road laws) (fn 3494). Comparables: NSW guidance on principles is useful, but NSW guidance on the length of custodial sentences is unhelpful in Victoria (different maximum penalties; some Victorian culpable driving may be charged as manslaughter in NSW) (fn 3492).

title: Culpable driving causing death: forms of culpability; responsibility and causation
statement: Four forms: recklessness; gross negligence; alcohol, or a drug, to the extent of being incapable of proper control. There is no inherent distinction between negligence from intoxication and other negligence (mobile phone, fatigue), and no statutory hierarchy: gravity depends on the facts, and some gross negligence may be more serious than recklessness. For gross negligence, start with whether the offender was solely responsible for the manner of driving and whether it was the sole cause of death, and whether another’s conduct qualified either. The offender may qualify moral culpability by establishing that another person or an external circumstance was partly responsible for the decision to drive or the manner of driving, and causation by showing something else, outside their control, that was also a material cause of death. A passenger’s willingness to travel with an intoxicated or fatigued driver does not by itself make this showing; distraction by a passenger has limited mitigating effect. A victim not wearing a seatbelt will usually not, on its own, qualify causation (it must be shown on the balance of probabilities it would have prevented death, and even then weight is relatively modest; drivers are responsible for passengers’ seatbelts; compare the NCSI-by-driving treatment, guide.injury.ncsi_driving_gravity). Alcohol or drug use may not aggravate culpable driving under s 318(2)(c)–(d), but may under s 318(2)(b) (fn 3494).

title: Dangerous driving causing death or serious injury; negligently causing serious injury by driving
statement: Dangerous driving causing death or serious injury is inherently serious, ordinarily attracting significant imprisonment. Dangerous driving causing death and negligently causing serious injury share a maximum (10 years; dangerous driving causing serious injury is 5 years); because negligent conduct is often more serious than dangerous driving conduct, the two may be regarded as similarly serious. Gravity turns on moral culpability and objective dangerousness (and, for serious injury, the extent of injuries); the extent to which the offender should have foreseen the consequences informs moral culpability. Culpability is higher where risks were known, lower for momentary inattention or misjudgment or external contributing circumstances (e.g. poor intersection design). Ask what degree of care and alertness was reasonably expected; dangerousness reflects the likelihood of something going wrong and the extent of resulting harm.

title: Failing to stop or render assistance after an accident causing death or serious injury
statement: For the s 61 offences (driver of the motor vehicle, s 61(3)) the maximum rose from 80 penalty units or two years to 10 years, a fivefold increase signalling markedly greater gravity (the s 61A(3) offence — driver of the other vehicle — has a Level 6, 5-year maximum in the register). Offences under s 61(3) are intended to deter fleeing the scene; excuses usually carry no weight, and failing to stop because of the quality of driving or capacity to drive aggravates. Rarely, the reason may mitigate (e.g. PTSD-driven panic; leaving to get help for an injured passenger; fear for physical safety). Promptly reporting to police (e.g. 15 minutes later) may mitigate as the main benefit (avoiding detection) is lost. It is error to consider grief and loss from a death where the offender is not convicted of an offence about the manner of driving. For s 61(3) the licence must be cancelled with a minimum disqualification (first offence: at least 4 years if a conviction is recorded, 2 years otherwise; subsequent offence: at least 8 years, or 4 years) — enforced by audit.mandatory_ancillary_orders.

title: Driving offences: purposes; reduced weight of youth, good character and remorse; driving record
statement: General deterrence is often the principal consideration; the seriousness and need for deterrence mean youth, good character and remorse carry less mitigating weight. In culpable and dangerous driving cases a poor driving record (especially serious driving offences, drug/alcohol driving, disqualified driving) is important, affecting moral culpability, rehabilitation, specific deterrence, community protection and denunciation — but prior convictions cannot be used in aggravation to increase the sentence (factor.prior_and_subsequent_convictions). Community protection is usually significant, but less so where fatigue rather than speed, drugs, alcohol or deliberate wrong-side (“hooning”) driving triggered the offence.

title: Driving offences: multiple victims, cumulation and double punishment
statement: Avoid double punishment while recognising each victim: consider whether deaths or injuries arose from one course of driving; whether an act or omission forms part of more than one offence; order cumulation for different incidents, offences and victims; ensure each victim is recognised in the total and non-parole period (not a “meaningless statistic” — 50% cumulation for a second culpable driving victim is not uncommon); keep within totality. A single failure to stop affecting two victims is one act; separate failures to assist are separate acts (in Vasilevski the Court said it may have been more appropriate to cumulate on the failure to assist charges and little or none on the failure to stop charges, but refused leave because the total was appropriate and recognised both victims). Significant cumulation is required where offences from one accident are very different (e.g. dangerous driving and failing to stop).

title: Culpable driving by alcohol/drugs plus a related summary offence: wholly concurrent
statement: Where culpable driving is by intoxication (s 318(2)(c)–(d)), additionally punishing a related summary offence such as exceeding the prescribed blood alcohol concentration is double punishment; sentences should be wholly concurrent. This does not arise for other forms of culpable driving or for dangerous driving.

title: Sexual offences: the maximum is fixed by the offence date (not a later increase; a later reduction applies)
statement: Sexual offences are often prosecuted years later; the Manual says the relevant maximum is the one in force at the time of offending, not at sentence, and that this is a common area of mistake. Read with 5.1.3, a later increase is disregarded but a later reduction must be applied (unless the maximum was reduced and then increased again before sentence to the same magnitude or higher, when the court may apply the original maximum: 5.1.3; audit.maximum_applicable (2)) (historic sexual-offence tables include reductions, e.g. Level 6 from 7½ to 5 years on 1 September 1997). The Manual does not reconcile the two statements (flag.maximum_at_offence_vs_later_reduction); audit.maximum_applicable applies 5.1.3.

statement: Sentences for serious sexual offences have increased, most significantly for rape and incest, following Dalgliesh (practices for incest inadequate; current practices not controlling).

title: Historic sexual offences: practices at sentence, equal justice and the old maximum
statement: Many sex offences are prosecuted years after they occurred. “Current sentencing practices” are those at sentence, and contemporary understanding of the impact on victims may be applied. Equal justice also requires regard to practices at the time of offending if it can be shown they would have required a materially lesser sentence; but if the offender’s own conduct made contemporaneous sentencing impossible, they may not be able to contend they should be treated as if responsibility had been established then. Practices are only one factor; past cases are not precedents and may not show a material difference. (The historical-practice inquiry is not an inflexible rule and applies only if reasonably practicable: csp.historic_offences.) The Manual notes a tension between these requirements and the need to consider them in light of the maximum in force at the time of offending — an area where care is required (guide.sexual.maximum_at_offence_date).

title: Sexual offences against adults: rape ordinarily attracts immediate custody
statement: Absent exceptional circumstances, rape usually attracts immediate custody with a substantial part actually served. Rape covers a wide spectrum; factors (usually in combination) such as an early plea, diminished culpability, genuine remorse and victim support or forgiveness may be exceptional and justify a suspended, non-custodial or substantially reduced term. Caution: the Manual states this without date limits, but rape is a Category 1 offence for an adult offender (custodial sentence required for offences on or after 20 March 2017) and suspended sentences have been progressively abolished since 1 May 2011 — a suspended or non-custodial term is open only outside those schemes; the hard checks govern (flag.rape_noncustodial_vs_category1). Other adult sexual offences have a wider range and little guidance; sentences imposed alongside more serious offences may be of little guidance.

title: Sexual offences against children: imprisonment is justified; non-custodial terms rare
statement: Sexual offending against children, particularly in the offender’s care, is a gross breach of trust justifying imprisonment; there is no tariff, but non-custodial terms are likely rare and particularly inappropriate for many victims over a long period. The same physical acts do not make cases relevantly comparable. For the Category 1 child offences (those marked “#” in 24.1.2) a non-custodial term is not available for an adult offender at all (cat1.custodial_required).

title: Incest: “dramatic change in sentencing parameters”
statement: In 2016 the Court of Appeal and the High Court found mid-range incest sentences disproportionately low (three years six months for incest resulting in pregnancy was given as inadequate); for incest in the mid-range of seriousness, sentencing must now take into account the dramatic change in sentencing parameters. Longer sentences involve long periods, younger children or multiple victims, threats or violence, or multifaceted, perverse or depraved offending; planned offending to capture child abuse material calls equally for a stern penalty.

title: Harm of sexual offending
statement: Sexual offences are crimes of violence causing appalling, often irreparable harm. Rape’s impact (physical invasion and the loss of rights and freedoms) must be given proper weight. Harm from child sexual abuse is severe and long lasting; severe psychological repercussions are presumed from incest and may be a primary consideration.

title: Presumption of harm to children (Clarkson): apparent consent is not mitigating
statement: A child under 16 cannot consent to sexual penetration; the prohibition protects children from harm and deters adults, and rests on a presumption of long-term harm unaffected by apparent consent, which is not mitigating. The presumption is rebuttable, and the offender bears the onus of rebutting it (fn 3602); rebuttal will be likely to succeed only in very limited circumstances (freely given consent reflecting genuine affection; focus on the circumstances, ages, exploitation or breach of trust); a child’s statement is not sufficient; independent expert evidence will normally be required; only in a very clear case might a material reduction be warranted. It applies to cybersex and in person offending with children under 16, preparatory offending (procuring, grooming) and child abuse material (including material depicting 16–17 year olds). The victim’s attitude, conduct or “attractiveness” is irrelevant. The degree of harm varies with the objective gravity and explicitness. It does not apply where there is no child victim (e.g. a police officer posing as a child) — but culpability and gravity are not thereby lessened (flag.police_child_presumption). The Manual does not say whether it applies to the care/supervision offences against 16- or 17-year-olds or to the non-contact offences (see link_conditions). The presumption rests on protecting children from “premature sexual experience of all kinds”; in person and cybersex offending share the same objectives, so there is no basis for distinguishing them; that the child may be exploring their sexuality online or enjoy the offender’s attention is irrelevant.

Presumption of harm to children (Clarkson): apparent consent is not mitigating
A child under 16 cannot consent to sexual penetration; the prohibition protects children from harm and deters adults, and rests on a presumption of long-term harm unaffected by apparent consent, which is not mitigating. The presumption is rebuttable, and the offender bears the onus of rebutting it (fn 3602); rebuttal will be likely to succeed only in very limited circumstances (freely given consent reflecting genuine affection; focus on the circumstances, ages, exploitation or breach of trust); a child’s statement is not sufficient; independent expert evidence will normally be required; only in a very clear case might a material reduction be warranted. It applies to cybersex and in person offending with children under 16, preparatory offending (procuring, grooming) and child abuse material (including material depicting 16–17 year olds). The victim’s attitude, conduct or “attractiveness” is irrelevant. The degree of harm varies with the objective gravity and explicitness. It does not apply where there is no child victim (e.g. a police officer posing as a child) — but culpability and gravity are not thereby lessened (flag.police_child_presumption). The Manual does not say whether it applies to the care/supervision offences against 16- or 17-year-olds or to the non-contact offences (see link_conditions). The presumption rests on protecting children from “premature sexual experience of all kinds”; in person and cybersex offending share the same objectives, so there is no basis for distinguishing them; that the child may be exploring their sexuality online or enjoy the offender’s attention is irrelevant.

title: Sexual offences: gravity generally (no hierarchy of penetration; trust; the victim’s home)
statement: Sexual intrusion is serious (maxima up to 25 years) — but see Traeger (fn 3613): indecent assault is serious, but given the two maxima significantly less so than rape. Gravity depends on the facts; there is no hierarchy of penetration (digital rape is not necessarily less serious). Breach of trust, or offending in the victim’s home, is particularly egregious.

title: Rape: gravity and culpability factors (maximum 25 years; standard sentence 10 years for ss 38(2)–(3))
statement: Rape is always very serious (maximum 25 years; for rape under ss 38(2)–(3) the standard sentence is 10 years — the 24.1.1 table prints no standard sentence against s 39(2) rape by compelling sexual penetration, which the register treats as outside the scheme, with a caution: flag.sso_rape_by_compelling): an act of violence even without other violence; all non-consensual penetration is objectively serious. There are no inflexible principles; the range is wide; there is no rule that partner rape is more or less serious than stranger rape; consider all circumstances, not just the elements. The relevant factors (below) are descriptive, not exhaustive, and explain seriousness even without violence or physical harm. For multiple rapes, care is needed not to doubly punish and to respect totality (fn 3638). Consent obtained by deceit bears on gravity (e.g. “stealthing”: consent to penetration does not extend to further penetration after a condom is removed without the victim’s permission or knowledge).

title: Sexual offences against children: gravity and culpability factors
statement: Sexual crimes against children are abhorrent and without question serious, particularly with breach of care or trust. Dalgliesh’s observations on seriousness apply to all such offending. Common factors are listed below. The absence of a listed factor is not necessarily mitigating; it may simply be the absence of an aggravating factor. Passage of time since the offending is irrelevant to gravity and culpability. title: Incest: gravity, culpability and the value of a plea
statement: Incest (commonly penetration of one’s children, step-children or a partner’s children) is mostly an aggravated form of child sexual offending, condemned in the strongest terms, especially where it breaches parental care. A guilty plea is entitled to more than the usual utilitarian benefit (sparing the victim and family a trial). Maximum 25 years for a parent against a child (ss 50C, 50D). Consider nature, extent, frequency, duration and circumstances. Particular considerations: violence or threats (inherent violence; penetration at the very high end; any sexual touching by a parent is very serious); breach of trust (very high culpability); degradation (filming, posting online, offending before family or involving others); concealment or continuation by bribes, coercion or secrecy. A representative charge may be significantly more serious than a single act. The two other incest offences (s 50E: the junior adult party in parent-child incest; s 50F: siblings; both 5 years) are generally not the target of the strongest comments, but share some of the same condemnation; a s 50F offence by a much older sibling may bear all the characteristics of the most serious incest offences (fn 3703).

title: Online grooming to procure children for overseas abuse (Commonwealth provisions)
statement: The Commonwealth suite of online child sexual abuse provisions (outside this app’s Victorian scope) responds to the growing use of the internet to groom adults to procure children for overseas abuse: where the grooming occurs is immaterial if the intent is to procure a child for abuse outside Australia, and it does not matter that the child is fictitious, that the abuse is impossible, or that no sexual activity “in real life” is involved. The essence of the offence is the intention to use the internet to gain access to children; a fictitious child does not lessen culpability; actual harm aggravates but the absence of a “real victim” does not mitigate; it is predatory, manipulative and corrosive behaviour that can never be anything but serious.

title: Child abuse material: gravity (Minehan factors; ANVIL/CETS levels; numbers; possession is not victimless)
statement: CAM offences are especially grave and increasingly prevalent; the internet’s anonymity hampers detection. Minehan’s thirteen factors guide gravity (the twelve listed below; the thirteenth, any other matter in s 16A of the Crimes Act 1914 bearing on objective seriousness, concerns Commonwealth offences and is outside the app’s scope). The six-level ANVIL/CETS scale helps, but the actual content matters, not just the level (Level 1 images are not benign; absence of higher levels does not minimise lower-level possession); the number of children depicted matters. Numbers of images are not determinative and gravity is not a mathematical comparison with other cases. Prose describing child sexual abuse can itself be abhorrent. Possession is not victimless (it creates a market); possession for sale or distribution aggravates; active distribution increases culpability whether or not profit was made or payment given (but see Schulz, fn 3746: possession falls at the lower end of seriousness if the images are few and unsolicited). Also relevant: how long material was kept, whether stored or sorted, and the duration of offending. The authority for “the absence of material in higher categories cannot … minimise” (fn 3739, “Ibid 820–21 [71]”) appears to be Garside, not Hutchinson (flag.ibid_fn3739). The expanded breadth of internet offending and the increased maxima indicate gravity; possessing only a “moderate” number of images does not mean the offending cannot be serious; using the internet to exploit children is grave even if the offender is not procuring the exploitation.

title: Child sexual offences: good character excluded only if it assisted the offending
statement: The court must not have regard to prior good character or lack of prior convictions if satisfied it assisted the commission of a child sexual offence. This requires an affirmative finding of a connection (with submissions; the Crown appears to bear the burden); taking advantage of that status is one way but not the only one; it requires a material contribution, not a high causal threshold.

title: Sexual offences: purposes
statement: Courts emphasise general and specific deterrence, just punishment, community protection and denunciation. General deterrence has primacy for child pornography offending. Rehabilitation, especially for historic offending, may mitigate depending on the case.

title: Sexual offences: cumulation reflects separate harms
statement: Although cumulation is less likely for a single incident with one victim and no fresh harm, for sexual offending acts closely associated in time represent separate and substantial harms appropriately recognised by cumulation; total gravity informs it. Counting penetrative acts is crude; punishing successive degradation is not double punishment. Sending an explicit image to a child is separate criminality from attempts to procure. Cumulation is not a mathematical exercise, but an effective 4 months for each of three penetrations of a child under 10 was “simply too low”, despite very significant mitigation. But see Flynn (fn 3768): in a single-transaction case, cumulating one third of a second rape sentence on the first was “significantly out of kilter”.

title: Causing injury: mandatory minimums for gross violence and protected workers; the four special-reason exceptions
statement: The Act specifies minimum sentences for most causing injury offences in circumstances of gross violence or against a protected worker. 25.1.3.1 describes “four exceptions” — the four special-reason categories: assistance or an undertaking to assist; proven (balance of probabilities) mental impairment causally related to the offending that substantially and materially reduces culpability or would make imprisonment substantially and materially more burdensome (not where the impairment was caused substantially by self-induced intoxication: fn 2007); a proposed Court Secure Treatment Order or Residential Treatment Order; or substantial and compelling reasons that are exceptional and rare. The last requires powerful circumstances wholly outside run of the mill factors; the offender bears a heavy burden to show a special reason. The list is not exhaustive of the exceptions: 9.1.2.2–9.1.2.3 add an offender under 18; liability by complicity (for the protected-official minimums only where the offender proves on the balance of probabilities that their involvement was minor); and, for protected-official offences other than gross violence, a youth justice centre order for offenders under 21 on the 9.1.2.3 conditions (flag.mm_exceptions_25_1_3_1). The gating is done by the mmnpp.* hard rules with the full 9.1.2.x lists; this item is guidance only.

title: Intentionally causing serious injury: current practice
statement: ICSI sentences have increased; immediate imprisonment is generally called for (more so than RCSI). Intent to cause serious injury makes it graver in that respect than unintentional homicide; some cases warrant sentences like or exceeding manslaughter. The Court of Appeal has said Nash and Cedic are yardsticks where serious injury is intended and severe injury results, and that ICSI with life-threatening or catastrophic injuries or ongoing serious impairment “should usually attract” more than 10 years (a Court of Appeal statement about that category, not a floor).

title: Recklessly causing serious injury: current practice
statement: RCSI is triable summarily; as the principal offence in the higher courts it generally attracts custody, which is usually required. In 2010 the Court of Appeal said glassing sentences (as RCSI) did not reflect the inherent dangerousness of the conduct and should be increased (csp.uplift_glassing). Where facts closely resemble ICSI (glassing; “king hit”) no meaningful difference is warranted. Caution in comparing older cases after Kilic and Dalgliesh.

title: Negligently causing serious injury by driving: current practice (uplift)
statement: In 2015 practice for upper-end NCSI–Driving was held inadequate and to be uplifted, with flow-on to mid and low range; the maximum had been increased to 10 years without corresponding sentence increases. The most serious cases involve negligence of the very highest order; do not draw detailed distinctions between precise injuries in upper-end cases. A court may have regard to car NCSI sentences when sentencing the driver of a motor boat for the same offence (neither should be treated more leniently). NCSI–Driving and culpable driving share features (speed, inattention, intoxication, priors) allowing comparisons. Some cases may suit a CCO or combination sentence, less likely as negligence and injury increase.

statement: For a serious-injury offence the injury must be regarded as serious, but on a plea to a lesser offence (RCI or ICI) the offender cannot be sentenced for a more serious offence, even if intent might be inferred or the injury might meet the definition of serious injury. title: Causing injury: shared gravity and culpability factors
statement: Shared factors (below): proven intent; seriousness of injury (present and future; physical and psychological; impact; how inflicted; obstruction of medical help; assessed when sustained); vulnerability; weapons (blades significantly aggravating — see also Ranger, fn 3822: slight injuries and the offender’s disabilities); persistence (an attack “of a relatively short duration” is not mitigating: fn 3823); company; violence (kicking, punching by trained fighters, choking); family violence (serious breach of trust, especially in the home; controlling conduct such as monitoring the victim; “I snapped” does not mitigate) and duties to children (exposure to domestic violence when young may explain but cannot excuse or reduce culpability for harming a child); post-offence conduct such as shifting fault illuminates moral culpability; public, alcohol-fuelled unprovoked violence (youth and rehabilitation take a back seat); premeditation; part of the body attacked. Provocation may significantly lessen culpability, but not for revenge or punishment; here it is limited to words or deeds causing near-immediate loss of control; cooling off lessens it; cultural sensitivity to language (swearing) may not suffice. In homicide the Manual states provocation more broadly (as a sentencing factor not limited by the common-law test for reducing murder to manslaughter; may be cumulative; may count even where the conduct was excessive): apply each statement to its own offence class and caution where both arise (flag.provocation_injury_vs_homicide).

title: ICSI (maximum 20 years) and RCSI (maximum 15 years): key indicators
statement: ICSI: the Court of Appeal endorsed the first six shared factors as a useful, non-prescriptive framework; key indicators are proven intent, seriousness of injury and manner of infliction (persistence and repeated head blows may show intent; a finding of higher intent than the basis of the plea requires an opportunity to be heard: fn 3851). Not foreseeing the precise injuries does not reduce culpability (but see Marino, fn 3855, RCSI king-hit: a substantial disparity between the injury foreseen and the catastrophic injuries sustained); worse injuries being possible does not prevent a serious characterisation. Glassing is serious ICSI (worse if offender sober and victim intoxicated) and, all things being equal, intentional glassing should receive more than reckless. RCSI: consider the probability of serious injury and the seriousness of the probable injury foreseen — acting in the face of both shows high culpability — and the impact on the victim (a key consideration, albeit only one). An offender may be highly culpable for gross violence RCSI without inflicting the injuries or being present. RCSI glassing is not in a lower category than RCSI with conventional weapons.

title: Negligently causing serious injury by driving: gravity and responsibility
statement: NCSI–Driving sits above dangerous driving causing serious injury and below dangerous driving causing death; gravity is assessed by the degree of negligence and seriousness of injury. Aggravating features listed below; their absence does not necessarily put the offence at the lower end; remaining and assisting at the scene is not mitigating. Start from the presumption that the offender was solely responsible for the driving and its consequences (qualifiable by evidence). A passenger’s knowledge of intoxication or fatigue does not, by itself, reduce responsibility, and the passenger’s failure to wear a seatbelt does not demonstrate it was a contributing cause — and even if it did, the driver remains responsible, given the legal obligation to ensure passengers are wearing seatbelts (compare culpable driving, where a seatbelt failure proved on the balance of probabilities to have caused the death gets relatively modest weight: guide.driving.culpable_driving). Victim conduct matters only if it bears on the driving or choice to drive (e.g. urging faster driving); the offender may establish factors outside their control that were a material cause of the injuries, which should reduce the penalty. Loss or injury of one’s own child may be relevant in both mitigation and aggravation.

A passenger’s knowledge of intoxication or fatigue does not, by itself, reduce responsibility, and the passenger’s failure to wear a seatbelt does not demonstrate it was a contributing cause — and even if it did, the driver remains responsible, given the legal obligation to ensure passengers are wearing seatbelts (compare culpable driving, where a seatbelt failure proved on the balance of probabilities to have caused the death gets relatively modest weight: guide.driving.culpable_driving). Victim conduct matters only if it bears on the driving or choice to drive (e.g. urging faster driving); the offender may establish factors outside their control that were a material cause of the injuries, which should reduce the penalty. Loss or injury of one’s own child may be relevant in both mitigation and aggravation.

title: Administering substances, stalking and assault
statement: Administering substances (rarely charged): given the statutory language, its gravity would appear to turn significantly on the dangerousness of the substance and the motive. Stalking (usually Magistrates’ Court; in the higher courts it is usually not the principal offence but does result in immediate custody — a practice observation): serious because it intends physical or mental harm or fear; psychological harm can be devastating. Statutory assaults’ seriousness is often limited by overlapping offences with higher maxima; common law assault is limited by the availability of causing injury and threat offences.

title: Kidnapping and false imprisonment: current practice
statement: Kidnapping is uncommon but extremely serious, generally warranting a substantial custodial sentence (as do related offences such as false imprisonment). For kidnapping only (not child stealing or taking away a child, whose maximum is 5 years): kidnapping for ransom or leading to sexual offending often attracts sentences in “double figures”; total effective sentences of eight to nine years for “payback” kidnappings are not unusual; over seven to just under ten years is not uncommon for kidnapping generally and associated offences (whole-case total effective sentences).

title: Kidnapping, false imprisonment and child stealing: gravity
statement: Gravity is indicated by the maxima (kidnapping 25 years). Kidnapping has been described as a form of terrorism; for ransom, extortion, advantage or subjugation it is particularly grave; trickery is not less serious than force. Child stealing is very serious. For false imprisonment, knowing a further serious assault would follow, leaving the bound victim to further assault, and whether steps were taken to end the imprisonment are relevant. Gravity and culpability may be increased by: premeditation; length of detention; violence, threats, fear or harm (victim or family); breach of trust; motives such as perverting justice or intimidating a witness; isolation; vigilantism; exposure to serious health and safety risks.

title: Blackmail, extortion and threats: gravity
statement: Blackmail (threat to expose/accuse, or threat of violence — the Manual says it is debatable which is worse) is inherently serious: a direct attack whose fear, stress and anxiety may resemble violence. Threat gravity turns on the nature of the threat; bomb threats call for heavy sentences, their gravity does not depend entirely on proof of the means then and there to carry out the threat, and they are serious where multiple, menacing and distressing; an imitation device reinforces the threat but its incapacity to harm is also relevant. Also relevant: impact and fear; planning; stand-over tactics; persistence and duration; weapons; breach of trust; number of victims and family relationships; purpose of deterring enforcement of a legal right.

title: Endangerment offences: gravity
statement: Key factors: the nature and degree of risk and whether a weapon was used; deliberately firing a firearm at close quarters toward a person (especially police on duty) is among the most serious. Disregarding risks to others to serve one’s own ends (even self-harm) must expect a substantial price. Injury or death is not aggravating but shows the risk was real. Genuine (even mistaken) fear may mitigate, but does not extinguish criminality — particularly for a prohibited person in possession of a weapon who fires after the danger has passed (fn 3953); taking the law into one’s own hands or acting to intimidate or retaliate may place it at the upper end.

title: Other offences against the person: focus on actual harms; purposes; schemes
statement: These offences are broad and hard to categorise (person v property); focus on the actual harms in the case. Purposes: deterrence, just punishment/denunciation, community protection. Not CCE or sex offender registrable; blackmail, extortion with threat to kill and extortion with threat to destroy property are automatic forfeiture offences (26.5 does not name the threat-to-injure limb of s 27). The serious offenders regime may apply (serious_offender.regime) — the Manual says “may apply” / “might be imposed”; an indefinite sentence requires a “serious offence”.

title: Violent property offences: current practice (robbery, aggravated burglary, home invasion, carjacking)
statement: In all but the most exceptional case, an offender convicted of robbery or armed robbery should expect a recorded conviction and a custodial sentence. Hogarth held that practice for “confrontational” aggravated burglary (then commonly around two years) was inadequate and needed to be uplifted; offences of the kind described in Hogarth are now the offences of home invasion and aggravated home invasion; the ruling was expanded to all “more serious forms” of aggravated burglary (rigid application of the categories discouraged), and terms of five to seven years are regularly imposed in these cases (aggravated burglary only; the Manual gives no practice figure for home invasion or aggravated home invasion — for their seriousness relative to aggravated burglary see guide.property.violent_common_features, which records that “a class of home invasion offences” is, other things being equal, to be regarded as more serious, and flag.home_invasion_mandatory_scheme_fn4044). Guidance on carjacking is limited and still evolving: robbery considerations may guide carjacking, and armed robbery aggravated carjacking (which, unlike armed robbery, has a minimum non-parole period). Each proposition applies only to the offences of its limb (below).

title: Deception (white collar) offences: current practice
statement: Deception ranges from isolated instances of credit card fraud, through false information or identities, to the largest systematic fraud on institutions and investors. For serious instances of white-collar offending long terms of imprisonment are to be expected, and dispositions without an immediate term of imprisonment with a non-parole period are likely to be inadequate. Secret commission offences will almost inevitably attract a custodial sentence.

title: Arson: current practice (maximum 15 years); manslaughter as a guide for arson causing death

title: Theft and burglary: gravity
statement: Theft cannot be put in a hierarchy; gravity turns on what was taken, its value, from whom, and all circumstances including purpose. Value is commonly key but not decisive (generally, the greater the value the greater the culpability), and may be completely subordinate where another harm to the victim is involved. Key elements are planning, role and value. Particularly serious: brazen offending; breach of trust by a burglar who is or was employed by the victim; prolific and persistent offending. Distinguish poorly planned, haphazard thefts from highly organised commercial offending, though incompetence is not mitigating and a high degree of persistence may elevate seriousness. There is little distinction between burglary of commercial and residential premises: both are serious for different reasons (dwellings: breach of privacy, fear and terror, loss of sentimental items; commercial: often greater planning and professionalism). Vehicle theft is not categorically less serious. Going equipped has no noticeably different gradations of seriousness.

title: Theft of a firearm
statement: Theft of a firearm is particularly serious (maximum 15 years v 10 for theft) because it feeds the illegitimate flow of firearms; the risk exists whether opportunistic or premeditated; plainly premeditated offending (bringing down gun safes with chains attached to the offenders’ vehicle) cannot be categorised as “low level offending”.

title: Handling stolen goods
statement: Handling is generally more serious than theft (greater maximum), as it encourages and ensures the success of thefts; no general sentencing practice exists. Most serious where planned, of significant scale and sophistication, where the offender leads or organises (not a passive recipient), abuses power or trust (e.g. disguising goods as stock-in-trade), or handles specialised or unique property (sentimental items from domestic burglaries).

title: Violent property offences: common features of gravity
statement: Violent property offences are serious: terrifying for victims and threatening the community’s sense of security. Sentencing decisions on home invasion as a form of aggravated burglary remain directly relevant to the new offence. By introducing mandatory sentencing requirements for a class of home invasion offences, the legislature signalled that those offences are, other things being equal, more serious than aggravated burglary (which class the Manual means is unclear: fn 4044 says the mandatory imprisonment scheme applies to aggravated home invasion but not home invasion, yet home invasion is a Category 2 offence — flag.home_invasion_mandatory_scheme_fn4044; the register’s Category 2 status governs). Value matters less (and may be irrelevant) than violence, threats and fear. Common features are listed below. As with burglary, there is little distinction between commercial and residential premises.

title: Aggravated burglary and home invasion: gravity; post-entry and uncharged conduct; no subtraction reasoning
statement: Hogarth’s six categories (intimate partner, sexual assault intent and confrontational most serious; intent to steal, rob and spontaneous encounter less so) are not to be applied rigidly. Other instances of the offence must be considered, but the absence of an aggravating factor seen in another case does not make the instant case necessarily less serious; reasoning by subtracting absent features is impermissible two-stage sentencing. Ordinarily relevant: intent at entry; mode of entry; weapon; company; time; what the offender knew about occupants; whether the victim was particularly frightened of the offender. Family violence context does not make the offending less serious, and the law now recognises the fundamental importance of general deterrence in domestic violence. The extent to which post-entry conduct is relevant is “not entirely straightforward”: conduct that could have been charged as a more serious offence (e.g. false imprisonment, assault) should not be treated as aggravating, and if not charged that criminality cannot be taken into account adversely — the principle that the judge considers all circumstances of the charged offence gives way to the principle that no one is punished for an uncharged offence. But carrying a loaded firearm during a home invasion has been held a “very significant aggravating feature” even where no firearm offence is charged, because it revealed premeditation, illuminated the intention at entry and greatly increased the danger of the entry (the boundary is not stated: flag.uncharged_firearm_clark). Separately charged conduct must not be double counted. Post-entry conduct may prove the intent at entry (sexual assault intent generally more serious).

title: Weapons in violent property offences
statement: All weapons are serious (risk of serious injury or death; terror); a weapon of “great lethality” bears directly on gravity, and how a weapon is used is relevant to criminality. Unloaded firearms, imitation weapons and innocuous items plainly carry less risk and so are less dangerous than the genuine article, but can still instil terror, cause serious emotional damage and are dangerous given potential police responses (on the competing general authorities see flag.imitation_weapon_competing_authority). Where carrying a weapon is an element it is not an aggravating circumstance, but its nature, potential for harm and manner of use may be considered; the use of a weapon in aid of a carjacking will almost always heighten the gravity of aggravated carjacking, even though it is the qualifying circumstance. Do not double count separately charged firearm possession or discharge, though carrying a loaded firearm is generally a significantly aggravating feature (an uncharged firearm in an aggravated burglary or home invasion: flag.uncharged_firearm_clark). The absence of a weapon commonly places casual, opportunistic aggravated burglary at the lower end, but not necessarily otherwise grave offending. Examples: pointing a firearm while threatening to shoot has been characterised (in one case) as a “mid-range” armed robbery; pulling the trigger (a misfire) was particularly egregious; firing shots aggravates; lacerating a victim with a chainsaw or box cutter greatly elevated the criminality. Serious offending stays serious even with relatively minor injuries.

title: Deception and corruption offences: gravity; motive; absence of loss
statement: Deception offences are serious (calculated courses of conduct, repeated dishonesty, significant losses; hard to detect, expensive to prosecute, most often devoid of excuse). Particularly egregious: dishonesty by a solicitor or accountant in professional practice, or other abuse of a position of power, trust or responsibility to facilitate or camouflage the offending; an appalling breach of trust; a very large amount; systematic, deliberate dishonesty over a period, particularly where the offender persists despite opportunities to desist (voluntary cessation before exposure by a third party earns a real discount); a significant or “tragic” impact on small or vulnerable investors, on victims including both individuals and institutions, or where no funds are recovered. Value gained is generally an important indicator, but the extent, breadth and sophistication may make offending involving smaller sums more serious. Absence of loss significantly reduces gravity but must not unduly erode general deterrence. Greed versus need is a slight and usually illusory difference; the absence of greed is not uncommon, and motive may bear on the genuineness of remorse, specific deterrence or rehabilitation; extreme financial pressure only extremely rarely mitigates a significant breach of trust, and people in desperate financial straits cannot expect special leniency. Secret commissions threaten institutional and commercial integrity; profit, duration and scale matter.

title: Criminal damage and arson: gravity
statement: Criminal damage varies greatly; offences charged as arson are generally of substantial gravity and arson causing death is the most serious; computer and contamination offences are commonly at the lesser end — but the maximum still governs (e.g. sabotage, Level 2 – 25 years). Bushfire damage is always serious. Particularly serious arson or damage: multiple arsons; a leading role; substantial loss; revenge or reward motive; knowledge the building was occupied; risk to others (neighbours); fire danger periods, total fire bans or hot windy days; fires hard to detect. The offender’s intention characterises the seriousness; men directing violence (arson or damage) at former partners should expect condign punishment. At common law reasonably foreseeable unintended consequences could be considered; ss 5(2)(daa) and (db) have displaced that requirement: the court considers victim impact and the extent of loss or damage. Planned offending is generally more serious, but unplanned “add-on” arson may still be very serious; method dictates seriousness; landscape and spread risk matter. Arsonists are not uncommonly injured: whether such injuries mitigate is unsettled and depends on the circumstances (the cases go both ways: flag.extra_curial_test_scope).

title: Money laundering / dealing with proceeds of crime: gravity (Victorian Division 2A v Commonwealth s 400)
statement: The Manual’s principles “have so far emerged from the authorities on Commonwealth offending” (the first, the seriousness of the offence within the s 400 scheme, is Commonwealth-only), and it marks the Victorian differences: Division 2A grades seriousness by the fault element, not by value, and for Victorian offending value is relevant but not dominant (for Commonwealth offending value is highly significant and the primary identifier of the maximum). The court considers the precise circumstances of the conduct, including the nature of the dealing, its duration, and the number of transactions (in general, prolific offending involving small amounts will be more serious than a single larger transaction), the offender’s role, authority and initiative, and the extent of their belief or knowledge that the money is proceeds of crime. Do not consider what sentence might have followed for the predicate offence.

title: Deception offences: reduced weight for good character; reputational loss
statement: Personal circumstances including good character ordinarily get less weight in deception offending, as white collar offenders typically have good character, references and prospects — often what gave them positions of trust and helped them avoid detection. Mitigating weight may be given to reputational damage and loss of capacity to practise their profession.

title: Property offences: purposes
statement: Theft: the scale of the offence and the offender’s personal circumstances will generally be the strongest determiners of the dominant purpose; general deterrence is key for theft, burglary and handling (especially prevalent offences such as shoplifting and vehicle theft, and burglaries of vulnerable “soft targets” such as rural properties); just punishment and general deterrence are the key purposes for handling; specific deterrence matters for serial offending; going equipped is a deterrent or “preventative” offence in itself. Violent thefts: just punishment, denunciation, general deterrence and community protection, especially for vulnerable victims (a special protective obligation); aggravated home invasion forfeits liberty for a very long time; youth and rehabilitation are secondary in serious cases (rehabilitation may rarely displace deterrence where reform is a real prospect; it may be emphasised for less serious cases or young offenders without significant priors). Deception: white collar thefts are said to deserve utmost condemnation; general deterrence and strong denunciation of breach of trust; personal mitigation such as good character generally gets less weight than general deterrence; specific deterrence often minor. Arson: said to be hard to detect and to call for deterrence (easy to commit, destructive); both general and specific deterrence matter for violence towards former partners, “misguided vigilantism”, total fire bans and significant risk to others; community protection is key. Secret commissions (hard to detect, often committed by people of good character) and money laundering: general deterrence.
