title: Property offences: serious offender scheme (arson), Category 1 and 2, forensic samples, forfeiture and CCE offences
statement: Each scheme applies only to the offences of its limb (below). Serious offender scheme: only arson offences (arson, arson causing death, causing a bushfire, and the listed Forests Act and CFA Act offences, conspiracy and interstate equivalents). Category 2 (offender 18 or older; offence on or after 20 March 2017): armed robbery only where the offender had a firearm, a victim was injured as a direct result, or it was committed in company; home invasion; carjacking; arson causing death (the register carries each condition). Aggravated home invasion and aggravated carjacking are Category 1 offences (offender 18 or older) with a three-year minimum non-parole period unless the offender was under 18 at the offence or special reasons are found (mmnpp.aggravated_home_invasion_carjacking_3y; 9.1.2.5 gives s 10AC for aggravated home invasion and s 10AD for aggravated carjacking; the 27.1.1.2 table footnotes cite s 10AD for both: flag.ahi_minimum_provision_10ac_10ad). All Victorian offences in the chapter are forensic sample offences except going equipped, dealing with property suspected of being proceeds and ss 247G–247H; civil forfeiture applies except to suspected proceeds and ss 247G–247H. Automatic forfeiture applies to the listed offences where the property is $50 000 or more (or $75 000 or more across multiple charges on the same facts or a series). The listed offences are continuing criminal enterprise offences where the property is $50,000 or more (dealing with proceeds of crime only under s 194(1)–(3); destroying or damaging property under s 197(1)–(3), (6)–(7)); a rolled-up count with one transaction of $50,000 or more is treated as a CCE offence (9.4 says the transaction must exceed $50,000; at exactly $50,000 the app does not rely on the doubled ceiling, and a sentence above the ordinary maximum but within it is a caution, not an error: flag.cce_value_threshold, cce.regime). Whether the property values are met must come from the user.

title: Cumulation: burglary/aggravated burglary and the ulterior offence
statement: Where a burglar is sentenced for the trespass with intent and the ulterior offence, cumulation reflects separate criminality but totality limits the total; factors common to several offences must be reflected in cumulation. Do not cumulate the whole aggravated burglary sentence on an ICSI sentence from the same occasion.

title: Commercial trafficking and cultivation: current practice (Gregory uplift; Fernando relativities)
statement: Generally, an immediate custodial sentence will be imposed for commercial trafficking or cultivation offences. Gregory held that practice for commercial-quantity (CQ) trafficking was inadequate and compressed at the upper end; because practice did not reflect the gravity, community impact and high maximum, courts are no longer constrained by existing practice, and relativities between the quantity-based offences must be maintained. The Court expected sentences to be spread across the statistical range, but said double figures might be expected where one or more listed features are present (a not guilty plea and relevant priors appear in the list, but neither can increase a sentence: see the caution). Pre-Gregory sentences and statistics need caution. Gregory said LCQ sentences will similarly need to increase substantially — obiter, but consistently followed since. Fernando: the uplift affects the upper range most, with a diminishing effect toward the middle and lower categories. The uplift is not controlling (Dalgliesh) but cannot be ignored. Each limb applies only to its own offences (plain trafficking, s 71AC, is not a CQ offence).

title: Cultivation: current practice (hierarchy and relativities; trafficking comparators and the Nguyen uplift for CQ cultivation)
statement: Cultivation offences form a deliberate hierarchy, so what was said in Gregory about relativities applies equally to cultivation. For commercial-quantity cultivation, trafficking cases may be considered in assessing current practice (given the overlap), and Nguyen found mid-category CQ cultivation sentences inconsistent and compressed at a low level, capped by the overlap with LCQ cultivation, and required the range to be uplifted and substantially expanded (its “by increments” requirement has since been overruled; the uplift does not reach sentences previously reserved for less culpable offenders such as crop sitters: csp.uplift_cultivation). Each limb applies only to its own offences.

title: Quantity as a comparator: use a common denominator
statement: Trafficking (and importation) is quantity-based, so quantity is a key indicator of seriousness and of comparison, and must be presented simply and clearly. Where different drugs are compared, raw quantities, multiples of a minimum quantity or estimated wholesale or retail values are not a sensible common denominator (28.1.4.2); convert to a common denominator — preferably the commercial quantity or large commercial quantity (multiples or percentages). Value may still indicate scale and the offender’s benefit (28.3.2.2, 28.3.2.5); the Manual states the role of value in both ways (flag.drug_value_comparator). Tables of comparable cases help only with sufficient case features, not mere numbers. Quantity is only one factor; comparing by weight alone departs from principle. (Commonwealth: the Commonwealth scheme does not distinguish a CQ from an LCQ — outside the app’s Victorian scope.)

title: Conspiring, inciting, aiding and abetting or attempting State drug offences: same maximum as the primary offence
statement: The primary forms of extended liability for State drug offences carry the same maximum penalty as their reference offence. The chapter 32 tables confine this to DPCS s 79 conspiracy and s 80 incitement to “certain drugs offences, including trafficking, cultivation, supply to a child, and possession”, and to attempts within ss 71–71AC, 72–72B and 73; these rows displace the Crimes Act inchoate rows and the fn 4805 life-to-15-years cap (guide.inchoate.maxima_notes). (Commonwealth: under federal law these are “extended liability” offences and, except incitement, carry the same maximum as the reference offence — outside the app’s Victorian scope.)

title: Statutorily mitigated forms (onus on offender, balance of probabilities); possession v trafficking (De Simoni)
statement: The DPCS Act provides lower maxima where statutory mitigating factors are proved by the offender on the balance of probabilities: cultivation not for trafficking; possession of a small quantity of cannabis; possession unrelated to trafficking (cannabis or any drug); using cannabis. The mitigated possession forms that raise whether the possession was related to trafficking must be approached with care: a person convicted of possession cannot be sentenced as if for trafficking — “possession for sale” is not a valid basis for aggravation (De Simoni), but “possession for a purpose relating to trafficking” may aggravate if proved beyond reasonable doubt, unless that purpose amounted to trafficking (this arises most where the s 73(1)(c) “any other case” band applies). (Commonwealth: the Criminal Code creates scaled offences but no offence provable in a mitigated form — outside the app’s Victorian scope.)

title: Quantity is the primary statutory factor; no judgments of relative drug harm (Pidoto: trafficking and cultivation)
statement: Quantity is the primary statutory factor of seriousness; because Parliament created a quantity hierarchy (a harm-based scheme would look very different), courts must not judge the relative harmfulness of different drugs (Pidoto) — that would need special expertise, detailed investigation and extensive information. Schedule 11 sets large commercial, commercial, traffickable and small quantities. The drug’s identity is not a primary basis for distinction (except for cannabis, it is relevant only to whether an aggravated or mitigated form was committed). The harm of drugs generally to users and the community remains legitimate, and quantity is not the only factor. Pidoto is limited to trafficking and cultivation: possession, use, trafficking to a child and supply to a child are excluded — but 28.3.1 also states the no-hierarchy proposition for “possessing, or using” (flag.pidoto_scope_possession_use).

title: Measuring quantity: purity, plants, continuing (Giretti) trafficking, co-offenders, aggregation
statement: It appears that the “small” and “traffickable” quantities refer to pure substance. A drug may be treated as pure if it meets the prevailing purity standard (British Pharmacopeia judicially noticed). Plant weight is measured as at the offence (a green crop’s actual weight), though usable yield matters to gravity; a cutting becomes a plant when it develops a root (even if it dies). A continuing business of trafficking can be one Giretti offence with accumulated quantities (mixed drugs permitted). Quantities are not divided among co-offenders. Mixture components may be aggregated by adding proportions of the relevant threshold (exceeding one qualifies), but not across separate counts; the drugs in a concoction do not create as many offences as there are drugs, and that the substances are mixed may be taken into account.

title: Traffickable quantity (evidentiary presumption only); small quantities (cannabis fine); s 76 adjourned bond
statement: A traffickable quantity does not affect the maximum (in either scheme); possession of it is prima facie evidence of trafficking. Small quantities affect the maximum only for cannabis possession (fine of five penalty units instead of one or five years’ imprisonment if established). Apart from this, the only relevance of the small quantity is s 76: under it, a person charged with possession or use (or the inchoate forms) should presumptively be released on an adjourned bond without conviction “if other strict criteria are met” — and the table says cultivation unrelated to trafficking (s 72B(a)) “may qualify” too. The criteria are not set out in the Manual (flag.s76_scope_cultivation): s 76 is possibly available — ask the user; never pass or fail a sentence on s 76 alone.

title: Drug offences: information the court needs; common gravity features
statement: Drug offences are a substantial social evil. It is counsel’s duty to provide the court with the drug’s identity, how it can be used, what is known of its effects, and its wholesale or retail value. Common features found relevant to gravity and culpability: quantity (actual or attempted); role in the hierarchy; financial gain or motive; knowledge or belief; size and sophistication; duration; assistance to authorities; criminal history; prospects of rehabilitation. Criminal history appears in that list, but prior convictions cannot be used to increase a sentence (flag.priors_as_aggravation_30_3). On duration the Manual notes contrary authority (fn 4326, Quah: the character of the possession, not its duration; flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6).

title: Quantity, purity, plants, value and yield as indicators of gravity
statement: Maxima range from 10 years to life at the upper end; generally, the higher the quantity, the more serious, reflecting Parliament’s ascending order of seriousness — but giving quantity chief importance without other factors is error. The standard sentence’s middle-range notion is harder to apply where quantity is central. No mathematical adjustment between several offences by quantity. Large seizures support inferences (not for personal use; large-scale business; expected profit). Purity matters (higher purity increases gravity; where the purity of a mixture is known, comparing the pure proportion with the pure threshold is not error). Commercial by number of plants but not weight may indicate lower seriousness (e.g. Belbruno, charged among other things with trafficking a commercial quantity of cannabis: 168 plants, potential weight a little over 10 kg, described as a low to mid-range commercial quantity). Value can indicate scale and may give some basis for comparison, and is regularly accepted as a guide to gravity where it reveals the offender’s actual or anticipated benefit — but the legislation emphasises quantity (flag.drug_value_comparator). Potential yield and value matter for cultivation, though hard to estimate; much may depend on the plants’ stage of development and the care needed.

title: Role in a drug enterprise (labels are not the focus; Olbrich)
statement: Role is significant: principals are typically more culpable than couriers or middlemen, who are more culpable than street dealers and users — but the terms used vary widely, labels are not the focus, there is no rigid benchmark, there is no reason to think enterprises are formally structured, and courts sentence on the known facts. Olbrich: identifying the precise role is not essential (nor required in every case; its utility depends on what is known); “courier” and “principal” may be a useful shorthand, but cannot obscure what the offender did, and the label should not distract from the tasks performed, relationships and the trust and responsibility given (e.g. living at the crop premises; many communications about quantity and price can show a principal role). In serious drug offences couriers and other low-level participants are important, if not essential, and deserve suitable punishment, and a sole proprietor of a “one man” cultivation is not a mere crop sitter: normally, offending even at that level calls for immediate imprisonment (limbs below: the commercial offences; for non-commercial trafficking and cultivation the scope of “serious drug offences” is unresolved, a caution: flag.serious_drug_offences_low_level_custody). Steps such as possession, movement and storage can show an executive function; a precise equivalence between co-offenders is not required (an evaluative judgment). What others in the hierarchy stood to gain is irrelevant. (Commonwealth importation and possession: the R v Nguyen principles — e.g. a rebuttable inference of profit; good character of less weight; attempted possession no less serious than importation — outside the app’s Victorian scope.)

title: Financial gain or motive
statement: Greed is more culpable than funding one’s own addiction; willingness to harm the community for reward increases culpability, and in these circumstances general and specific deterrence “loom large”. Larger expected reward means more serious offending; the offender may prove on the balance of probabilities little or no benefit, or a lower value of the drug (consistently lower sentences for GHB reflect its reward differential). Pidoto bars harm differentiation, not consideration of reward. Giving proceeds to family is not significantly mitigating; failing to obtain a reward or complete a sale is generally not mitigating; providing armed support to a sale may be as culpable as organising it. (fns 4370 and 4418 cite [2021] VSCA 26 as “Mourkakos”, which the Manual elsewhere names “Navaratnam”: flag.vsca_2021_26_two_names.)

title: Knowledge or belief; sophistication and scale
statement: Absent contrary evidence, the court may sentence on the basis the offender knew the quantity (no speculation about a lesser belief); recklessness as to the substance is no different from knowledge; knowingly returning to selling the same drug may make a later offence comparable to a more serious one. Sophistication and scale elevate seriousness (quantity primarily, price also); lack of sophistication or impossibility matters little where quantity is serious; specialised equipment supports inferences of scale; the strain on community resources from extensive police involvement and investigation may also indicate scale; a sophisticated, large cultivation may permit an inference of a principal role (its fn 4390 authority is uncertain: flag.fn4390_nguyen_2017). (Commonwealth importation: ignorance of the pure quantity is not unusual, and expected reward may then be a better guide — outside the app’s Victorian scope.)

Sophistication and scale elevate seriousness (quantity primarily, price also); lack of sophistication or impossibility matters little where quantity is serious; specialised equipment supports inferences of scale; the strain on community resources from extensive police involvement and investigation may also indicate scale; a sophisticated, large cultivation may permit an inference of a principal role (its fn 4390 authority is uncertain: flag.fn4390_nguyen_2017). (Commonwealth importation: ignorance of the pure quantity is not unusual, and expected reward may then be a better guide — outside the app’s Victorian scope.)

title: Trafficking: attempts, potential harm, fake drugs
statement: Trafficking includes attempts, but attempts are not necessarily sentenced as completed offences; the 16-year standard sentence for LCQ trafficking does not apply to attempted trafficking (sso.scope). Trafficking is no less serious because the drugs did not reach consumers: seriousness may be assessed by potential consequences and intentions; potential harm is as serious as actual harm; absence of actual harm gets little weight where distribution is thwarted by arrest, covert police or ineptitude. Supplying a substance purporting to be a drug is objectively serious, though the criminality may be less than a genuine plan to supply drugs (fn 4394, a NSW case).

title: Cultivation: custody; overlap with trafficking; theft of electricity
statement: The Court of Appeal has said that, save perhaps in exceptional circumstances, commercial-quantity cultivation requires custody (“possibly wholly suspended, if still available”) — but for offending on or after 20 March 2017 by an adult, CQ cultivation is a Category 2 offence and LCQ cultivation Category 1 (the register; cat2.custodial_unless, cat1.custodial_required), and suspended sentences have been progressively abolished from 1 May 2011 (the dates by court and offence class: suspended.abolished). Where possession for sale is the basis of a trafficking charge, cultivation and trafficking overlap, with the same maxima at commercial and large commercial levels: examine the common factual elements as a matter of common sense, not semantics — only the elements not in common are separately punished. Cultivation is often charged with theft of electricity (crop farmers commonly bypass meters to power grow lights): sentencing judges should consider what impact this might have on orders for cumulation; though the theft may be an integral part of the hydroponics system, it is a discrete offence, and a measure of cumulation may be appropriate.

title: Sale to children; police involvement; violence in trafficking
statement: The DPCS Act creates separate offences for trafficking or supplying drugs to children, and “supply or trafficking to children within 500 metres of a school is a statutory factor leading to qualification for a higher maximum penalty”; the child’s age and the circumstances also bear on gravity. Which offences carry the 20-year “within 500 metres of a school” maximum is stated inconsistently (the table prints it for s 71AC and s 71B; 28.3.6 and fn 4409 point to sale to children, ss 71B(1A) and 71AB(2)): apply it only when the user confirms the statutory condition (flag.school_500m_condition). Police involvement may affect culpability (a spectrum; the primary focus is how it bears on the offender’s culpability), but little where police merely facilitate offending the offender was ready to commit; factors listed below. Trafficking that relies on violence and intimidation is more serious and warrants a heavier sentence (using violence to complete a transaction is more culpable).

title: Drug offences: offender circumstances (character, age, addiction, status, cooperation)
statement: Age is relevant but carries less weight in drug cases because competing considerations (gravity, deterrence, denunciation) “may assume greater significance” (for young offenders see audit.youth_principles). title: Drug offences: concurrency within a single transaction; Giretti charges and commonality (Dang)
statement: Drug sentencing commonly requires decisions about concurrency and cumulation. Offences in a single transaction should generally be concurrent (e.g. possession that was a consequence of manufacture was consumed by the plea to trafficking, and cumulating part of the sentences was error; punishment on a count may even be unlawful). A Giretti charge is not duplicitous because trafficking is a continuing activity. Separate Giretti charges may share commonality: conduct indistinguishable in time or behaviour, no differentiation by victim or result, no separate obligations, part of one ongoing course relied on as a Giretti charge, or a single business selling different drugs. Counterweights: that different drugs are trafficked deserves separate recognition (subject to totality), and some cumulation is appropriate where a hydroponic operation involves theft of electricity (fn 4430).

title: Drug offences: no indefinite sentences; serious offender offences; forfeiture and CCE; serious drug offender
statement: No drug offence is a “serious offence”, so indefinite sentences are unavailable. Serious offender offences: trafficking LCQ or CQ, cultivation LCQ or CQ, and conspiracy, incitement, aiding/abetting or preparatory acts for them (certain Commonwealth convictions can qualify an offender; the serious offender consequences do not apply to Commonwealth offences). Forfeiture and CCE offences: any indictable Victorian drug offence or Schedule 2 offence (including producing, selling or supplying, and advertising a psychoactive substance); the Manual does not say whether, or how, the $50,000 test of 9.4 applies to a drug offence (flag.cce_drug_offences_value). Automatic and civil forfeiture: trafficking LCQ, CQ, to a child, trafficking; cultivation LCQ, CQ; and conspiracy, incitement, aiding/abetting of those. A serious drug offender declaration (s 89DI; a person sentenced for repeat offending of the same kind) makes community protection the principal purpose (disproportionate sentence permitted), presumes cumulation and must be recorded. Each list applies only to the offences of its limb. (The footnotes cite these DPCS provisions as “The Act”: flag.fn4438_4468_the_act_dpcs.)

title: Commonwealth drug quantity scheme (Criminal Code): commercial, marketable and trafficable quantities; pure quantities; comparisons
statement: The Criminal Code identifies commercial, marketable and trafficable quantities (Criminal Code Regulations 2019 schedules); the thresholds for the same drug may differ as a controlled and a border-controlled drug (e.g. heroin). Criminal Code quantities are of the pure substance, and combined quantities may be calculated where an organised criminal activity is proved; the trafficable quantity creates a rebuttable presumption whose nature depends on the offence. For comparisons, DPP (Cth) v KMD converts quantities to percentages of a CQ; a high-end marketable quantity offence may be more serious than a low-end CQ offence, so some CQ cases may be comparators; a Commonwealth CQ is generally equal to or higher than a Victorian LCQ, and expressing an importation as a multiple of the CQ shows its scale and allows comparison across drugs. Outside the app’s Victorian scope; for Victorian offences see guide.drugs.quantity_as_comparator and guide.drugs.measuring_quantity.

title: Offences against justice: little guidance on practice
statement: Perverting (or attempting to pervert) the course of justice carries 25 years, but caution is needed: rarity and varied circumstances mean little guidance and minimal assistance from the high maximum (limb: s 320 only). Authoritative guidance on the range for contempt is similarly limited; for the at-large contempt of the Chief Examiner, the five-year maximum of the cognate offence of refusing to take an oath or affirmation “may be a useful comparator” (fn 4474). The contempt rows have their own maxima in the register (from 1 month or 5 penalty units — fine-only rows from 10 penalty units — to at large). The authority for fn 4477 is uncertain (flag.ibid_fn4477).

title: Perverting or attempting to pervert the course of justice: gravity
statement: It strikes at the heart of the justice system; an attempt is an equally serious substantive offence (not inchoate). Gravity depends on the circumstances (factors below, with the Manual’s footnote qualifications). The likelihood of success has substantially reduced significance; potential consequences may weigh more. “Justice” includes the proceedings of judicial tribunals, and the attempt can be committed before curial proceedings have begun (e.g. intentionally frustrating or deflecting police from prosecuting), including action to prevent the institution of proceedings.

title: Perpetrators and targets within the legal system
statement: Gravity and culpability may be highest where the offender is embedded in the legal system (police, judicial officers, lawyers, other trusted personnel). Police abuse of power can undermine public confidence in the police (abusing criminals may be considered more serious; culpability is not reduced because victims are offenders; an experienced officer who tries to corrupt a more junior one may be more culpable). The public is entitled to expect that only people of good character are appointed to judicial office, so a judicial officer’s good character gets far less weight. Offences against justice by a lawyer, or by someone who intends to enter the profession, are treated especially seriously; where a lawyer attempts bribery or uses other means to pervert the course of justice, the status as a lawyer automatically increases seriousness. Offending may also be aggravated where the offender holds another trusted position in the legal system (e.g. a rehabilitation provider giving false evidence). Targeting police (bribery — refusal of the bribe does not meaningfully reduce seriousness; entrapment may reduce sentence; less serious without threats) or judges (treated very seriously: the public must not be left with the perception that judges do not treat bribery seriously) is serious; as with police, actions against lawyers may also be serious (e.g. threats to a prosecutor to secure the withdrawal of charges).

title: Contempt: gravity (wilful v inadvertent; jurors and witnesses; disobedience; refusal to give evidence)
statement: Contempt is serious in any form (threat to the rule of law); wilful (deliberate or contumacious) contempt is more serious than inadvertent or technical. Interfering with jurors (naming, threatening, abusing) is very serious, and so is interfering with witnesses (who may not give evidence at all, or may shade it); prejudicial publication needs no intent, but absence of intent is an important mitigating factor. Orders must be strictly obeyed until discharged, even if their validity is doubted (the Manual notes the limits of this principle for orders of an inferior court without jurisdiction: fn 4518, flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6); public defiance may increase gravity; continuing disobedience despite notice of the order and of the contempt proceedings aggravates; contempt by a large representative body (like a union) is more serious than by an individual; and a public disturbance requiring considerable resources to maintain order is more serious; distinguish the tendency to frustrate the order (gravity) from the contemnor’s intentions, which 29.2.2.2 says are only relevant to culpability — though it ends by saying that the consequences of publication are relevant to culpability (flag.contempt_gravity_culpability_29_2_2_2). For refusal to give evidence, consider the gravity of the underlying offence and, where possible, the likely weight of the evidence withheld (often not possible, and unreliable); refusal is generally more serious than a false claim of inability (perjury).

title: Contempt: considerations in punishment; endorsement rule; aggravation proved beyond reasonable doubt
statement: Consider whether disobedience was wilful or based on an honest though unreasonable belief. Protect jurors; consider the type of threat and capacity to carry it out and the objective effect on the trial. Where an order lacks the indorsement the Supreme Court rules require (a warning that non-compliance exposes the offender to imprisonment for contempt), hesitate to imprison — though a fine for wilful contempt is not precluded; waiver should not be done lightly and requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of awareness of obligations and consequences. Non-exhaustive considerations are listed below (the weight of having sought legal advice depends on what the evidence discloses of it; an offender who maintains privilege cannot complain if it gets little weight; an organisational system for preventing contempt is an important mitigating factor, undercut by failing to comply with it). Bankruptcy does not preclude a fine nor justify imprisonment, and financial difficulty does not discount a fine. Aggravating factors must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

title: Perjury: gravity
statement: Perjury is serious whatever the motive (easy to commit, hard to detect; undetected perjury produces injustice and erodes confidence), even for seemingly minor matters such as a false driver nomination to avoid a parking or traffic fine. Curial perjury is more serious than non-curial; curial perjury not producing a false conviction or acquittal may be less serious than perjury exposing another to conviction. Perjury by police and lawyers is more serious; repeated (not spur of the moment) perjury is more serious; foreseeable impact on a third party is relevant.

title: Offences against justice: purposes
statement: Perverting calls for sentences that denounce (even lower-range conduct) and deter. title: Offences against justice: formulation (cumulation; contempt penalties and the Sentencing Act; perjury custody)
statement: Perverting offences are indictable, forfeiture and forensic sample offences, not triable summarily; cumulation may suit attempts linked to avoiding detection for other offences. Contempt should be approached, so far as possible, consistently with criminal conduct generally: in the higher courts the penalty is at large, and in all courts common-law principles apply (parsimony, single course of conduct, totality); penalties include imprisonment for a definite or indefinite term, fines, sequestration, and (Supreme Court) a suspended sentence, including on a condition of unpaid community work; coercive punishment of indeterminate length may suit an ongoing refusal to give evidence. There is “some question” how far the Sentencing Act applies — it does not apply in its entirety (sections specifically held to apply include: non-parole periods, order of sentences, concurrency and cumulation, youth detention orders, imprisonment, fines, recording or not recording a conviction, discharge and dismissal), and some community-based options might be inconsistent with the superior court’s power to commit for a fixed term — so the hard order checks treat a contempt sentence as a caution, not an error (flag.contempt_sentencing_act_and_orders). A conviction may be recorded only for criminal contempt, which is more likely to lead to imprisonment. Costs may be awarded, but imprisonment in default of costs is improper; no statutory categories apply. Perjury: full concurrency would be very rare; for curial perjury custodial sentences should be imposed unless there are exceptional circumstances; indictable, forfeiture and forensic sample offence; may be heard summarily.

title: Riot, violent disorder and affray: offences and current practice
statement: Common law riot, rout and affray were abolished in 2017 (replaced by violent disorder and statutory affray). Riot prosecutions are rare and practice cannot be discerned (most 2016–2021 sentences relate to one serious prison riot, which cannot indicate practice for riot in general); violent disorder is too new. Affray practice varies widely: short custodial sentences are common where serious injury or death occurs; CCOs, fines or good behaviour bonds are within range for less serious cases with compelling mitigation.

title: Riot (by analogy, rout) and violent disorder: gravity and individual culpability
statement: Riot derives gravity from numbers (crowd psychology, sudden escalation); principal factors are size (numbers, duration, alarm), actual violence and harm. Participants bear some responsibility for collective harm, adjusted for their part and blame; an individual’s culpability is not assessed in isolation. Culpability factors: leadership/encouragement (aggravating); no planning or premeditation (mitigating); attacks on police or prison officers (aggravating; generally custody); disguises (relevant to whether the participant intended violence); harm to persons or property; knowledge or foresight of danger or injury. The Manual states this reasoning for riot; apply it to rout by analogy. Violent disorder does not replicate riot but is intended to capture much of its conduct (a violent mob mentality); maximum 10 years, or 15 years for the aggravated form (face covering) — where aggravated violent disorder is charged, the face covering is an element and must not also be counted as aggravating (limb below).

title: Affray: gravity and individual culpability
statement: Affray requires unlawful violence or threats that would terrify a reasonably firm person; seriousness varies with duration, numbers, weapons and injuries. It is a collective offence: individual acts are not taken in isolation, as any participation promotes the totality of the affray. Statutory affray (s 195H): maximum 5 years, or 7 years for the aggravated form (face covering — then an element, not separately aggravating); common-law affray had a 5-year maximum and no aggravated form (register). Factors: extent of injury (but do not sentence for more serious offending the offender is not responsible for); location (public and moving; private with witnesses or children); planning (pre-arranged armed meetings are serious); weapons (aggravating even if unused); role (leadership, capacity to stop it, recruiting, enthusiastic participation).

Affray: gravity and individual culpability
Affray requires unlawful violence or threats that would terrify a reasonably firm person; seriousness varies with duration, numbers, weapons and injuries. It is a collective offence: individual acts are not taken in isolation, as any participation promotes the totality of the affray. Statutory affray (s 195H): maximum 5 years, or 7 years for the aggravated form (face covering — then an element, not separately aggravating); common-law affray had a 5-year maximum and no aggravated form (register). Factors: extent of injury (but do not sentence for more serious offending the offender is not responsible for); location (public and moving; private with witnesses or children); planning (pre-arranged armed meetings are serious); weapons (aggravating even if unused); role (leadership, capacity to stop it, recruiting, enthusiastic participation).

title: Public order offences: purposes, parity and double punishment
statement: Riot: general deterrence is key (especially prison riots). Affray: general and specific deterrence, denunciation and community protection (courts frequently condemn groups of men who go out drinking and “throw their weight around”; where the motive is revenge, general deterrence and denunciation are important). Rehabilitation may get more weight for youthful offenders. Parity across many offenders: pragmatic approach from the first sentence, explaining disparities without mathematical precision. Where affray and offences arising from or contributing to it are sentenced together, take care to avoid double punishment: the affray sentence cannot be increased for shared elements (e.g. causing injury), and cumulation should be limited consistently with totality.

title: OHS offences: scope; summary jurisdiction; forfeiture
statement: Most OHS offences are under the OHSA (other safety statutes and the harmonised WHS laws are outside the chapter). title: Offences before 1 July 2005: OHSA 1985 general penalties and the s 53 additional penalty for prior convictions
statement: Most of the OHSA commenced on 1 July 2005; earlier offending fell under the OHSA 1985, s 47 general penalties: indictable 500 penalty units (individual) / 2500 (company); summary 100 / 400. All OHSA 1985 breaches were indictable; breaches of regulations could be summary. With a prior OHSA 1985 conviction, s 53 allowed an additional penalty: indictable — individual 10–500 penalty units and up to 5 years’ imprisonment, company 50–2500 penalty units; summary — individual 10–200 penalty units and up to 2 years’ imprisonment, company 50–400 penalty units. Where s 53 is invoked the court identifies the further penalty and omits prior convictions from the base penalty (no double counting), without a two-step process (this statutory additional penalty is not a breach of the rule against using priors in aggravation: audit.priors_and_remorse_not_aggravating). Factors: nature and number of priors, proximity, relevance, character, and whether the priors and present convictions show a systemic, general or flagrant failure to comply. The current OHSA has no additional-penalty provision. The intake must capture the offence date.

title: OHS: gravity is the breach and the risk (“measure of evidenced disregard”); the outcome illuminates the risk
statement: OHS offences are not merely quasi-criminal (heavy maxima). Company and individual (even a sole director) are assessed separately. Punish the gravity of the breach, not its consequences: the scheme is generally risk-based (death or injury is not an element of most OHS offences, though s 32 requires serious injury), and death or injury is relevant to gravity only so far as it shows the seriousness of the risk; harm proved beyond reasonable doubt to have resulted directly is also taken into account as victim impact (31.3.2.4, 31.6.1) — the Manual states both positions (flag.ohs_outcome_relevance). Gravity = seriousness of the departure from duty + extent of risk (likelihood of an endangering event and potential gravity of the consequence): the “measure of evidenced disregard”. High consequences from an unforeseeable, low-end breach remain low-end; the next level is a failure, through inadvertence or negligence, to appreciate a risk the offender should have dealt with; the gravest is wilful disregard of a known risk; where a risk is self-evident or identified, having no system for it (especially at no cost) increases moral culpability. Employers cannot let employees improvise or rely on their skills, and must ensure the person responsible for safety is appropriate; directing dangerous work significantly aggravates; wilful disregard by the responsible person aggravates; employees’ foolish risks do not lessen seriousness.

title: OHS: foreseeability of risk; notice; special or obvious risks
statement: Foreseeability concerns the risk, not the precise accident (an accident may be evidence of whether the risk was reasonably foreseeable). No prior incidents or complaints does not reduce gravity (the employer must ensure safe systems), but ignoring explicit notice (inspector warnings, prior incidents or checks) aggravates (the Manual notes contrary authority: fn 4681, flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6). Employers must be alert to special or unexpected industry risks; failure to foresee them is not exculpatory unless nothing more could reasonably be done; exotic or unforeseen risks (e.g. activity outside training) may mitigate. Failures regarding self-evident or inherent risks, or obvious equipment defects, are serious departures.

title: Workplace manslaughter: negligent manslaughter principles apply
statement: Principles for negligent manslaughter are useful (the Manual cross-refers to 22.2.2); the degree of negligence and its duration matter: continued or repeated negligence despite obvious risks, or blatant disregard, is more culpable than an aberration or temporary lapse; seriousness is assessed substantially by the measure of evidenced disregard for safety.

title: OHS: responsible actor, safety systems, worker non-compliance, harm and causation
statement: Most OHSA offences are absolute liability; the origin of the failure matters to culpability. Each duty-holder’s duties are unaffected by others’ failures; sentence depends on control and involvement; senior employees with safety responsibility generally receive higher sentences. The OHSA requires reasonably practicable steps: the key is the failure to do what was reasonably practicable, not the incident — failure to follow management’s systems v failure to establish them. Employers need not prevent all accidents but must take reasonably practicable measures; high-risk environments require strict, rigorous, religiously maintained standards; systems are judged in context (industry practice is relevant). Worker contraventions do not excuse the employer (being “let down” is not mitigating; the employer cannot claim incapacity to control employees, especially when a known disregard of procedures continues); systems must be actively implemented (31.3.2.3). Exposure of anyone present is relevant; the actual result is of very limited relevance to gravity, though direct injury or death may be considered as an impact of the offence — but causation is not part of the offence, may be difficult to determine after conviction and must be proved beyond reasonable doubt before it is used, and a court using injuries to assess risk must ensure a causal relationship (31.3.2.4; flag.ohs_outcome_relevance). Long or ongoing breaches and vulnerable exposed persons are serious.

title: OHS: offender circumstances (remorse, plea, priors, size, community involvement)
statement: Objective seriousness takes precedence; offender circumstances matter less. Post-incident rectification may show remorse and rehabilitation, but less so after considerable prior disdain (and may show risks were easily avoidable); examples: independent audits, training and maintenance, going above and beyond WorkSafe requirements. Pleas retain utilitarian value (less if late). No adverse finding from declining an interview; trial conduct may bear on remorse. Evading responsibility (qualifications, liquidation or phoenixing, litigating against employees) may show an absence of genuine remorse; supporting employees and paying debts, and executives attending, count in favour; remorse is judged through authorised representatives (the Manual notes contrary authority on phoenixing and corporate remorse: fns 4723, 4728, flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6). Prior convictions are viewed in context (the company as a whole; historical convictions of previous entities of limited relevance; scale of operations and exposure to risk; directors of new companies); a good safety record mitigates. Size does not affect the standard of care or culpability but is relevant to means (fine), context and exposure, criminal history, and the offender’s position (e.g. statutory bodies); charitable and community activity indicates good corporate citizenship (directors’ to a limited extent).

title: OHS: purposes (general deterrence; specific deterrence for corporations)
statement: General deterrence is significant: Parliament’s high maxima require a penalty sufficient to compel attention to safety and prevent future risks; hopelessly inadequate systems or a cavalier attitude increase the need for punishment and denunciation; rarely, a widely publicised incident may itself deter. Retribution and rehabilitation have very little role for corporations (authority drawn from antitrust cases: fn 4747); specific deterrence is the means (previous OHS convictions may bear on its importance, though isolated priors may not show persistent disregard; remorse and cooperation reduce it; failing to remediate or comply with notices increases it). Liquidation does not automatically reduce specific deterrence (those behind the company; but 31.7.2 says that for a company in liquidation specific deterrence has little or no part: flag.ohs_liquidation_specific_deterrence).

title: OHS: rolled-up charges, VIS, conviction, fines, aggregate fines, and OHSA orders
statement: Breaches of one provision in ss 21–32 from the same facts may be rolled up (single penalty; same maximum). Although OHS offences are generally risk-based, the court must take into account injury, loss or damage resulting directly from the offence, including through victim impact statements. Usual sanction is a fine (adjourned undertakings possible). Not recording a conviction against a company is significant leniency; serious offending should still be convicted (the Manual notes contrary authority: fn 4760); a conviction may be recorded against the company but not the director. Fines: not a valuation of a life; the court must consider the offender’s financial circumstances as far as practicable, but they cannot immunise a company — the fine must be commensurate with objective seriousness and general deterrence, and its symbolic importance must not be overlooked; inability to pay does not prevent a fine; fines may be ordered against insolvent companies (general deterrence); for a company in liquidation, the judge must ignore the fact that it is in liquidation and that the fine will never be paid, and consider its assets and prospects at the time of trading (31.7.2: specific deterrence then has little or no part — but 31.5 says liquidation does not automatically reduce it: flag.ohs_liquidation_specific_deterrence); post-incident safety spending is not deducted; stays or instalments must not let the fine become a cost of doing business. Directors may be made jointly and severally liable where the company cannot pay and insolvency was foreseeable, unless they reasonably believed solvency and took reasonable steps. For separate penalties on company and director (especially a sole director and shareholder), consider the aggregate, who bears the penalty, each one’s capacity to pay, and whether the company will meet the fines (e.g. phoenixing); a sole director affects quantum, not the penalty itself. Aggregate fines (including for rolled-up or representative charges; not exceeding the sum of maxima) may reflect totality; different duties to different classes of persons may warrant individual penalties (but see fn 4784: flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6). OHSA orders: reinstatement or damages for discrimination; adverse publicity orders (protective; on the court’s initiative or the prosecutor’s application; costs not exceeding the maximum; notice of the offence, consequences, penalty and related matters, with evidence to WorkCover); improvement projects (conditions; costs not exceeding the maximum); release on a health and safety undertaking for up to two years — equivalent to a release on adjournment and available in addition to other penalties — with three mandatory conditions and special conditions.

title: Inchoate maxima: the register row for the charge; general rows yield to specific ones; life is not a “prescribed maximum”; attempt 60% rule
statement: Use the register row for the charge. Many inchoate maxima are “the maximum penalty which applies to the primary offence” (for multiple offences, the accumulated maxima). The general Crimes Act rows for a mandatory penalty and a penalty “at large” apply only “unless otherwise covered by another item in this table” (fns 4804–4807). Conspiracy or incitement where the penalty is at large (s 321C(1)(b), s 321I(1)(b)): Level 4 – 15 years. Because life imprisonment is not “a prescribed maximum penalty”, the operative maximum for a Crimes Act conspiracy (or incitement) to commit an offence punishable by life is 15 years (Dimozantos; fn 4805, repeated in fn 4807) — but not for conspiracy or incitement to murder or treason (s 321C(1)(ba), s 321I(1)(ba): Level 1 – life; the footnotes’ carve-out is worded inconsistently: flag.inchoate_life_maximum_footnotes), and not where another row covers the charge: DPCS s 79 conspiracy and s 80 incitement to certain drug offences carry the primary offence’s maximum (guide.drugs.extended_liability). Summary-only offences: Level 6 – 5 years or the primary maximum, whichever is greater. Attempts: s 321P(1)(a) “as set out in the table” (not reproduced: flag.attempt_table_not_reproduced; it applies with necessary changes to interstate penalties); where the penalty is not specified by a Level in that table, 60% of the maximum for the offence (s 321P(1)(b)); at large, Level 6 – 5 years; attempted murder or treason, Level 2 – 25 years; a lower penalty in another enactment prevails (s 321P(2)); an attempt outside Victoria carries the maximum in that place (a penalty above life is read as life); attempts within DPCS ss 71–71AC, 72–72B and 73 carry the primary offence’s maximum, and s 191(1) (attempting to fraudulently induce investment) is Level 4 – 15 years. The Commonwealth rows (32.1.2) are outside the app’s scope.

title: Inchoate offences: current practice (conspiracy, incitement, attempts)
statement: Conspiracy does not inevitably attract less than the completed offence. Incitement convictions are relatively rare (most commonly incitement to murder, which may merit more than some murders; upper-range incitement to murder indistinguishable from conspiracy to murder should align with conspiracy sentences). Attempts ordinarily attract less than completed offences even without a lower maximum — an approach that accords with the Crimes Act penalty scheme (s 321P(1)(a)) — because an attempt usually causes less harm (treating attempted murder as seriously as murder is “an affront to common sense”; an attempted aggravated sexual assault is not as serious as the completed offence) and to preserve the incentive to desist. The significant exceptions are attempted drug offences (many DPCS offences include attempted conduct without differentiation in penalty) and attempting to pervert the course of justice; where a benign substance was substituted by authorities there is little difference between attempt and completion.

title: Inchoate offences: gravity (content and probability of success; plotting is dangerous)
statement: Inchoate offences vary widely; seriousness is coloured by the substantive offence, and an attempt at a serious offence is serious. Equal maxima for some conspiracies show Parliament’s view; attempts are not ordinarily commensurate with conspiracy (different elements; a lower maximum). Conspiracy’s essence is joint plotting, which is inherently dangerous (likelihood, capability, further plans, difficulty of detection). Gravity of conspiracies and attempts turns on the content (the offence contemplated or attempted and the consequences if completed) and the probability of success (distance travelled, real prospects, performance, duration and reality; sophisticated or naïve, serious or half-hearted, competent or mismanaged). The improbability or impossibility of success is relevant to the criminality of most conspiracies and attempts (commonly little weight for incomplete drug offending); lack of equipment, means or intelligence may reduce criminality; withdrawal or failure to proceed from a very early stage may be less serious (each case on its merits); a sophisticated near-success weighs more than a naïve attempt. Thwarting by police, prevention measures, luck or bungling does not reduce criminality. Content and probability are weighed in all the circumstances: a hopeless attempt at a serious offence is not necessarily less serious than a near-complete attempt at a lesser one, though the difference between well- and poorly planned attempts diminishes as the substantive offence’s seriousness decreases. Harm caused or avoided is relevant, but attempted violent thefts that terrify are not much less serious. For incitement the key is the offence incited.

title: Conspiracy: individual culpability
statement: Besides the content of the conspiracy and its probability of success, culpability depends on role, benefit and participation (instigators and greater beneficiaries more culpable; the sentence reflects the organisational nature of the conspiracy and the offender’s role, not only acts performed; involvement may vary between co-conspirators, and comparative financial gain may guide), duration, planning and sophistication (deliberately hard to detect), and persistence despite detection or desistance before it.

title: Inchoate offences: victims, remorse, purposes and overt acts
statement: Intended victims (or those who would have been present) are victims once relevantly affected by learning of the plan. Remorse takes the form of contrition for the prospective damage. General deterrence is normally primary for conspiracy; general deterrence, denunciation and just punishment are important for incitement and attempts, coloured by the substantive offence. Where overt acts are one transaction with the conspiracy, no separate sentence may be appropriate; overt acts are not aggravated merely because part of a conspiracy; where separate sentences are imposed, avoid double punishment by limiting the sentence on the conspiracy or the overt acts, or by identifying their separate criminality.

title: Firearms offences: scope of the chapter; prohibited persons
statement: The Firearms Act 1996 contains a spectrum of summary and indictable offences (possess/use/carry for prohibited and non-prohibited persons; acquire/dispose; discharge; firearm prohibition orders; manufacture; safety, alteration, administration, storage). The chapter focuses on prohibited person possess firearm, discharge offences and contravening a firearm prohibition order, plus imitation firearms (Control of Weapons Act) and (Commonwealth) importation. A person may be a prohibited person in several circumstances, including having served (in the past 15 years) or serving a term of imprisonment for an indictable offence or some drug and weapons offences, or being subject to a final family violence or personal safety intervention order or a community-based order (Firearms Act s 3). A “prohibited weapon” includes an imitation firearm.

title: Prohibited person possess firearm: current practice (Berichon categories)
statement: Practice generally follows Berichon: (1) possession not associated with ongoing criminal activity — usually a low order of imprisonment unless criminal history warrants more (normally under two years); (2) possession for a criminal activity or purpose (security, enforcement) — more severe. The categories do not fetter discretion: each sentence turns on the particular circumstances of the offending and the offender. Imprisonment is most common; avoid double punishment with sentences for offending related to the same firearm (fn 4875 cross-refers to “1.4.1 – Double punishment below”; the chapter’s double punishment discussion is 33.4.1); a combination of imprisonment and a lengthy CCO may suit compelling mitigation, but may be out of range alongside other serious offences. On the use of criminal history see flag.firearm_status_priors_aggravation.

title: Firearm possession offences: gravity
statement: Possession offences are very serious: obvious risk of serious injury or death, heightened by association with criminal enterprise even without use. Objective gravity is primarily influenced by the Berichon categories (possession without a criminal purpose is generally less morally culpable), but they are not fixed sub-categories. Factors that may elevate seriousness even without a criminal purpose: criminal history (especially firearms priors); circumstantial evidence of unlawful purpose (but be cautious — absent direct evidence, a criminal purpose should be inferred only if it is the only reasonable inference; lack of a credible explanation may be insufficient); ammunition; no lawful use; cut-down firearms (little leniency). Factors that may aggravate: number; nature (modified, home-made, high-powered); loaded or with ammunition; insecure and readily accessible; duration (longer may aggravate; short possession by design to avoid detection may not mitigate); prohibited person or FPO status and the nature and extent of prior history; value. Less serious: non-functional firearm (cannot be fired, not merely unloaded) and no ammunition. Each possession offence also has its own policy considerations (guide.firearms.specific_possession_offences). Criminal history and status: they must not lift the sentence beyond what the offence warrants, and where the status is an element it is not counted again (flag.firearm_status_priors_aggravation).

title: Prohibited persons, traffickable quantities, imitation firearms and firearm prohibition orders
statement: Prohibited person possession reflects the Act’s purpose of public safety and peace by keeping firearms from those who cannot meet community standards (e.g. prior criminal history, intervention orders, criminal enterprises); criminal history and criminal associations are particularly relevant; possession may be less serious where the prohibition stems from unrelated minor matters (e.g. a previous intervention order) with no firearm or violence history. Traffickable quantity (prohibited and non-prohibited persons alike) targets the prevalence and harm of illegal firearms, their commercial movement, the risks of accumulation and the difficulty of detection; the threshold was reduced from 10 to three to two; the number above the threshold corresponds to seriousness. Imitation firearms: seriousness varies with prohibited status; for prohibited persons the same maximum “suggests” equal severity, but sentences treat them as less serious than real firearms (flag.imitation_weapon_competing_authority); victims may believe they could be shot, so incapacity to fire may be of limited relevance; possession unconnected with a criminal purpose may be less serious. Firearm prohibition orders (introduced 2018; made in the public interest by the Chief Commissioner where a firearm may be used to endanger public peace and safety): contravention is particularly aggravated if soon after service; deliberate defiance significantly increases culpability.

title: Importing firearms (Commonwealth offences)
statement: Importation offences are Commonwealth offences (outside this app’s Victorian scope): Customs Act tier 2 goods, 10 years; Criminal Code import prohibited firearms, 20 years, and life for 50 or more firearms within six months. They are very serious because firearms are a grave danger and more durable than drugs (a lasting threat until seized); relevant factors include the nature and number of firearms, ammunition, motives, planning, concealment and difficulty of detection; an attempted importation is still serious. A person punished for a Criminal Code traffick-firearms offence cannot be punished again for the same conduct under the Customs Act.

title: Discharging a firearm with reckless disregard (at premises or vehicles)
statement: Maximum 15 years (s 131A(1)); 20 years if while carrying out a serious indictable offence (s 131A(2): the table and the register say “serious indictable offence”; the 33.2.3 text says “an indictable offence”). The high penalties reflect potentially lethal consequences; the offence was introduced in 2018 in response to a perceived increase in drive-by shootings (before then it would likely have been charged as reckless conduct endangering life or serious injury, 10 and 5 years). Key aggravating feature: discharge at a person, or at premises or vehicles where people may be present (e.g. the bullet strikes the victim; residential premises when occupants are likely present; a vehicle known or inferred to be occupied). Other indicia: premeditation and planning (stolen or hired vehicles, sourcing a weapon, stealth); nature of firearm (semi- or fully automatic, high-powered); motivation; aim and penetration; role; whether anyone was injured. Discharge with no one nearby may be less serious; the indicia measure the risk and the offender’s culpability. The 33.2.3 discussion is of s 131A; for Crimes Act s 31C(2) (discharge reckless to the safety of police or protective services officers, 15 years) the Manual gives no offence-specific gravity guidance (limb).

title: Firearms offences: double punishment with related charges; the s 7C(2) bar
statement: Firearm possession is often charged with other offences whose elements overlap (e.g. armed robbery) or which it aggravates (e.g. threat to kill). Where the firearm aggravates another charge and a prohibited person possession charge is also laid, the possession charge must not be elevated to the criminal-purpose category because of that other offending, nor include penalty for that use; it may be elevated only on evidence of a distinct criminal purpose (then modest cumulation is not double punishment). If possession is sentenced in the serious category, it cannot also aggravate the other charge, though totality may justify a higher individual sentence and cumulation where possession materially adds to overall criminality. Multiple charges about the same firearm (possession and discharge; possession and disposal; FPO contraventions) risk double punishment — do not treat possession more seriously because the firearm was discharged in other criminal activity that is separately punished — but distinct criminality (especially FPO contraventions) may warrant higher sentences and some cumulation; aggregate sentences may avoid double punishment. The Manual cross-refers to 3.4.7 (double punishment, weapons offences).

title: Terrorism offences: almost exclusively Commonwealth; the Victorian s 4B(1) offence
statement: Terrorism offences are governed almost exclusively by the Criminal Code (Cth) after the 2002 referral of State powers; the chapter covers terrorism offences and related post-sentence orders, primarily Parts 5.3 (terrorist act including preparatory acts; terrorist organisations; financing) and 5.5 (foreign incursion and recruitment); other “terrorism offences” (Division 72 Subdivision A, Division 80 Subdivision B, Charter of the United Nations Act) are outside the Manual. The Victorian offence listed is providing documents or information facilitating terrorist acts, Terrorism (Community Protection) Act 2003 s 4B(1), Level 5 – 10 years (from 16 April 2003). Most guidance in this chapter derives from Commonwealth cases; apply it to the Victorian offence with that caution, and never apply the Commonwealth regimes (guide.terrorism.cth_regimes) to it.

statement: Few cases limit the utility of a range. Victorian sentences have been uplifted (the gap with NSW arguably closed); in 2017 the Court of Appeal said the Benbrika sentences seemed unduly lenient and would not be imposed today, so pre-2017 practice should be approached with caution.

title: Terrorism: general gravity considerations; victims; conspiracy; impossibility
statement: Terrorism offences are inherently serious. Considerations: planning, research, complexity, sophistication and commitment; duration; depth of radicalisation (extremist material, communications); indoctrination of others and their vulnerability; the maximum. Prolonged planning to massacre civilians is of extremely high gravity (particularly where the offender appreciates the wrongfulness); targeting police, public events on national holidays and willingness to kill civilians suggest very high moral culpability. Continued adherence to a violent ideology is not ordinarily aggravating, but its abandonment (proved by the offender) mitigates; relatively superficial conviction may attenuate gravity. Victims’ circumstances and harm (including witnesses) must be considered (the Manual’s source is Commonwealth: Cth Crimes Act s 16A(2)(d)–(e), fn 4958; for the Victorian s 4B(1) offence see factor.statutory_victim_and_harm); harm includes harm to the public and polity, not mathematically related to victim numbers. Terrorist conspiracies are more serious than individual offending (agreement more advanced, joint effort more likely to succeed, harder to detect and shut down, more enduring zeal). Incompetence or impracticability does not diminish a serious offence.

title: Terrorism: gravity of document-making offences
statement: Relevant considerations: length and detail of the document; whether intended to result in violent attacks and incite others; clandestine distribution (dark web, rallies); recruiting others to review drafts; time spent. That the ideas are “fanciful, immature rubbish” unlikely to produce an attack may be of no mitigating consequence. These factors are stated for a Commonwealth document-making offence (DPP (Cth) v Galea, fn 4971); the Manual does not say they apply to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence, so apply them by analogy, with that caution.

title: Terrorism: offender circumstances (renunciation, plea, mental condition, youth)
statement: Mitigating personal factors get substantially less weight. Respectful, co-operative conduct at trial may be disregarded as mitigation, and disruption need not be treated as aggravating. Renunciation of extremist beliefs is crucial to rehabilitation (adherence at the time of the offence and at sentencing is a crucial question; if the views are no longer held, the court must make an allowance); the offender must prove it on the balance of probabilities (public renunciation especially compelling; transformation without contrition, or in sheltered custody, is viewed sceptically; conversion to another religion is unnecessary). The plea’s utilitarian value has no special weight; it may cautiously indicate relenting; late pleas, or prior explicit contempt (remorse then credible perhaps only if given in oral evidence and tested), weaken remorse; boasting admissions earn only a modest discount. Mental condition may make the offender an inappropriate vehicle for general deterrence, reduce specific deterrence or make custody more onerous, and a causal relationship with extremist beliefs has sometimes been taken into account. Young offenders can plan carefully: youth is relevant but its weight may diminish measurably for planned extreme violence (general deterrence and denunciation may take primacy; rehabilitation moderated); radicalisation at 17 did not of itself reduce culpability (Alou), though immaturity rather than fanaticism may earn significant consideration (Bayda).

title: Terrorism: purposes
statement: Purposes: prevent circumstances increasing the likelihood of terrorist acts, punish and denounce, incapacitate and protect the community — substantial weight to denunciation, general deterrence, community protection and just punishment; personal mitigation gets substantially less weight. Intending to die does not reduce deterrence (the Manual notes contrary remarks: fn 5071, flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6). Preparatory offending is denounced in the strongest terms even where no harm results. Community protection looms large where views are retained (the concern is the perfection of the very crime); for lone wolf attacks community protection, punishment and general and specific deterrence are the focal points. Rejection of extremist views and rehabilitation may reduce specific deterrence and protection (lower head sentence and NPP), reflecting the community’s interest in minimising reoffending.

title: Commonwealth terrorist act and advocacy offences: gravity
statement: Engaging in a terrorist act spans mass murder to lesser property damage; look at all the circumstances. Religious and ideological motivation and intent to intimidate government distinguish it from private crimes, so comparison with (e.g.) attempted murder is wrong — though the public/private division is not binary (an unseen attack intended to advance an extremist cause and intimidate the public is no less serious, Shoma); spontaneity does not diminish gravity where the act grew from longstanding extremist views. An adult who equips and encourages a child to commit a terrorist act may be as culpable as the principal. Advocating terrorism is serious (it heightens the probability of an act in Australia) but, with a 5-year maximum, one of the least serious terrorist offences; relevant matters include the number and duration of acts of advocacy, social media, graphic imagery, enthusiasm, audience, original or reposted material and reference to Australia. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

title: Commonwealth terrorist organisation offences: gravity and culpability
statement: A terrorist organisation is one directly or indirectly engaged in preparing, planning, assisting or fostering a terrorist act, or a listed organisation. Its history bears on objective seriousness and culpability; seriousness depends on whether it advocates or engages in indiscriminate killing of civilians, is well organised and resourced with intention and capacity, is geographically confined, directly threatens Australia, and recruits children, engages in sexual violence or uses landmines. The court does not evaluate the merits of its ideology (a matter for the legislature) though it may take into account proved dangerousness; claimed commitments to international humanitarian law or to targeting only government forces may not reduce culpability; participation in a non-international armed conflict is irrelevant. Joining an established organisation “eyes wide open” may be more culpable than joining a “rag-tag collection of malcontents” after indoctrination, but membership is always very serious. Membership spans leadership to informal participation; knowledge of objectives and methods and duration matter; a passive, sympathetic chronicler is towards the lowest order; belief in the cause may not of itself affect culpability; membership connected to personal trauma and intergenerational persecution may reduce culpability, and a primary motive to oppose genocide may mitigate somewhat. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

title: Commonwealth preparatory terrorist offences: the two axes of seriousness
statement: Preparing for or planning a terrorist act is an offence even if no act occurs, without a specific target, or for more than one act; the provisions bite early; the life maximum is a salient indicator of seriousness. Because plots are often detected early and preparatory acts are indefinite, culpability is measured not only by the steps taken but by the nature and extent of the act contemplated — two axes: “actions in contemplation” (the criminal objective) and “acts actually done”; the most serious examples are far advanced on both. On the first axis (of fundamental importance) killing is more serious than property damage, deliberate killing than risk of death, many deaths than few; the absence of a finally selected target carries little weight; planning an attack on police or prison officers is very grave; the offender’s state of mind may be assessed from actions and plea. The second axis is assessed by the general considerations (34.2.1); considerable premeditation and methodical planning elevate dangerousness, and an intention still held at arrest, thwarted only by interception, is much more serious. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

The second axis is assessed by the general considerations (34.2.1); considerable premeditation and methodical planning elevate dangerousness, and an intention still held at arrest, thwarted only by interception, is much more serious. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

title: Commonwealth financing terrorism offences: gravity
statement: Relevant factors: the amount, the identity of the organisation, and the offender’s surrounding conduct. Even a relatively small amount ($5,000 enabling travel to assist Islamic State, Atai) may be a serious example, and elaborate steps over a long period magnify criminality (a significant organisational role). Where an undercover operation meant the funds could never reach the organisation, the offence may still be substantially serious (a broad analogy with drug supply that does not reach the public): that the funds did not arrive is relevant, but the intention to provide them and the failure to stop the transaction remain primary. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

title: Commonwealth foreign incursion and recruitment offences: gravity; not a “species of terrorism”
statement: Since 1 December 2014 these offences are in Part 5.5 of the Criminal Code (CFIRA repealed); the life maximum for most plainly reflects increased gravity. CFIRA principles remain relevant and vice versa, bearing in mind the different penalty regimes (CFIRA’s “services” language does not exist for the Criminal Code offences). Gravity factors (Alqudsi): the nature and extent of the services, their intention and intended effect; others include duration, planning, commitment, range of conduct (reconnaissance, weapons, armed guard), personal involvement in overthrowing a government, awareness, allegiance, contact with organisations, indoctrination of others, whether an undercover operation was needed for the offence, extremist religious thinking, rank, and the risk of return with enhanced capabilities. Poor planning (a plot foredoomed, success extremely remote) may reduce gravity. Though now within the Cth Crimes Act definition of a terrorism offence, they should not be regarded as a “species of terrorism” (the Manual notes contrary authority: fn 5027, flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6) and must not be sentenced as terrorist act offences (their fault element lacks the ideological or coercive intent). The Manual says it is uncertain how far the designation has affected their inherent gravity: depth of radicalisation may be considered for Criminal Code offences, but extremist ideology may matter less for CFIRA offending, and statements of extremist belief, though synthesised, do not elevate CFIRA objective seriousness. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

title: Commonwealth terrorism offences: the s 19AG three-quarters non-parole rule
statement: For a Commonwealth terrorism offence (and attempt, incitement or conspiracy to commit one; other minimum non-parole period offences include Division 80 and espionage offences) the court must fix a single NPP of at least three-quarters of the head sentence, for all federal sentences the person is to serve, whether or not imposed at the same sitting; it supersedes a recognizance release order; for a federal offence that is not a minimum NPP offence sentenced with one, the rule is calculated by reference only to the minimum NPP offence(s). Life is taken to be 30 years (so a minimum NPP of 22 years 6 months). The court need not find what NPP would otherwise apply; it must not fix the NPP and work back, but impose a proportionate head sentence and then apply the rule, without ameliorating the head sentence to offset s 19AG. The rule applies only to imprisonment and does not affect other options. For an offender under 18, the rule applies unless exceptional circumstances justify a shorter NPP, treating community protection as paramount and the person’s best interests as primary. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

title: Commonwealth terrorism offenders: warning about post-sentence orders
statement: When sentencing for a specified terrorism offence, contravention of an extended or interim supervision order, or (if the DPP informs the court a warning must be given) contravention of a control order, the court must warn that an application may be made under div 105A for a continuing detention order or an extended supervision order, and that contravention of a continuing detention order is an offence; it must state when the AFP Minister may apply (before the end of that sentence, or any later sentence while continuously detained; for control order contraventions, before the end of that sentence), and may note that whether orders are made is for a court at the time. Failure to warn does not affect the sentence’s validity or prevent an application. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

title: Commonwealth post-sentence orders (div 105A): continuing detention and extended supervision orders
statement: Terrorist offenders who would pose an unacceptable risk of committing a serious Part 5.3 offence may be subject to post-sentence orders (PSOs): a continuing detention order (CDO: further detention in prison) or an extended supervision order (ESO: conditions after release; contravention is an offence); maximum 3 years each, successive orders possible; interim orders up to 28 days, totalling no more than 3 months per type absent exceptional circumstances. The Supreme Court may make them for an offender at least 18 at sentence end, detained in custody in a prison for a specified terrorism offence (Division 72 Subdivision A; a serious Part 5.3 offence, i.e. maximum 7 years or more; Part 5.5 except recruitment advertising; the repealed CFIRA except recruitment advertising), or already subject to a PSO. Application: by the AFP Minister, no earlier than 12 months before the sentence (or order) ends, after reasonable inquiries for facts that would support no order (no particular risk report is required); the Manual notes a sunset: no PSO may be applied for, affirmed or made after 7 December 2026 (fn 5120). Experts: a preliminary hearing within 28 days; the court may appoint experts; the offender must attend, and what they say is inadmissible against them except in div 104/105A proceedings. CDO: satisfied to a high degree of probability, on admissible evidence, of an unacceptable risk, and that no less restrictive Part 5.3 measure (control order, ESO) would be effective; “unacceptable risk” is flexible, weighing likelihood and seriousness, and need not be linked to a specific offence; the AFP Minister bears the onus; if not satisfied the court must consider an ESO. ESO: satisfied on the balance of probabilities of an unacceptable risk and that each condition and their combined effect is reasonably necessary and reasonably appropriate and adapted to protect the community (the object of div 105A is paramount); contents prescribed; an ESO revokes any CDO in force. Relevant considerations are listed (s 105A.6B). Conditions: broad (exclusion zones, residence, travel documents, non-communication, technology bans, programs), no more than 12 hours a day at specified premises; exemption conditions; variation on application. Review: the AFP Minister must apply within 12 months of commencement or the last review, or the PSO ceases. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.
