title: Confiscation orders: not part of the sentence, but may affect it
statement: The Confiscation Act 1997 is the primary mechanism (other legislation may also require confiscation). A confiscation order is not part of the sentence but imposed in addition; forfeiture can mitigate where it puts the offender in a worse position than before the offending (punitive and deterrent) — but see anc.confiscation.effect_on_sentence: orders disgorging profits are not considered, and the automatic forfeiture of a serious drug offender’s property must not be taken into account. Applications are best heard with or close to sentence. On appeal, confiscation orders are treated as part of the sentence.

title: Forfeiture orders and pecuniary penalty orders
statement: On conviction of a Schedule 1 offence (including a Schedule 2 offence) the court may, on application, order forfeiture of “tainted property” (specifying interests) or defer sentencing until the application is determined; property may be restrained around the time of charge. On application it may make a pecuniary penalty order equal to the benefits derived (reducible by restitution or compensation paid), and may defer sentence until that is determined. The Manual identifies Schedule 1/2 offences only for drug and property offences (28.7, 27.5.1: guide.drugs.statutory_schemes, guide.property.statutory_schemes); for other offences, (app policy) membership (and whether an application has been or will be made) must come from the user.

title: Automatic forfeiture (Schedule 2 offences; serious drug offenders)
statement: On conviction of a Schedule 2 offence where a restraining order was made and no exclusion order has been made, the property is automatically forfeited 60 days after the restraining order or conviction, whichever is later. Almost all property of declared serious drug offenders is automatically forfeited.

title: “Tainted property” and “benefits”
statement: Tainted property: property used or intended to be used in or in connection with the offence, or derived or realised from it or from the offence. “Used” has its ordinary meaning, and property is “used” only when it, or some feature of it, is turned towards bringing about the offender’s purpose; “in connection with” widens it; connection is a matter of degree and fact (no substantial connection needed); the nature and significance of use bear on the discretion; merely doing an act in or on property is normally insufficient; passive use makes connection less likely. Benefits (for PPOs) include money received (regardless of expenses), property derived, services or advantages, increases in property value, profits from depictions of the offence, and anything else the court considers appropriate.

title: Magistrates’ and Children’s Court limits on confiscation
statement: The Magistrates’ and Children’s Courts may not make forfeiture orders over real property, or orders whose value exceeds the Magistrates’ Court civil jurisdictional limit (unless personal injury damages are claimed); the Supreme or County Court may then make the order.

title: Considerations for forfeiture of tainted property
statement: Considerations include use of the property; hardship to anyone; others’ claims; value; nature and gravity of offending; involvement and history; other property confiscated; the penalty; the offender’s interest; drug value or crop size; acquisition with drug proceeds; utility to the offender; involvement in the offence; deterrence; and effect on rehabilitation. The discretion is broad.

title: Confiscation and sentence: proportionality, punishment, remorse and cooperation
statement: Proportionality requires due consideration of confiscation, but it is not always mitigating: does it have a disproportionate or deterrent effect? Forfeiture must be proportionate (unacceptable hardship can be critical). Orders disgorging profits are not considered; forfeiture of lawfully acquired property or PPOs exceeding profits may be; automatic forfeiture of a serious drug offender’s property must not be taken into account. Confiscation beyond profits is punishment and failing to consider it may be error; possible future forfeiture is considered with sufficient evidence, the offender bearing the burden on the balance of probabilities (credible material on lawful source; proof of loss beyond profits). A forfeiture order may indicate remorse or cooperation (no deeming); cooperation requires conscious facilitation, not a pragmatic decision.

title: Confiscation appeals; fresh evidence of true impact
statement: Anyone with an interest may appeal a forfeiture order or PPO (or refusal) as if part of the sentence; it may be confirmed, discharged, varied or remitted. Where the true impact emerges after sentence, it may be fresh evidence enlivening resentencing.

title: Compensation orders: civil, ancillary, additional to sentence
statement: Courts may order compensation for personal injury and property loss or damage, and restitution of property. Compensation is additional to sentence — a convenient mechanism for victims; an application is a civil proceeding ancillary to sentencing on the civil standard. The VOCA Act scheme operates independently and is not considered in the Manual. The Act has two independent, parallel schemes (personal injury; property).

title: Personal injury compensation: who, what injury, time limits
statement: A guilty or convicted person may be ordered to compensate someone who suffered any injury as a direct result of the offending (including other occurrences within a representative charge). “Injury” is defined as physical harm; mental illness or disorder (or exacerbation); pregnancy; grief, distress, trauma or other significant adverse effect; combinations — but not property loss. Only on application by the injured person (or on their behalf: for children or incapable persons; the DPP, informant or police prosecutor in the Magistrates’ Court; the DPP otherwise). Apply within 12 months after the finding of guilt or conviction (extendable in the interests of justice — viewed liberally, the court balancing finality and rehabilitation against the rights of victims; for a guilty plea time appears to run from sentence; for a person who has been convicted the Manual says it is unclear whether time runs from plea or finding of guilt or from sentence, although a person is generally “convicted” when the verdict or plea is accepted: flag.compensation_time_limit_start). Extension considerations: likely success in time; length of and reasons for delay; prejudice to rehabilitation; forensic disadvantage.

title: Property loss or damage compensation: application, court’s inquiry, own motion, timing
statement: On the victim’s application (or by the DPP; or DPP, informant or police prosecutor in the Magistrates’ Court). Where evidence of property loss or damage is presented the court must ask the prosecution whether an application will be made (its failure to ask does not prevent an application). The court may act on its own motion if the beneficiary does not oppose and the offender has been heard — but only for offences whose hearing commenced on or after 31 January 2013. Apply as soon as practicable (interpreted broadly, but no open-ended right; waiting to assess means is not as soon as practicable).

title: Compensation: procedural fairness; facts must sufficiently appear; clear cases only
statement: Procedural fairness applies; evidence may be given and tested. The court must hear and determine the application unless the relevant facts (commission, identity, injuries, impact, special expenses, causation) do not sufficiently appear; undisputed prosecution statements of facts and documentary evidence may be used. Orders suit only clear cases; significant unresolved factual conflicts, contribution and joint/several liability questions may make it too complex (leaving civil remedies), though the victim’s burden of civil proceedings is weighed.

title: Compensation: assessing the amount (synthesis; means; rehabilitation; no punitive damages; children $1000)
statement: The court intuitively synthesises seriousness, relationships, degree of injury, the offender’s financial circumstances, the effect on rehabilitation and the burden of payment. Means are relevant, not controlling; inability to discover means does not prevent an order. Balance compensation against rehabilitation (and denunciation). Child offenders cannot be ordered above $1000 and their means must be considered. Amounts follow common law damages principles (possibly contributory negligence) with heads expanded by statute; no punitive damages; amounts may be reduced to avoid over-compensation where claims cannot be tested (no blanket discount). Joint offenders: apportionment (not automatic) or joint and several liability; complexity may justify declining.

title: Compensation: heads of claim, causation, grief factors, property value cap, discounts, method and costs
statement: Personal injury heads: pain and suffering; reasonable counselling, medical and other non-property expenses (incurred or likely). “Direct result” uses tort causation and remoteness (a significant role or substantial operating cause; may develop gradually or appear later; feelings about the trial are too tenuous). Grief factors: circumstances of death, effect on hearing, closeness, applicant’s age, extent of suffering. Property compensation cannot exceed the property’s value; no order if property is recovered without loss. Reduce by VOCA awards (same head) and amounts repaid; avoid double compensation. Instalments may be ordered. Each party bears its own costs unless the court orders otherwise.

title: Compensation: combination with sanctions; priority over fines; appeal; judgment debt
statement: A compensation order is an independent discretionary consequence; it may accompany dismissals, discharges and adjournments and offences taken into account; it cannot be a condition of a CCO (but may accompany one as an ancillary order). The Manual says compensation orders are “relevant to assessing whether to impose a fine” (the court must consider their effect on the offender’s finances), while 12.3.1 says finances are irrelevant to whether to fine and are considered only after deciding to fine (flag.compensation_whether_to_fine; (app policy) compensation is treated as reducing the means available for a fine’s amount and payment, not as deciding whether to fine). If the offender cannot pay both, compensation has priority. It is “considered a sentence” under the Criminal Procedure Act, so an appeal is an appeal against sentence (leave required). Compensation and restitution orders are not regarded as punitive and so are not considered as punishment in sentencing (7.7.1, contrasting confiscation orders), though their effect on the offender’s finances bears on a fine (above); (app policy) it is not counted in the maxima or s 6AAA checks. It is a judgment debt; civil rights are unaffected.

title: Restitution orders (stolen goods)
statement: Where goods are stolen and a person is found guilty of a connected offence, the court may order return of the goods or replacement goods, payment of their value from money in the offender’s possession at arrest, or payment to good-faith purchasers or lenders. title: Forensic sample orders: not part of the sentence; forensic sample offences
statement: A forensic sample order directs a procedure to take a sample; commonly made at sentence but not part of it. title: Forensic sample orders: application, time limits, hearing, determination, reasons, review, retention
statement: Application usually by police (DPP in higher courts) specifying intimate or non-intimate sample; notice required for child offenders. Time: any time after the finding of guilt but no later than six months after the appeal period (or appeal determination); a 12-month limit applies in narrow circumstances to certain old drug offences. The offender is not a party and cannot call or cross-examine witnesses (adults may only respond to the court’s inquiries; children may address seriousness and justification). The court must consider the seriousness of the circumstances of the offence and be satisfied the order is justified in all the circumstances (the seriousness of the circumstances is the only mandated consideration; beyond it the discretion is very broad: recidivism risk is a common circumstance, the gravity of the offending may justify an order even without that risk, and social utility may also be relevant). The court must give reasons, serve the order and reasons, and inform that reasonable force may be used. Not appealable as part of sentence (judicial review). No order is needed to retain a sample already taken from an adult who is found guilty (or not guilty because of mental impairment) of one of the listed indictable offences; it may then be retained indefinitely, and must be destroyed if that finding is set aside on appeal unless retained for non-identifying statistical purposes. A retention order for a child requires a finding of guilt of the offence for which the procedure was conducted, an offence arising out of the same circumstances, or an offence on which evidence from the procedure had probative value, and an application within six months of the appeal period; retention orders for children follow the same considerations, and the same process applies on a finding of not guilty because of mental impairment, but not to an offence heard and determined summarily (19.4.2; whether that exclusion covers only the mental-impairment extension is not clear).

title: Alcohol exclusion orders (Sentencing Act): mandatory when criteria met
statement: A court must make an AEO if it records a conviction for a relevant offence and is satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the offender was intoxicated — defined as speech, balance, coordination or behaviour noticeably affected by the consumption of liquor (not drugs) — and that the intoxication significantly contributed, and the offender is not and has not been subject to a previous AEO for the current offence. AEOs last two years (from release if combined with or during custody; otherwise from the making of the order). Relevant offences are described by category (homicide, causing injury, administering substances, threats, endangering, kidnap and assault, certain resisting arrest and assisting offender offences, firearm use, certain adult and child sexual offences, CAM offences) and are not mapped to register ids, so (app policy) membership must be confirmed where the offence is not plainly within a category. An AEO prohibits consuming or attempting to consume liquor in licensed premises and entering or remaining at major events; exemptions are permitted for good reason where otherwise appropriate. With an AEO the court may not also make an EO or attach an alcohol exclusion condition to a CCO, but may combine an AEO with a CCO. Contravention: maximum Level 7 imprisonment. An AEO is capable of being punitive because it restrains liberty in addition to a sentence of imprisonment; those restraints are part of the circumstances the court must generally consider in the synthesis, and any further punitive element depends on the offender’s circumstances. Its punitive effect on sentence follows the principles printed at 11.4.2.8 (“The following principles apply to an alcohol exclusion order”; flag.aeo_principles_placement): an offender contending for additional punitive impact must say so expressly, with evidence, addressing the s 89DE(5) exemption, and the court should then make a finding and explain its effect.

title: Exclusion orders (Liquor Control Reform Act)
statement: An EO may be made if the offender is found guilty of a specified offence committed in a designated area, is not sentenced to 12 months’ imprisonment or more, and the EO may be an effective and reasonable means of preventing further specified offences there. title: Confiscation: the chapter’s scope; “used”; Magistrates’ and Children’s Court limits; a possible forfeiture is considered
statement: The Manual identifies only the parts of the Confiscation Act relevant to sentencing. For tainted property, “used” has its ordinary meaning (employed or made use of for a particular purpose or end). The Magistrates’ and Children’s Courts may not make a forfeiture order over real property, or (for a particular offence) a forfeiture order or PPO whose value exceeds the Magistrates’ Court civil jurisdictional limit unless personal injury damages are claimed. Where at sentence there is only a possibility of forfeiture, the Court of Appeal has held it should nonetheless be considered because it might constitute “substantial additional punishment” (subject to sufficient evidence: anc.confiscation.effect_on_sentence).

title: Compensation: extensions of time; “as soon as practicable”; order of the inquiry; facts that must be easily determined
statement: On an extension of time for personal injury compensation the court balances finality and rehabilitation against victims’ rights, viewing out-of-time applications liberally (a criminal, not civil, statute) but not permitting late applications that may significantly prejudice rehabilitation. For property, “as soon as practicable” depends on the circumstances and is read broadly for the claimant, but there is no open-ended right. Once compensation is applied for, the court first considers whether to grant it before the amount, and also whether the case is too complex; it should be able to determine the listed matters easily (including each offender’s order reflecting their individual contribution to the victim’s pain and suffering, and the offenders’ financial circumstances and burden — though an order may be made despite an inability to discover them). Difficulty may mean the facts do not sufficiently appear or the issues are too complex; no information may indicate the facts do not appear.

title: Compensation amount: the synthesis; the offender’s circumstances and rehabilitation; untested claims; pain and suffering; causation; grief
statement: Where there is an entitlement the court intuitively synthesises all the material circumstances (the listed matters). It may look at the offender’s personal circumstances (character, antecedents, age, health and any custodial burden) in assessing the burden, and most importantly the burden on rehabilitation. Because offenders may not be able to fully test the claims, the amount should give the victim “an appropriate measure of justice without running the risk of doing injustice to the offender”. “Pain and suffering” is undefined and assessed by intuition and experience. Causation: the damage must be reasonably foreseeable and not tenuously related; “direct” does not mean immediate, proximate or obvious — the crime must play a significant role or be a substantial and operating cause — assessed in a common-sense way (injury may be directly caused despite extraneous contributions, such as earlier abuse). Grief or trauma is assessed by the listed factors; the award is highly discretionary and views will differ widely. Depending on the circumstances the court may order no or reduced compensation, defer payment or order instalments; alternatively, it may order full compensation regardless of the offender’s circumstances, as long as they are taken into account.

title: Compensation: fire-fighting costs excluded; overlapping awards; Wrongs Act provisions; instalments; costs
statement: Compensable “property” may include motor vehicles and inheritances, but not a public authority’s costs of extinguishing a fire. Where awards overlap for the same head of damage the amount is reduced (the rest untouched); for overlaps not prescribed by legislation the court may reduce to avoid double payment, especially where the offender is serving a life sentence. After describing Part VBA of the Wrongs Act (thresholds for non-economic loss) the Manual says “These provisions do not apply to orders under the Act” (whether this covers only Part VBA or the Wrongs Act provisions generally is not stated: flag.wrongs_act_provisions_referent). A debtor may apply for an instalment order under the Judgment Debt Recovery Act 1984 s 6 even if the court did not order instalments. On costs the court considers the impact on the victim, complexity, the number of offences against the applicant, the time between offending and the award, the need for proper representation and the need for specialist medical opinions.

title: Restitution: the available orders; combined orders; timing; appeals and stays; when to leave parties to civil remedies
statement: A restitution order may direct that the goods be returned to the entitled person; that replacement goods (goods that “directly or indirectly represent the stolen goods”) be returned; that the goods’ value be paid to the entitled person from money in the offender’s possession at arrest; or that the purchase price be paid from that money to a third party who bought the goods in good faith or lent money on their security. Where goods are intermingled, only the parts that were stolen may be ordered restored. A combined order for replacement goods and money is allowed if the entitled person does not recover more than the goods’ value. Apply as soon as practicable after the finding of guilt or conviction. The offender may appeal, or the DPP where there is an error and it is in the public interest; a Supreme or County Court order is stayed during the appeal period unless otherwise directed. Parties should be left to civil remedies where there are significant factual conflicts requiring a complicated or extensive inquiry, where the evidentiary limits in s 84(8) cause difficulty, or where taking accounts or moulding equitable relief is required.

title: Alcohol exclusion orders: comparison-table criteria; application timing; content; exemptions and variation; the prohibitions
statement: In the Manual’s comparison table, the AEO column requires a recorded conviction for a relevant offence, no previous AEO for the offence circumstances, and satisfaction on the balance of probabilities that the offender was intoxicated and the intoxication significantly contributed; its conditions include a prohibition on consuming alcohol. The application must be filed and served before the first mention, committal mention or first directions hearing (or later with leave). An AEO must contain the offender’s name, the grounds, the prohibited conduct and any exemptions, and when it takes effect and its duration; exemptions (e.g. for weddings or sporting events) should be detailed. The court may vary an AEO if satisfied that new facts or circumstances have arisen and that there is a good reason why the offender should or should not be allowed to enter specified premises or an event, and it considers the variation appropriate; it may impose, vary or remove exemptions and must specify when the varied AEO takes effect. An AEO offender must not knowingly or recklessly enter, remain or attempt to in a prohibited place, or consume or attempt to consume liquor in licensed premises; it is not a contravention if caused by circumstances beyond their control and they took reasonable precautions.

title: LCRA exclusion orders: specified offences; the effectiveness considerations; the prohibitions
statement: Specified offences include causing injury and assault; threats, endangering conduct and administering substances; being armed with criminal intent and prohibited weapons; rape and sexual assault; destroying or damaging property; and offensive and obscene behaviour, disorderly conduct and failing to leave licensed premises. To decide whether an EO may be an effective and reasonable deterrent the court must consider the nature and gravity of the specified offence; prior findings of guilt for a specified offence in the designated area; any EO for another specified offence; the likely impact on the offender, any victim, public safety and public order; and any other relevant matter. An EO offender must not enter, re-enter or attempt to enter the designated area or licensed premises, and on contravening must obey a police officer’s lawful direction to leave. The offender, the DPP or a police officer may apply to the court that made the EO to vary it; the court may vary it in any way it considers appropriate if satisfied that facts or circumstances have arisen since the order (or its last variation) that make variation appropriate.

title: Each sentence is within the maximum applicable at the date of offending
statement: Misidentifying the maximum is appealable error unless immaterial. For offences before a change in penalty the court applies any reduction but never an increase, except that where the maximum was reduced and then increased again before sentence the court may sentence under the original maximum if the current one is of the same magnitude or higher. Counsel must check the maximum, and the parties’ agreement on it does not bind the court.

title: Penalty level and printed term disagree

Maxima for periods before 1 September 1997 use level/term pairs that do not follow the current table, and the Manual does not set out the scale then in force.

title: Magistrates’ Court jurisdictional limits
statement: Victorian summary offences: maximum two years’ imprisonment. Indictable offences heard summarily: two years per offence; cumulative terms for offences committed at the same time not over five years; fines up to 500 penalty units (2500 for a body corporate; 12.2 states the 2500-unit limit for a body corporate in any matter heard summarily). The limit is jurisdictional only. The Drug Court Division of the Magistrates’ Court is subject to the same limits.

title: Category 1 and Category 2 offences: imprisonment without a CCO (subject to the exceptions)
statement: For most Category 1 offences the court must imprison and not attach a CCO; the exception is for Category 1 offences that are also mandatory minimum offences against protected officials. For Category 2 offences it must imprison (without a CCO) unless a listed exception is established; the residual “substantial and compelling, exceptional and rare” exception is stringent. A special reason is an exception the mandatory minimum provisions provide (9.1.3): for a Category 1 offence with no mandatory minimum it does not exist.

title: Mandatory minimum non-parole periods and terms
statement: For the five groups (manslaughter, gross violence, protected officials, driving against protected officials, aggravated home invasion or carjacking) the court must impose imprisonment with at least the minimum non-parole period unless an exclusion applies (under 18 at the offence; the accessory rules stated for each group; the protected-official youth justice centre alternative) or a special reason is found and recorded in writing.

title: Non-parole period rules
statement: Imprisonment of two years or more requires a non-parole period unless inappropriate; none may be fixed if the total is under 12 months; it must be at least six months shorter than the total; standard sentence offences require at least 30 years (life), 70% or 60% unless not in the interests of justice (with reasons); an offender serving the non-parole period of a prior sentence gets a new single non-parole period; an unusual non-parole period should be explained.

title: CCO availability, duration, combination and condition limits
statement: A CCO requires an offence punishable by more than five penalty units, a pre-sentence report (unless only unpaid work of 300 hours or less), and consent. Duration limits: Magistrates’ Court two/four/five years by number of offences; higher courts five years; cumulative CCOs five years. A combination sentence’s imprisonment cannot exceed one year after pre-sentence detention (except arson). Conditions: at least one Division 4 or justice plan condition, none for restitution, compensation, costs or damages; unpaid work up to 600 hours; curfew two to 12 hours a day for up to six months; electronic monitoring only in the higher courts and only for a curfew or place exclusion. No CCO with a youth justice centre order, and none on a Category 1/2 charge except through the Chapter 9 exception routes.

title: Aggregate sentence availability and ceiling
statement: An aggregate sentence is available for two or more offences founded on the same facts or forming (part of) a series of offences of the same or similar character; it cannot be imposed on a serious offender for a relevant offence, if any offence is a standard sentence offence, or for a mix of parole-violation and other-time offences; it cannot exceed the total of separate sentences; the decision, reasons and effect must be announced. It may be inappropriate in some circumstances, though not necessarily erroneous.

title: A sentence for each charge; base sentence and cumulation; time served declared
statement: A sentence must be imposed for each offence (unless aggregate); cumulation and concurrency should be made by reference to a base sentence, ordinarily the most severe; the head sentence and any non-parole period stated; time already served declared and noted (nil days where the court otherwise orders, for good reason).

title: Orders that require (or exclude) a recorded conviction
statement: Imprisonment can only be imposed if a conviction is recorded, and youth justice and youth residential centre orders are made only on conviction; a discharge requires a finding of guilt and a recorded conviction; a dismissal is solely a non-conviction order. A CCO, a fine and an adjourned undertaking may be made with or without conviction (the court should expressly say which).

title: Section 6AAA statement of the sentence that would have been imposed but for the plea
statement: Where a less severe sentence is imposed because of a guilty plea and the sentence is a custodial order, imprisonment, a CCO of two years or more, a fine over 10 penalty units or an aggregate fine over 20 penalty units, the notional sentence (and notional non-parole period) must be stated for the overall sentence and recorded. The plea may change the form of the sentence itself, so the notional sentence may be of a different (more severe) type. Failure is an irregularity that does not of itself invalidate the sentence.

title: Section 5(2AB): announcing a less severe sentence for cooperation
statement: If a court imposes a less severe sentence because the offender has undertaken to assist the authorities, it must announce that it is doing so and have the undertaking’s details recorded. The Manual also states the requirement for cooperation generally; whether it extends to past assistance without an undertaking is not settled. Non-compliance does not automatically vitiate the sentence.

title: A sentence indication binds the judicial officer who gave it
statement: A magistrate who indicated a sentence of a particular type must not impose a more severe type (but may impose a less severe one); a higher court that gave an indication must not impose a more severe sentence type, or a longer total effective sentence, than indicated. An indication binds only the judicial officer who gave it.

title: Fines: availability by level, maximum, body corporate, aggregate fines
statement: No fine for Level 1; for Level 2 only in addition to imprisonment (natural person) unless otherwise stated; none where a dismissal, discharge or adjournment would serve. The maximum fine is in the provision, else follows the level; where the maximum is in years only, 10 penalty units per month; a body corporate up to five times. Fines for several offences are cumulative; an aggregate fine cannot exceed the sum of the maxima and is not available if any offence is a standard sentence offence.

title: Youth detention: age, prerequisites, serious youth offences, maximum, aggregate and custody
statement: A youth justice centre order is for offenders aged 15 to under 21 at sentence (youth residential centre under 15); it needs a pre-sentence report and a finding of reasonable prospects of rehabilitation or vulnerability in adult prison, and the court must consider the nature of the offence and the offender’s age, character and history; for Category A (or B with a prior) serious youth offences exceptional circumstances are required; maximum four years (higher courts) or two years (Magistrates’ Court) regardless of the number of convictions, also capping cumulation across occasions.

title: Adjourned undertakings, DATOs, RTOs, CSTOs, court assessment orders, suspended and indefinite sentences: limits
statement: An adjourned undertaking may be up to five years and needs the offender’s agreement. A DATO is made only by the Drug Court within the listed eligibility and exclusions, with a custodial part of no more than 2 years (Magistrates’ Court) or 4 years (County Court) and no non-parole period. An RTO is limited to five years, to eligible offences and to eligible offenders, and RTOs cannot be cumulated. A CSTO must not exceed the imprisonment otherwise imposed and needs a non-parole period. Suspended sentences are abolished for offences after the listed dates. An indefinite sentence is exceptional and requires a high degree of probability of serious danger.

title: Mandatory ancillary orders: licence cancellation and disqualification; alcohol exclusion orders
statement: Licence disqualification is mandatory for serious motor vehicle offences (16.1 “found guilty or convicted”; 2.4.3 “found guilty and convicted”: flag.licence_guilty_or_convicted), and on conviction for dangerous or negligent driving while pursued by police and for stealing a motor vehicle, with statutory minimum periods; the form of the order depends on the licence held. An AEO must be made where a conviction is recorded for a relevant offence, the offender was intoxicated by liquor and the intoxication significantly contributed, and there has been no previous AEO for the offence.

title: Displacing presumptive cumulation for prison offences, escape and parole offending; youth centre escape or damage
statement: For a prison offence, escape, breach of parole or offending while on parole, a court must find exceptional circumstances before displacing the prima facie cumulation of the new sentence on the previous sentence. Youth detention for escaping from or damaging a youth justice or residential centre must be cumulative on other detention unless the court orders otherwise and gives reasons.

title: Other statutory presumptions of concurrency and cumulation
statement: Sentences are concurrent unless ordered otherwise, but cumulation is the default for listed categories (offending on parole or bail, prison offences and escape, serious offenders, fine default, specified driving and emergency-vehicle offences); good reason is needed to depart from any presumption; for fine default, serious offenders, bail and the protected-worker driving offences the court has a wide discretion and totality can justify departure (but for serious offenders the Manual warns against directing concurrency simply to achieve totality).

title: Representative, rolled-up and course of conduct charges; offences taken into account
statement: A representative charge does not increase the maximum; a rolled-up charge is limited to the maximum for a single charge; a course of conduct charge carries the maximum for the substantive offence; offences taken into account under s 100 cannot lift the sentence above the maximum for the offences formally sentenced, and treason and murder cannot be taken into account.

title: Facts relied on are within the plea or verdict and proved to the right standard

Facts adverse to the offender must be established beyond reasonable doubt; favourable facts on the balance of probabilities; both must be proved by evidence and mitigation cannot be inferred from an absence of evidence. Disputed harm in a victim impact statement used to increase sentence needs causation proved beyond reasonable doubt.

title: Instinctive synthesis, not two-tier sentencing or quantified discounts
statement: Sentence is reached by identifying all relevant factors, discussing their significance and making a value judgment. Two-tier sentencing — a benchmark taken from one consideration followed by proportional additions or deductions for others — is error, as is synthesising in stages; but the prohibition is not on sequential reasoning, or even arithmetic deductions, in certain cases. Quantifying a discount is inconsistent with the synthesis, except where the Act requires the plea discount to be identified (s 6AAA). For cooperation, the undiscounted sentence need not be stated, and stating it is undesirable save in the simplest cases. Classing offending as “low”, “mid-range” or “high” risks reading current practices for that class without the circumstances of the case.

title: Sentencing statistics and medians are not used as the answer
statement: Statistics are a yardstick only: they do not identify the range, cannot substitute for the synthesis and do not by themselves establish a sentencing practice; a median is an accidental or contingent statistic. Selecting a median and placing the offending above or below it risks an improper two-stage approach. Used correctly, statistics may help to check whether a sentence accords with current sentencing practices.

title: Comparable cases (including retrieved case summaries) used as yardsticks only
statement: Current sentencing practices must be considered but are one factor among many. Comparable cases indicate a range that does not set the outer limits; a few cases do not define a range; detailed analysis to find the “right” sentence is wrong; comparisons are of limited use for widely varying offences. Strict regard must be had to the offence under consideration; a range that appears contrary to principle should not be followed; cases with idiosyncratic features are unlikely to be useful comparators; cases predating an appellate statement that practices were inadequate need great caution, as do cases decided under a lower maximum (an increase signals that existing sentences were insufficient); Victorian courts do not often give substantial weight to other States’ practices. For historic offences, caution is called for where the maximum is now higher, and equal justice may require regard to historical practices — but an offender whose own conduct prevented contemporaneous sentencing may not be able to rely on them (24.1.8.1). Where a party relies on a strikingly similar case, the court must ordinarily explain how it informed the discretion.

title: Standard sentence taken into account as a guidepost; relationship stated; only scheme sentences as practice
statement: The standard sentence is a legislative guidepost like the maximum. The key requirement is that it be taken into account as a relevant sentencing factor, but it must not be given too much weight; the court does not start from it and work up or down, and must state how the sentence relates to it by identifying the facts, matters and circumstances bearing on its judgment, without classifying the offence against a hypothetical mid-range instance. For a standard sentence offence a court may only consider sentences previously imposed under the scheme as current practice, though principles established in earlier cases remain usable.

title: No reliance on adverse matters the user has not supplied; assumptions surfaced
statement: A party must be made aware of any information on which an adverse determination may be based and given an opportunity to respond; a court may not sentence on a fact it considers important (e.g. prevalence, whether a factor aggravates) without identifying it, nor on material not before it. Where the facts of the offence are disputed, no adverse inference may be drawn from the offender’s failure to give evidence on the plea except in rare and exceptional circumstances. (For a fine, an adverse inference may be drawn if the offender declines to disclose their financial circumstances.)

title: An element of the offence is not counted as aggravating or mitigating

title: Uncharged conduct: aggravating only within the De Simoni limits
statement: The circumstances of an offence are not confined to its elements: uncharged or discreditable conduct may be treated as aggravating. But it may not be taken into account where it constitutes an aggravated version of the offending or should have been alleged as a separate charge entirely, and uncharged acts cannot aggravate where they warrant conviction for a more serious offence; the court sentences only for the offence of which the person is convicted or to which they plead. The Manual’s permitted examples include an uncharged injury when sentencing for recklessly exposing an emergency worker to risk (no separate injury charge) and offending while on conditional liberty or in breach of court orders; uncharged offending may also be mentioned as part of the narrative. The line is fine and fact-dependent.

title: No double punishment or double counting (separate harms excepted)
statement: A person must not be punished twice for the same criminal conduct or for common elements; a wholly subsumed offence is not separately sentenced even concurrently; conduct separately sentenced cannot also aggravate another charge; breach of trust cannot both aggravate and diminish good character. But where a single act reflects separate harms, particularly against different people, each may be punished separately even when linked by time and place, and an appropriate measure of cumulation may be called for (e.g. culpable driving causing several deaths or serious injuries). The Manual describes the area as complex and ambiguous, with varied outcomes.

title: Mandatory and statutory considerations addressed (and only proper ones)
statement: All relevant factors must be identified and their significance discussed; where legislation directs that a matter be considered, it should be discussed, not merely recited. The maximum penalty and current sentencing practices are mandatory considerations, as is the standard sentence for a standard sentence offence. The s 5(2) matters include the nature and gravity of the offence, culpability and degree of responsibility, the circumstances of the victim, any injury, loss or damage resulting directly from the offending, the impact on any victim, a hatred or prejudice motive, personal circumstances, the plea and previous character. title: Prior convictions, lack of remorse and a not guilty plea are not aggravating
statement: Prior criminality cannot be used in aggravation to increase a sentence or to doubly punish, but it may indicate moral culpability, persistent lawlessness or a propensity to commit particular crimes and so inhibit mitigation such as rehabilitation; subsequent convictions cannot increase the head sentence. Absence of remorse is not aggravating, but it may show a need for specific deterrence and, where it reveals a contemptuous attitude to the victim or the law, may bear on moral culpability and prospects for rehabilitation. A not guilty plea is never aggravating. Some offence chapters use looser language; those passages are flagged and the flags are shown with this check.

title: Verdins applied only on cogent evidence, limb by limb
statement: Generally, Verdins need only be considered where the issue is clearly raised with a sufficient evidentiary basis; it is wrong to assume it applies because an impairment exists. Cogent evidence, normally expert evidence, must establish on the balance of probabilities that the principles are enlivened; the Manual also says expert evidence is required but not determinative, and the court decides whether and how each limb applies. Some connection between the impairment and the offending is required to moderate general deterrence or reduce culpability (a causal connection is not required). General deterrence should not be moderated where the impairment arose as a reaction to the discovery of the crimes or the prospect of imprisonment (that does not matter for the burden-of-imprisonment limbs). A self-induced impairment may reduce the mitigatory effect. A court may infer, without direct evidence, that a prisoner with a severe mental health condition would find prison more burdensome.

title: Intoxication, addiction and good character given only their proper weight
statement: Intoxication will rarely mitigate (only in exceptional circumstances) and may aggravate, particularly where the offender knew the likely consequences of ingestion. Addiction may bear on culpability and other purposes, but its weight is greatly diminished above street level, someone with repeated opportunities for reform should not expect to rely on it, and if the lack of an addiction is used to show the offender acted solely from greed it must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. Good character is assessed apart from the current offending, carries reduced weight for offences commonly committed by people of otherwise good character, and in sentencing for a child sexual offence cannot be considered if the court is satisfied that it helped the offender commit the offence.

title: No differential sentencing on race, ethnicity, culture, religion or gender in themselves; Bugmy applied correctly
statement: Ethnicity, culture and race are not in themselves bases for differential sentencing, though associated considerations may be, depending on their connection with the offence; a cultural norm must be established by evidence relevant to the offender and cannot give rise to a different range of sentences for a group; treating Aboriginal offenders as generally less culpable is racial stereotyping, though deprivation mitigates to the same extent for all; there can be no difference in sentencing based solely on gender, though closely associated factors such as pregnancy may be considered; general deterrence must not be used to target an ethnic community. Religious practices likely to make an offender a target in prison may be taken into account. It is an error to require an offender to demonstrate “significant childhood deprivation”; at some point mitigation for disadvantage must yield to serious violent offending and community protection, particularly in domestic violence.

title: Plea: utilitarian value, timing, remorse and application of the discount
statement: The Act requires the court to consider whether the offender pleaded guilty and at what stage. In all but exceptional cases the utilitarian value of a plea must be acknowledged by a reduction; the strength of the Crown case has no bearing on that value; pleading guilty to some charges while contesting others does not diminish the weight of the plea. Timing is assessed from when a plea was first reasonably open; early pleas ordinarily attract a substantial discount, late ones generally less. A further reduction for remorse requires proper evidence of genuine penitence, and post-offence remorse may not be rejected merely because remorse was lacking at the time of the offending. The discount is applied to the head sentence and then the non-parole period. There are competing authorities on a discount in the worst category, and the pandemic augmentation was noted to have subsided by the end of 2023.

title: Cooperation with authorities: no tariff; nature of the assistance explained
statement: There is no mathematical process or tariff for a cooperation discount: it rises or falls with objective and subjective factors and the nature of the assistance (the highest levels of cooperation have attracted 50% to 66%). Reasons may need a restricted and a public version.

title: Delay and hardship: evidence and thresholds
statement: Delay is not an automatic discount. It has two limbs (unfairness to the offender; rehabilitation during the delay); the offender must provide some evidence for the limb relied on, though in some cases anxiety may be accepted without supporting evidence; it bears on both head sentence and non-parole period. Delay attributable to the offender carries less significance, and in sexual abuse prosecutions the accused often cannot rely on it. Hardship to the offender needs no exceptionality. Hardship to family or third parties is not normally mitigating; for Victorian offences the Manual records an earlier “exceptional” threshold and states that it now appears the hardship must rise above that commonly suffered by prisoners’ families and be so significant that it will weigh heavily — generally for an especially vulnerable dependant, on cogent evidence.

title: Prevalence used only with a disclosed basis and procedural fairness
statement: Prevalence is neither a circumstance of the offence nor of the offender; the better view is that reliance on it requires the court to disclose its source and give the parties an opportunity to address it, and a court may not sentence on a fact it considers important, such as prevalence, without first identifying it. Its principles are engaged only if it is used to aggravate. The evidentiary foundation remains unresolved, and recent cases focus on the content of the offending rather than a locality or ethnic community.

title: The sentencing purposes identified and weighed (general deterrence not overwhelming; youth; impairment; protection)
statement: The s 5(1) purposes overlap, and which purpose, if any, is paramount depends on all the circumstances and is discretionary. General deterrence plays a role in almost every case but must not cause injustice by overwhelming the other purposes; it has minimal relevance when sentencing a child, and for youthful offenders rehabilitation is usually far more important. A disproportionate sentence may not be imposed to extend the protection of the community save under the statutory regimes; before imposing one the court must be satisfied the offender will remain a danger beyond the proportionate term and give reasons, and the serious-offender power should be exercised rarely.

title: Executive action, registration and deportation consequences handled correctly
statement: The court must not consider the possibility that time in custody may be affected by executive action, and must assume every day of the head sentence may be served; but in fixing the non-parole period it may consider the possibility of parole, its rehabilitative potential and the offender’s suitability. It must not consider Sex Offenders Registration Act or Working With Children Act consequences, and it is error to lower a sentence artificially to avoid Migration Act consequences. An offender must not be denied parole eligibility because deportation is likely; the court should explain that the non-parole period was not increased because of it. Deportation is relevant only on evidence of its likely risk and impact; without evidence or a prosecution concession it need not be considered.

title: Victim impact, victim attitude, victim conduct and domestic context
statement: A victim impact statement informs the court of impact but is not to be used to punish or to produce an unjust sentence; a victim’s attitude to sentence is generally irrelevant (forgiveness may show lessened harm, treated with extreme caution in family violence); a victim’s failure to make a statement or take part is not mitigating; victim conduct, if established on the balance of probabilities, may bear on sentence but should not be labelled mitigating or “complicit”. Offending in a domestic context can never be mitigating and may be aggravating.

title: Parsimony, imprisonment as last resort, the Boulton question and the purposes of a CCO
statement: The sentence must be no more severe than necessary to achieve the purposes; imprisonment may be imposed only if the purposes cannot be achieved by a less severe sentence. For Victorian offences the Boulton question asks whether any feature of the offence or offender requires imprisonment given that a CCO could run for years with punitive and rehabilitative conditions; but the court need not give reasons for rejecting a non-custodial term, failing to ask the question does not by itself show error, and a CCO need not be expressly ruled out. A positive CCO assessment does not presume a CCO. It is erroneous to assume that in a combination sentence the imprisonment deals with punishment and the CCO only with rehabilitation, that the head sentence reflects punishment and the non-parole period rehabilitation, or that a CCO is entirely rehabilitative; equally, there will be cases where a CCO cannot adequately punish.

title: Proportionality: neither excessively lenient nor overly severe
statement: The sentence must be proportionate to the gravity of the offence in light of its objective circumstances; a longer term may not be imposed merely to cure a condition, protect the community or detain preventively; proportionality applies to every component, including the total effective sentence. There is no single proportionate sentence, and sentencing is not a stepped process that first fixes a proportionate term. The statutory power to depart from proportionality should be exercised sparingly, with adequate reasons.

title: Totality: individual sentences, then cumulation, then stand back; no crushing sentence
statement: The total must be a just and appropriate measure of the total criminality: preferably appropriate individual terms, then concurrency or partial cumulation, then stand back; shortcuts cause error. Where the preferred approach cannot be followed, the secondary “moderate and cumulate” approach may be used. Totality applies to offences cumulated on an existing custodial sentence. A crushing sentence should not be imposed absent special circumstances, but it is wrong to fix a minimum by the need to ensure “some measure of life after release”. For an aggregate sentence the individual sentences need not be announced. Where legislation presumes cumulation, totality must not be applied inconsistently with it.

title: Parity with co-offenders
statement: Any significant difference between co-offenders’ sentences must be capable of rational explanation (age, background, history, role; plea timing does not by itself justify a marked disparity); all components including non-parole periods are compared; using a co-offender’s sentence as a starting point and adjusting it is an inappropriate two-step process; where parity requires modification, err on the side of leniency — but an excessively lenient co-offender sentence cannot justify an inappropriately low one. Parity has only limited application between offenders sentenced under different systems (e.g. adult and juvenile).

title: Young offenders: rehabilitation emphasis; CYFA considerations for children; youth detention; adult minimums regarded
statement: For youthful offenders rehabilitation is usually far more important than general deterrence, though the weight of youth decreases as the seriousness of the offence increases; a youthful first offender should not, if avoidable, be given a custodial sentence; youth detention is available in the higher courts for young offenders. For a child sentenced in the Supreme or County Court the CYFA considerations must be addressed as far as practicable, and the CYFA dispositions are considered in their hierarchy (the Manual notes some ambiguity about the higher courts’ power); in CNK v The Queen a child before the higher court only because of a charge of which he was acquitted had to be sentenced on the remaining uplifted charges as if exclusively governed by the CYFA (flag.general_deterrence_childrens_court_charges). The higher courts, sentencing an offender aged 16 or 17 at the time of an indictable offence, must have regard to the adult minimum non-parole provisions when assessing gravity.

title: Recording a conviction; dismissals, discharges and adjournments
statement: Whether to record a conviction depends on all the circumstances including the nature of the offence, character and history, and the impact on economic or social wellbeing or employment; for serious offending, not recording a conviction is limited to out of the ordinary or exceptional circumstances that facilitate the offender’s rehabilitation. The Manual says a dismissed offence must be capable of being characterised as trifling, and also that dismissals may be granted for strong rehabilitative steps or where good character and post-offence conduct would make a conviction disproportionate. (Conviction requirements for imprisonment, youth detention and discharge are hard-checked by audit.conviction_requirements.)

title: Confiscation and compensation: effect on sentence and priority
statement: The Act distinguishes orders disgorging the profits of crime, which are not to be considered, from forfeiture of lawfully acquired property or a pecuniary penalty exceeding the profits, which may be; it prohibits taking into account the automatic forfeiture of a serious drug offender’s property. Confiscation that does more than remove profits is punishment and failing to consider it may be error, but there must be sufficient evidence of its likely effect. Compensation orders cannot be a CCO condition, and where the offender cannot pay both a fine and compensation, compensation must be given priority.

title: Extra-curial punishment

Whether public opprobrium as a result of conviction may be considered is unclear.

title: Reasons show the route to the conclusion; unusual features explained; references cited
statement: Reasons should usually state the findings of fact and their basis, the aggravating and mitigating factors, the impact on victims, the offender’s material circumstances and conclusions on the primary arguments — the route to the conclusion; an unusual factor that may carry weight (such as an unusual non-parole period) should be explained; statutory matters discussed rather than recited; intemperate or formulaic language avoided. Where there is a duty to give reasons, failure to do so is an error of law (the statutory statements are hard-checked elsewhere). Before a CCO or an adjourned undertaking the court must explain the order’s purposes, effect and consequences to the offender.

title: Category 2 residual exception and “special reasons”: the restricted reasoning
statement: The Category 2 residual exception is a stringent, non-discretionary test: are there substantial and compelling circumstances, and are they exceptional and rare? In applying it general deterrence and denunciation must be given primacy, personal circumstances less weight than the gravity of the offending, and regard must not be had to previous good character, an early guilty plea, prospects of rehabilitation or parity. For a mandatory minimum, a special reason may exist in four circumstances; for the residual “substantial and compelling reasons” the court must give primacy to general deterrence and denunciation, must not consider prior good character (other than an absence of prior convictions), an early plea, rehabilitation prospects or parity, and must have regard to Parliament’s intention that a custodial term should ordinarily be imposed. The offender carries the burden; the impairment ground must be proved on the balance of probabilities.

title: Fines: decide whether to fine before considering means; no harsher sentence for inability to pay
statement: An offender’s financial circumstances can be considered only after deciding to impose a fine; they are irrelevant to whether a fine should be imposed. A court should not impose a more severe sentence, such as imprisonment, because the offender cannot pay a fine that properly reflects the gravity of the offence. A fine beyond the offender’s reasonable capacity to pay is never just; the onus is on the offender to put material before the court about means, and capacity to pay is relevant but not dominant. Forfeiture, restitution and compensation orders must be taken into account. A fine with imprisonment may require the term to be reduced, and should not be imposed where default is likely.

title: Licence disqualification: the period reasoned, interaction with other sanctions, earlier suspensions
statement: Fixing a disqualification period is like the general sentencing discretion: aggravating and mitigating factors and the competing principles and purposes must be considered; a failure to give reasons for the period may indicate error; its effect on rehabilitation must be considered, and its interaction with other sanctions and its actual impact on the offender should be considered; failure to consider that interaction and impact may be error. A later suspension under the same specified provisions is presumed concurrent with the earlier one unless the court orders otherwise or the RSA requires the suspension or disqualification to be consecutive; and where the licence or permit has been suspended under Part 6B of the Road Safety Act and the court cancels and disqualifies, or suspends, it must take that period of suspension into account in fixing the period.

title: Standard sentence minimum non-parole period: short terms and the 12-month and six-month restrictions
statement: The s 11A(4) floor (60% of the relevant term) is stated without regard to the length of the term, but no non-parole period may be fixed for a total sentence under 12 months, and a non-parole period must be at least six months shorter than the total (arithmetic: 60% of a term exceeds the term less six months whenever the term is under 15 months). The Manual does not reconcile these, or define the “relevant term” where several offences are sentenced together. In those cases the app marks the non-parole period unresolved and cites all three restrictions.

title: Footnotes 4805 (conspiracy) and 4807 (incitement) are identical
statement: Both footnotes say that, because life imprisonment is not “a prescribed maximum penalty”, the operative maximum for “conspiracy” to commit an offence punishable by life is 15 years (other than incitement to commit murder or treason, covered by s 321I(1)(ba)). Footnote 4807 sits in the incitement table but speaks of conspiracy, and footnote 4805 sits in the conspiracy table but carves out by reference to the incitement provision (s 321I(1)(ba)), although that table’s own murder/treason row is s 321C(1)(ba). Check which offence each rule applies to before relying on it. Handling: the 15-year cap is enforced (error above it) for a Crimes Act s 321C conspiracy; for s 321I incitement it rests only on fn 4807, so a sentence above 15 years is a caution, not an error (guide.inchoate.maxima_notes; audit.maximum_applicable (4)).

title: Child sexual offence factors list “Did the offender lack remorse?”
statement: The list of factors “relevant in assessing gravity and the offender’s culpability” at 24.2.2.2 includes lack of remorse; 6.3.4.1 says the absence of remorse cannot be a circumstance of aggravation, although it may indicate a need for specific deterrence and, if it reveals a contemptuous attitude to the victim or the law, may bear on moral culpability and prospects of rehabilitation. Handling: lack of remorse is never treated as aggravating; it may bear on specific deterrence and (if it shows contempt) on culpability and rehabilitation; this caution is shown.

title: COVID-19: custody conditions “in the present time” and the augmented plea discount
statement: 7.6.5 asks courts to be mindful “in the present time” of more onerous pandemic custody conditions, and 7.1.1 (still in the present tense) gives a plea entered “during the currency of the pandemic” greater weight, while noting that as at the end of 2023 the pandemic’s effects on the Victorian criminal justice system had subsided; the Manual fixes no end date. Handling: custody — evidence of current conditions is required before giving this weight; pleas — augmentation is considered only where the plea date falls within the pandemic period, not for pleas entered after 2023, and with this caution for 2023 pleas.

title: Presumptive cumulation: two categories are in neither the “exceptional circumstances” nor the “wide discretion” group
statement: 8.4.1 lists the categories in which cumulation is the default, then says which need exceptional circumstances to displace it (prison offence, escape, parole) and which leave a wide discretion (fine defaults, serious offenders, bail, specified offences against emergency workers and custodial officers). The young-offender category (escape or damage to correctional facilities) and damaging an emergency vehicle are not placed in either group, so the test for departing from cumulation for them is not stated. Two readings are possible: the footnotes cite s 16(3D) for the young-offender, protected-worker driving and emergency-vehicle categories alike, and the exceptional-circumstances rule ss 16(3)–(3BA), which suggests the wide-discretion group; but the young offender’s “escape” limb may overlap “escape” in the exceptional-circumstances list. Handling: departing from cumulation for these two categories needs a stated reason and shows this caution (audit.cumulation_presumptions).

title: Special reason and Category 1: 9.1.3 (general) vs 9.1.1 (protected-official offences only)
statement: 9.1.3 says that if a special reason exists the court may decline to impose imprisonment “in the case of a Category 1 offence”. Read in context (9.1.3 opens with the mandatory minimum provisions, and footnote 2005, attached to that sentence, confines declining imprisonment to the protected-official injury and driving offences and then requires a therapeutic order), it means a Category 1 offence that also carries a mandatory minimum; 9.1.1 likewise confines the Category 1 exception to offences that are also mandatory minimum offences against protected officials. The literal words of 9.1.3 are wider. A special reason is itself an exception that the mandatory minimum provisions provide (9.1.3, first sentence), so the conflict is real only for Category 1 offences that carry a mandatory minimum (ss 15A/15B where the victim is not a protected official, ss 77B, 79A). Handling: for those offences the app follows 9.1.1 and footnote 2005 and proposes only imprisonment without a CCO; any other disposition proposed on a special reason (a non-custodial disposition, or imprisonment combined with a CCO) is shown as unresolved (caution) rather than passed, and not as an error (audit.category_1_2 (d), audit.cco_limits (6), cat1.custodial_required). For a Category 1 offence with no mandatory minimum (e.g. murder, rape) no special reason exists, so a non-custodial disposition is an error on every reading.

title: Category 1/2: “imprisonment” (9.1.1) vs “custodial sentence” (offence-table footnotes)

Handling: a youth justice centre order on a Category 1 or 2 charge outside that route is shown as a caution (audit.category_1_2), not passed or failed silently.

title: Good character: excluded outright (Category 2, 9.1.1) vs excluded except a lack of previous convictions (9.1.3)

Handling: for the Category 2 residual exception the app does not rely on good character; if the reasoning relies on an absence of prior convictions there, it shows this caution.

Handling: for the Category 2 residual exception the app does not rely on good character; if the reasoning relies on an absence of prior convictions there, it shows this caution.

title: CCE value threshold: “$50,000 or more” vs a rolled-up transaction that “exceeds $50,000”
statement: A CCE offence involves property or benefits “valued at $50,000 or more”, but 9.4 says a rolled-up charge qualifies only if a constituent transaction “exceeds $50,000”, while 2.4.5 says, of rolled-up charges themselves, a transaction “of $50,000 or more”. A transaction of exactly $50,000 is treated differently by these statements; the app shows this caution and marks the point unresolved. For the maximum check, the app does not rely on the doubled CCE ceiling for a rolled-up count whose largest transaction is exactly $50,000: a sentence above the ordinary maximum but within the CCE ceiling is shown with this caution, not failed (audit.maximum_applicable (7)); a charge whose value exceeds $50,000 only because of the rolled-up value does not qualify. 27.5.1 states the rolled-up rule as “at least one transaction of $50,000 or more”, as 2.4.5 does.

title: Aggregate fines: 12.5 bars one where an offence “is a standard sentence offence” but gives no test
statement: 12.5 says an aggregate fine is not available if one of the offences is a standard sentence offence. 9.2 defines a standard sentence offence as one for which the Act creating the offence or prescribing its maximum specifies a period as the standard sentence, and an attempt, conspiracy or incitement to commit one is not itself one (fn 2017). The Manual does not say whether the scheme’s limits of application (sso.scope: offences committed after 1 February 2018, offenders 18 or older at the offence, not heard summarily) also decide what is a standard sentence offence for 12.5. Handling: an aggregate fine including an offence that passes sso.scope → error (fine.multiple_offences, audit.fine_rules); including an offence that has a standard sentence but falls outside sso.scope → caution, never error.

title: Residential treatment orders: the “serious offence” list is introduced with “includes” and its footnotes skip paragraphs
statement: 14 makes an RTO available for sexual assault, sexual assault by compelling sexual touching, “or a serious offence, which includes:” a list of categories. title: Youth detention maximum across occasions: the unexpired part or the whole earlier term?
statement: 10.1.1.3 says the maximum period of youth detention also operates as the maximum that may be achieved by cumulation of sentences on several occasions, and that if the offender is already undergoing youth detention, cumulation orders only operate to the point when the maximum is reached. It does not say whether the earlier sentence counts in full or only its unexpired part. Youth detention is presumed concurrent with any other uncompleted term, whenever imposed (10.1.1.3). Handling (app policy): the cap is applied to what cumulation achieves — the unexpired part of the detention being served plus the part of the new detention cumulated on it is counted in the hard check (yjc.maximum, audit.youth_detention_limits), and new detention wholly concurrent with it adds nothing; where counting the whole earlier term instead of its unexpired part would take that total over the maximum, this caution is shown.

title: Youth detention commencement: “imprisonment that is cumulative on the sentence of detention” reads inverted
statement: 10.1.1.3 says that if a young offender is serving a sentence of imprisonment that is cumulative on the sentence of detention, the detention commences on the day the sentence of imprisonment is complete. Handling: the app does not compute commencement dates; where commencement matters, the reasoning states the order of service it assumes and shows this caution.

title: Aggravated home invasion minimum: s 10AC (9.1.2.5) or s 10AD (27.1.1.2 table footnote)?

title: Mandatory treatment and monitoring order with imprisonment: 11.9 (combination not limited) v 9.1.2.3 and 9.1.2.4 (“either … or”)
statement: 11.9 says the mandatory treatment and monitoring order (MTMO) provision does not limit a court’s ability to impose a combination sentence. 9.1.2.3 (the protected-official injury offences) and 9.1.2.4 (the protected-official driving offences, ss 317AC and 317AD) say that where special reasons are found the court must “either impose a sentence of imprisonment (without a CCO) or make” an MTMO, a Residential Treatment Order or a Court Secure Treatment Order. title: Fines for offences whose life or 25-year maximum is printed without a penalty level
statement: 12.1 says fines cannot be imposed as an alternative or in addition to imprisonment for Level 1 (life imprisonment) offences, and that for Level 2 offences (punishable by 25 years’ imprisonment) a fine can only be imposed in addition to imprisonment. Some register rows print a maximum of life or 25 years without a level. The Manual does not say whether the Level 1 and Level 2 fine rules apply to those offences. 12.1 excepts a body corporate from the Level 2 rule (a fine may be an alternative “if the offender is a body corporate”), and 5.1.1 excludes life imprisonment from the general fine of 10 penalty units per month. Handling: a 25-year maximum without a level — a fine alone, or as an alternative to imprisonment, imposed on a natural person → caution, unresolved (audit.fine_rules); a body corporate → no caution. A life maximum without a level — no general fine is available in any case (5.1.1; fine.maximum), which the maximum check enforces; a fine the row itself prints → caution. Never an error on the ground of the missing level.

title: Drug Court orders and sexual offences: “a sexual offence” (24.5) v “a schedule 1 sexual offence” (15A.3)

Read with its footnote, 24.5 appears to refer to the same schedule 1 class, and the Manual does not reproduce schedule 1 or say which offences it lists, for any of the chapter 24 offences. Handling: where the user states the offence is a schedule 1 sexual offence, a DATO is an error on either reading. Otherwise the point depends on this flag and is a caution, never an error: for the 24.1.1, 24.1.2 and 24.1.4 offences the app does not propose a DATO unless the user states that the offence is not a schedule 1 sexual offence (app policy, following 24.5’s words), and a DATO proposed for one is shown as unresolved (caution); for the child abuse material (24.1.3) and sexual servitude (24.1.5) offences the user is asked whether the offence is a schedule 1 sexual offence (intake.charges classes): unknown → caution.

title: Low-level participants in “serious drug offences”: normally immediate imprisonment — which offences?
statement: 28.3.2.4 says couriers and other low-level participants are important, if not essential, to serious drug offences and deserve suitable punishment, and that normally “drug offending even at this level calls for immediate imprisonment” (its footnote, fn 4360, cites DPP (Cth) v Bui). title: OHS offences, company in liquidation: specific deterrence “not automatically” reduced (31.5) v “little or no part” (31.7.2)
statement: 31.5 says liquidation does not automatically reduce the weight to be given to specific deterrence, because a company is controlled by directors who may operate in the industry in future. 31.7.2 says that the sentencing judge must ignore the fact that the company is in liquidation and that the fine will never be paid, and must consider the assets and financial prospects at the time of trading, and that specific deterrence will have little or no part to play. The Manual does not reconcile the two. Handling (app policy): fix the fine on the company’s assets and prospects at the time of trading; give specific deterrence of the company little weight, but the need to deter those behind it (31.5) may still be weighed; never fail reasoning that takes either view; show this caution where the company is in liquidation.

title: Indefinite sentence test: 4.4 (“a serious offender”; “or any special circumstances”) v 8.7 (“an adult offender … convicted of a ‘serious offence’”; “and any special circumstances”)
statement: 4.4 describes the indefinite sentence power as allowing a court sentencing “a serious offender for a serious offence” to impose an indefinite term if satisfied to a high degree of probability that the offender is a serious danger to the community “because of their circumstances, the nature or gravity of the offending, or any special circumstances”. 8.7, which sets out the scheme, says that an adult offender convicted of a ‘serious offence’ by the Supreme or County Court may be sentenced to an indefinite term, and that the court must be satisfied to a high degree of probability that, at the time of sentencing, the offender poses a serious danger “because of their circumstances, the gravity of the offending, and any special circumstances”. The two passages differ in the class of offender and in the connective (“or” v “and”). Handling: the gate (indefinite.requirements) and the audit follow 8.7, the section that states the requirements; reasoning that relies on 4.4’s wording (a single one of the matters, or the “serious offender” class) → caution, never an error on this ground. The app never presents an indefinite sentence as the expected outcome in any case (audit.adjournment_and_other_order_limits).

title: Sentences printed with garbled wording or an apparent slip (4.2.1, 6.3.3.1, 11.4.2.8, 11.8.1)
statement: Two sentences of the Manual are printed with words missing or duplicated: in 4.2.1 “Victorian courts have held that maintained that general deterrence has a role in the sentencing synthesis”, and in 6.3.3.1 “If any, for deprivation will not always ameliorate sentence, the court ‘must evaluate …’”. Two others contain an apparent slip: 11.4.2.8 “it may facility an offender’s rehabilitation” (for “facilitate”), and 11.8.1, in a passage on combining imprisonment with a CCO, “the Court has rejected the notion that a CCO is primarily punitive and Youth Supervision Order is primarily rehabilitative”. The rest of each sentence is clear. Handling: rely on the clear part (general deterrence has a role in the synthesis; deprivation will not always ameliorate sentence and the court must evaluate the extent of past disadvantage; an alcohol exclusion condition may aid rehabilitation; in a combination sentence neither component is assigned only punishment or only rehabilitation); quote the sentence verbatim and never repair it inside a quotation.

title: Dismissal: “dismissed without a finding of guilt” (13.1) although dismissal follows a finding of guilt
statement: 13.1 says a court that finds a person guilty may order dismissal of the charge without recording a conviction, and that the discretion to dismiss arises only when the court is satisfied that the charge is proved; it then says that once a charge is dismissed “without a finding of guilt”, it cannot be taken as a conviction for any purpose except as the Act provides. Read with the rest of 13.1, the phrase appears to mean “without conviction”. Handling: order.dismissal reads it so (a dismissal is not a conviction except as the Act provides); no hard check turns on the wording.

title: Fine work orders: commencement within three months (12.9) v a cumulative later order commencing on completion (12.9.2)
statement: 12.9 says the court must set the date on which a fine work order commences, and that it must not be more than three months after the order is made; 12.9.2 says that if the hours under fine work orders are cumulative, the later order commences once the earlier order is completed, which may be more than three months later. The Manual does not reconcile the two. Handling: a later cumulative order commencing on completion of the earlier one is not an error on this ground (caution); order.fine.work_orders states the three-month rule as a general one.

title: Compensation and the Wrongs Act: “These provisions do not apply to orders under the Act” — Part VBA only, or all?
statement: 18.1.4.4 says that Part IV of the Wrongs Act (contribution from concurrent wrongdoers) “may be applicable to compensation orders”, describes Parts IVAA and VB (saying Part VB may apply to negligent and reckless offences), then describes Part VBA and says “These provisions do not apply to orders under the Act”.
