Handling: the app does not resolve the referent; reasoning that applies or excludes a Wrongs Act rule in fixing a compensation order is shown with this caution, and substantial questions of contribution will frequently make the matter too complex for the summary compensation procedure, as 18.1.4.4 says.

title: Contempt by disobedience: intentions “only relevant” to culpability v “the consequences of publication” relevant to culpability (29.2.2.2)
statement: 29.2.2.2 says that, in assessing gravity, the extent to which the conduct tends to frustrate the order should be distinguished from the contemnor’s intentions, “which are only relevant to the related assessment of their culpability”; its example (a real and substantial risk that a suppression order might be breached by media publication) shows the tendency to frustrate the order, which goes to gravity. The passage then ends: “It is the consequences of publication that are relevant to assessing the contemnor’s culpability”. The Manual does not say how the consequences of publication bear on culpability when intentions are said to be the only matter for it. Handling: keep the tendency to frustrate the order for gravity; reasoning may weigh the contemnor’s intentions, and the consequences of publication, for culpability, shown with this caution; never an error on this ground.

title: Home invasion: fn 4044 says the “mandatory imprisonment scheme” does not apply to it, but 27.5.1 makes it Category 2
statement: 27.2.2 says the legislature introduced mandatory sentencing requirements for “a class of home invasion offences”; fn 4044 adds that “the mandatory imprisonment scheme applies to aggravated home invasion offences, but not aggravated burglary or home invasion” (citing s 10AC, the provision 9.1.2.5 gives for the aggravated home invasion minimum, fn 1992; the 27.1.1.2 table footnote on the aggravated home invasion row, fn 3972, cites s 10AD, which 9.1.2.5 gives for aggravated carjacking, fn 1993: flag.ahi_minimum_provision_10ac_10ad). Yet 27.5.1 lists home invasion as a Category 2 offence, and Category 1 and 2 offences are themselves a “mandatory imprisonment scheme” (fn 4200; 9.1.1). The Manual does not say which class it means. Handling: the register’s Category 2 status for s 77A governs the hard checks; fn 4044 is read as referring to the minimum non-parole period scheme, never as taking home invasion out of Category 2; show this caution where the “class of home invasion offences” reasoning is used.

title: Aggravated burglary and home invasion: an uncharged loaded firearm as “very significant” aggravation vs the uncharged-conduct rule
statement: 27.2.2.2 says uncharged post-entry conduct that could have been charged as a more serious offence should not aggravate, that such criminality cannot be taken into account adversely, and that the duty to consider all circumstances of the charged offence gives way to the principle that no one is punished for an uncharged offence — yet a loaded firearm carried during a home invasion has been held a “very significant aggravating feature” even where no firearm offence is charged, because it revealed premeditation, illuminated the intention at entry and greatly increased the danger of the entry. The Manual says the relevance of post-entry conduct is “not entirely straightforward” and does not state the boundary. Handling: allow an uncharged loaded firearm to aggravate an aggravated burglary or home invasion only for what it shows about the charged entry, with this caution; any other use of uncharged conduct follows audit.uncharged_conduct.

title: Drug value: “no meaningful guidance” (28.1.4.2) vs a guide to scale, comparison and gravity (28.3.2.2, 28.3.2.5)
statement: 28.1.4.2 says referring to the estimated wholesale or retail value does not “provide any meaningful guidance as to the seriousness of the offence”. 28.3.2.2 says value can indicate scale, “may provide some basis for comparison with other cases” and is “regularly accepted as a guide to gravity” where it reveals the offender’s benefit; 28.3 makes the sale value something counsel must provide; 28.3.2.5 says the low reward for GHB justifies “consistently lower sentences”. Handling: when comparing cases involving different drugs, use multiples of the CQ/LCQ, never value, as the common denominator; value may be used as evidence of scale and of the offender’s actual or expected benefit, with this caution.

title: Pidoto: “possessing, or using” included (28.3.1, first paragraph) vs excluded (28.3.1, last paragraph)
statement: 28.3.1 opens (citing Pidoto 278 [39], 279 [46]) by saying trafficking, importing, cultivating, “possessing, or using” one drug is generally no more or less serious than the same conduct with another drug; it ends (citing Pidoto 279 [47]–[48]) by saying Pidoto “limited its impact to trafficking and cultivation offences” and expressly excluded possession, use, trafficking to a child and supplying a child. Handling: apply the bar on relative-harm comparisons to trafficking and cultivation; for possession, use, s 71AB and s 71B follow the specific statement of Pidoto’s limits (the bar does not apply), with this caution.

title: Section 76 adjourned bond: described for “possession or use” (28.2.2.5), but cultivation s 72B(a) “may qualify” (fn 4248); criteria not stated

title: “Within 500 metres of a school” 20-year maximum: printed for s 71AC and s 71B, but described as supply or trafficking to children (ss 71B(1A), 71AB(2))

title: CCE offences: “any indictable drug offence” (28.7) vs every Schedule 1A class valued at $50,000 or more (9.4)

title: Contempt: the Sentencing Act applies only in part; suspended and indeterminate committals are available (29.5.2) despite 8.7–8.8
statement: 29.5.2 says there is “some question” how far the Sentencing Act applies to contempt, though “it does not apply in its entirety”; some of its community-based options “might be inconsistent” with a superior court’s power to commit for a fixed term; the Supreme Court “may also impose a suspended sentence” (under its rules: fn 4579), and coercive punishment of indeterminate length may be appropriate for refusal to give evidence. Elsewhere suspended sentences are abolished for offences after the listed dates (8.8) and an indefinite term needs a serious offence (8.7). The Manual does not reconcile these. Handling: for contempt (the 29.1.3 rows), a Supreme Court suspended committal, a coercive indeterminate committal or a CCO → caution citing this flag, never error; any other Sentencing Act-based hard check applied to contempt → caution.

title: OHS offences: death or injury “only relevant” to show the risk (31.2) vs harm that “must” be taken into account (31.3.2.4, 31.6.1)
statement: 31.2 says the OHS scheme is risk-based, not outcome-based, and that death or injury “will only be relevant in so far as it demonstrates the degree of seriousness of the relevant threat”; 31.3.2.4 says the actual result is of “very limited relevance” to gravity and may only illuminate the risk. Yet 31.3.2.4 also says death or serious injury “may be a relevant sentencing consideration as an impact of the offence or an injury, loss or damage resulting directly from the offence” (the Act ss 5(2)(daa), (db)), and 31.6.1 says a court “must take into account” such harm, including through victim impact statements. The Manual does not reconcile the two. Handling: measure gravity by the breach and the risk, using the outcome only to illuminate the existence, likelihood and potential gravity of the risk; take death or injury into account as an impact of the offence (s 5(2)(daa), (db)) only where causation is proved beyond reasonable doubt, and do not let the outcome stand in for the gravity of the breach; when comparing cases, compare the breaches, not the outcomes (31.1.3). Note that s 32 requires serious injury for that offence (fn 4667). Show this caution wherever death or injury occurred; never fail reasoning that treats proved harm as victim impact.

title: Firearm possession: criminal history and prohibited or FPO status listed as elevating or aggravating (33.2.1) vs the priors rule (6.3.1.2) and the element rule (5.2.8)
statement: 33.2.1 lists “an offender’s criminal history, especially any prior firearms convictions” among factors that “may elevate the seriousness” of a possession offence, and “the status of the offender either as a prohibited person or the subject of a firearm prohibition order, and the nature and extent of their prior criminal history” among factors that “may aggravate”; 33.1.3.1 says criminal history may warrant “a more substantial sentence”. But prior criminality “cannot be used in aggravation to increase a sentence or to doubly punish an offender” (6.3.1.2), and a factor that is an element of the offence cannot be counted as aggravating (5.2.8). For s 5(1), s 5(2), s 5AB(2), s 5AB(3) and s 112B the prohibited-person or FPO status is an element, and that status often arises from a prior term of imprisonment (fn 4865). The Manual does not reconcile these. Handling: criminal history may be used for what it shows about the purpose of the possession and the risk (33.2.1.1), to limit mitigation, and in specific deterrence (33.3), but must not lift the sentence beyond what the offence warrants; where the status is an element of the charge, do not count it again as aggravating, though the reason for the prohibition (serious offending v “unrelated, minor offending”, 33.2.1.1) may inform gravity. Show this caution; never fail reasoning on this ground alone.

For s 5(1), s 5(2), s 5AB(2), s 5AB(3) and s 112B the prohibited-person or FPO status is an element, and that status often arises from a prior term of imprisonment (fn 4865). The Manual does not reconcile these. Handling: criminal history may be used for what it shows about the purpose of the possession and the risk (33.2.1.1), to limit mitigation, and in specific deterrence (33.3), but must not lift the sentence beyond what the offence warrants; where the status is an element of the charge, do not count it again as aggravating, though the reason for the prohibition (serious offending v “unrelated, minor offending”, 33.2.1.1) may inform gravity. Show this caution; never fail reasoning on this ground alone.

title: YJC orders and CCOs: 10.1.2.1 says the Act provides for a YJC order “in combination with a sentence of imprisonment”
statement: After stating that a court may not impose a CCO in combination with a YJC order, 10.1.2.1 says “the Act only provides for a YJC order to be made in combination with a sentence of imprisonment” and that there is no provision for “one” to be made with a sentence of detention. Read with the preceding words and 11.8.1 this appears to mean a CCO, but the text is literally about a YJC order. The Manual is also silent on a YRC order with a CCO. It does not expressly address a CCO for one charge with a YJC order for another, but it describes combination sentences as spanning charges (a CCO for one offence with imprisonment for another, 11.8) and youth detention is not “imprisonment” (11.8.1), which suggests that case is also barred. Handling: a CCO combined with a YJC order is an error (11.8.1 independently); the other cases are shown as unresolved (caution).

title: Arson and the one-year combination ceiling: Magistrates’ Court position and the meaning of “arson offences”
statement: 11.1.3 says the one-year ceiling on imprisonment in a combination sentence does not apply to arson offences, “for which any sentence of imprisonment may be imposed by the Supreme or County Court”, and that the Magistrates’ Court remains limited to two years even for arson; 11.8.4 states the exception as “(except for arson)” with no court qualifier. Whether the Magistrates’ Court is freed from the one-year ceiling for arson is not stated expressly, and “arson offences” is not defined for this exception. Handling: Supreme/County Court arson — no combination ceiling; Magistrates’ Court arson — error above 24 months, caution between 12 and 24 months; whether a charge is an arson offence is asked of the user.

title: No fine for Level 1 offences (12.1) vs DPCSA “Level 1 – life and fine not exceeding 5000 penalty units”
statement: 12.1 says fines cannot be imposed as an alternative or in addition to imprisonment for Level 1 (life) offences. The Manual’s own penalty tables print “Level 1 – life and fine not exceeding 5000 penalty units” for trafficking a large commercial quantity (s 71), cultivation of a large commercial quantity (s 72) and trafficking a commercial quantity at the direction of a criminal organisation (s 71AA). The Manual does not reconcile the two. Handling: a fine on a Level 1 offence is an error unless the offence row prints a fine, in which case it is a caution (fine ≤ the printed amount).

title: Body corporate fines: five times the maximum for Crimes Act offences (5.1.1) or for every offence (12.2)?
statement: 5.1.1 says a body corporate found guilty of an offence against the Crimes Act 1958 may be fined up to five times the maximum; 12.2 says the body corporate maximum is five times the natural-person maximum “for the same offence”, without the Crimes Act limit. Both cite s 113D(1). Handling: use the printed company maximum where the register has one; otherwise five times the natural-person maximum is the highest ceiling either passage allows, so a fine above it is an error for any offence (unless the user identifies a provision setting a higher company maximum: caution, app policy); for an offence outside the Crimes Act, a fine above the natural-person maximum but not above five times it is shown with this caution, because 5.1.1 states the multiplier only for Crimes Act offences.

title: Dismissal: is “trifling” always required, or are rehabilitation and good character alternative grounds?
statement: 13.1 says that, moreover, the offence “must be” of such a nature that it can properly be characterised as trifling, and then that dismissals “may also be granted” where strong steps have been taken towards rehabilitation or previous good character and post-offence conduct would make a conviction disproportionate. The Manual does not say whether these are alternative grounds or factors within the trifling requirement. Handling: a dismissal relying only on rehabilitation or good character (offence not characterised as trifling) is a caution, not an error.

title: Court secure treatment orders: “must fix a non-parole period as if it were a term of imprisonment” for short terms
statement: 15.4.2 says a court making a CSTO must fix a non-parole period as if it were a term of imprisonment, but a non-parole period cannot be fixed for imprisonment under 12 months (8.3.1). The Manual does not say how the two apply to a CSTO whose notional term is under 12 months, or between one and two years, where fixing one is discretionary (8.3); nor whether, for a notional term of two years or more, the 8.3 exception (an npp need not be fixed where the nature of the offence or the circumstances of the offender make it inappropriate) carries over. Handling: for a notional term of two years or more, no npp and no stated reason → error, no npp with a stated reason → caution; for shorter terms — no npp for a notional term under two years, or an npp fixed for one under 12 months — caution, not error.

title: Compensation and restitution are “relevant to assessing whether to impose a fine” vs means irrelevant to whether to fine

Handling: compensation and restitution reduce the means available for a fine’s amount and payment, and take priority over a fine where the offender cannot pay both; the app does not use means to decide whether to fine.

title: Forensic sample orders: findings on 1 July 2014 (definition) and 1 July 1998 (availability) fall between the Manual’s “after” and “before”/“prior to” statements
statement: The broad definition of “forensic sample offence” applies to findings of guilt after 1 July 2014; for findings before 1 July 2014 the definition then in force applies. Handling: information only; ask the user to confirm the position for a finding on either date.

title: Gross violence (ss 15A/15B) against a protected official with a special reason: which disposition follows?
statement: The protected-official minimums include five years for ss 15A/15B (gross violence), but the s 5(2GA) route that follows a special reason (imprisonment without a CCO, or a mandatory treatment and monitoring order, RTO or CSTO) is stated only for charges of intentionally or recklessly causing serious injury or injury (ss 16, 17, 18; fn 2005 adds the protected-worker driving offences). 9.1.1 states the Category 1 exception for protected-official minimum offences generally. The Manual does not say what disposition follows a special reason on a gross-violence charge against a protected official. Handling: imprisonment without a CCO passes; any other disposition is unresolved (caution), not passed and not failed (audit.category_1_2 (c), audit.cco_limits (6), audit.mandatory_minimum).

title: Serious offenders: totality may justify departing from presumptive cumulation (8.4.1) vs wrong to do so simply for totality (3.3.2.1)

Handling: for a serious offender, totality may moderate the degree of cumulation but concurrency resting on totality alone is shown as a caution.

title: Plea timing: withholding a plea to avoid “forensic prejudice” (not late) vs to “avoid a forensic disadvantage” (not reasonable)
statement: 7.1.2.3 says a plea is not late when it is entered after the prosecution withdraws other charges and the accused was “reasonably avoiding forensic prejudice” by withholding it. The next sentence, resting on a Western Australian authority introduced with “See”, says an accused does not act reasonably if the object or effect of the delay is to “avoid a forensic disadvantage in relation to any other charged offences”. The Manual does not distinguish prejudice from disadvantage or reconcile the two. Handling: where a plea was withheld until other charges were withdrawn, do not treat it as late without addressing whether the withholding was reasonable; show this caution; do not reduce the discount on this ground alone.

7.1.2.3 says a plea is not late when it is entered after the prosecution withdraws other charges and the accused was “reasonably avoiding forensic prejudice” by withholding it. title: Section 6AAA: “may” state (7.1.4) vs “must” state (2.4.9 fn 361) for other sentence forms; “discounted” vs notional figures
statement: 7.1.4 says the s 6AAA obligation arises only for listed forms of sentence and that where it is not required a court “may still state” the notional sentence (fn 1434: s 6AAA(3)). 2.4.9 states the obligation without the list of forms, and its fn 361 says that for “all other offences it must state” the sentence, citing the same s 6AAA(3). 2.4.9 also says that for multiple offences the court “must state the discounted sentence and non-parole period … for the total effective sentence”, whereas 7.1.4 requires the notional (undiscounted) total effective sentence and non-parole period. Handling: the hard check runs only for the 7.1.4 trigger forms (imprisonment, including any order to serve a term; CCO of two years or more; fine over 10 penalty units; aggregate fine over 20 penalty units); a “custodial order” other than imprisonment → caution (flag.s6aaa_custodial_order_undefined); for other forms a caution recommends the statement; the notional (undiscounted) figures are always the ones stated.

title: Section 5(2AB) announcement: limited to an undertaking to assist (7.3.3.1) or any cooperation (2.4.9, 7.3.1)?
statement: 7.3.3.1 states the Victorian requirement (announce the less severe sentence; record the undertaking’s details) for a sentence reduced because the offender “has undertaken to assist”. 2.4.9 states it for a sentence reduced “because of an offender’s cooperation”, and 7.3.1 introduces it under assistance generally. 7.3.3.1 then contrasts the Commonwealth rule, which “only applies to discounts for future, not past, cooperation”, implying the Victorian rule is wider. The Manual does not say whether s 5(2AB) covers past assistance with no undertaking. Handling: where cooperation, past or promised, produced a less severe sentence, the output announces that and records the undertaking’s details where there is one; only an undertaking-based reduction that is not announced is an error; non-compliance “does not automatically vitiate” the sentence.

title: Plea discount for “worst category” offending: competing authorities
statement: The Manual records competing lines of authority on whether a plea to worst-category offending earns a discount: one holds that the more serious the crime, the greater the weight of the plea; more recent authority asks whether the enormity of the criminality means the plea’s utilitarian benefit must yield to public protection and the rule of law. Elsewhere the Manual says that in all but exceptional cases the utilitarian value of a plea must be acknowledged by a reduction. For the worst murders a plea is now generally held to be a necessary condition for fixing a non-parole period, but it does not necessarily save the offender from life imprisonment. Handling: for worst-category offending assume neither an enlarged discount nor none; state which line is applied and show this caution.

title: Prevalence: the evidentiary foundation is expressly unresolved
statement: The Manual says there remain unresolved issues as to the material or evidentiary foundation sufficient for a finding of prevalence. Prevalence need not be proved beyond reasonable doubt, but the court should be “sure” of it. Earlier cases treated some offences as so notoriously prevalent that no proof or prior canvassing was needed; the better view now requires procedural fairness and disclosure of the source. Evidence or official statistics may be tendered. Handling: no increase for prevalence without a stated, disclosed source and an opportunity to be heard (audit.prevalence); the source is recorded among the assumptions, and the message says the evidentiary standard is unresolved.

title: Hardship to family or third parties: “exceptional circumstances” (7.6) vs the current Victorian test (7.6.4)
statement: 7.6 says the family/associates limb “demands” that the offender establish exceptional circumstances, and the first paragraph of 7.6.4 says the same. 7.6.4 then records that Victorian authority previously required “highly exceptional” circumstances; that the NSW no-exceptionality approach for Commonwealth offences “is now followed by the Victorian Court of Appeal” (the Manual does not say whether only for Commonwealth offences); and, hedged (“It appears now”), that for Victorian offences the hardship must rise above the general hardship of prisoners’ families and be “so significant that they will weigh heavily in the sentencing calculus”. Handling: require cogent evidence and hardship that rises above the general and weighs heavily; where mitigation rests on that test without a finding of “exceptional” circumstances, caution, not error; never mitigate for third-party hardship without cogent evidence.

title: Public opprobrium as punishment: expressly unclear
statement: The Manual says loss of reputation may be a form of punishment, but it is unclear whether opprobrium resulting from conviction may be considered. It notes the tension with an offender who held, or exploited, a position of privilege or power, and lists only a few instances held relevant: seriously or significantly damaging publicity causing hardship; and loss of career from the conviction (less arguable if the career was used to offend; possibly mitigating where the offending is remote from the employment). Handling: give opprobrium weight only within the listed instances, with this caution; none where the offender used a position of privilege, power or career to offend, unless explained; record any such weight as an assumption.

title: Extra-curial punishment: the custody-framed Delzoppo test vs the broader uses and examples in 7.8.2
statement: 7.8.2 says that, for injury or loss to mitigate, the offender must argue it would “(a) add to the burden of the appellant’s imprisonment; and (b) constitute a form of extra-curial punishment” (Delzoppo). The same section says such injury or loss is generally taken into account and may bear on just punishment, the weight of remorse and general and specific deterrence, and its examples include losses that do not obviously add to the burden of imprisonment (forfeited police superannuation; a culpable driver whose own child died). The Manual does not say how limb (a) applies where the sentence is not imprisonment, or to losses that do not affect custody. Handling: for imprisonment apply both limbs; for non-custodial outcomes, or losses bearing only on just punishment or deterrence, give weight with this caution rather than failing it; illness caused by the offender’s reaction to the consequences of offending is never extra-curial punishment. For injuries an offender suffers in the course of offending (e.g. arson), 27.2.4.4 says whether they mitigate is “unsettled” and depends on the circumstances; its examples go both ways (fn 4129: “some punishment”; mitigation; a more onerous custody). Handling: show this caution and do not fail reasoning that gives, or refuses, weight to such injuries.

title: Imitation or unloaded weapons: the Manual records competing authority
statement: Legislation and most cases draw little or no distinction between an imitation and a real weapon, but some authority has found that using an imitation or unloaded weapon makes the offending less serious. The Manual does not choose. Handling: where the facts involve an imitation, replica or unloaded weapon, show both views, do not fail reasoning that adopts either, and widen the estimate band. For violent property offences, 27.2.2.3 takes a position: such weapons “plainly” carry less risk and so are less dangerous than the genuine article, but can still instil terror and serious emotional damage and are dangerous given the potential police response. Apply that chapter-specific statement to violent property offences, with this caution. For firearm offences, 33.2.1.3 says the same maximum for a prohibited person’s possession of an imitation firearm “suggests that imitation firearms are treated with the same severity”, yet sentences where both offences are charged suggest courts treat imitation firearms as less serious; and since victims may believe they could be shot, a firearm’s incapacity to fire may be of limited relevance in certain circumstances. Apply 33.2.1.3 to imitation firearm offences, with this caution.

title: Loss repaid by third parties: “little or no weight” (5.2.8.2) vs mitigation “not removed but may be lessened” (6.3.4.2)
statement: 5.2.8.2 says loss recouped from a third party such as an indemnity fund or insurer carries little or no weight in mitigation if it merely shifts the loss; 6.3.4.2 says restitution made by third parties or by court order does not remove mitigation but may lessen it. The Manual does not reconcile them (one may concern insurance recoupment, the other restitution paid on the offender’s behalf). Handling: where repayment came from someone other than the offender, show both statements, treat the weight as uncertain and do not fail either approach.

title: Verdins evidence: “normally” expert evidence vs “expert evidence is required”; inference without direct evidence
statement: The Manual says Verdins requires cogent evidence “normally in the form of expert evidence”, then that “expert evidence is required” but not determinative; it also allows a court, without direct evidence, to infer that prison is more burdensome for a prisoner with a severe mental health condition. Handling: without expert evidence, state the assumption and that expert evidence is normally needed; do not fail burden-of-imprisonment reasoning that relies on the inference for a severe condition shown by other evidence.

title: Footnotes that signal contrary authority (“But see”, “Cf”) to propositions stated without qualification (chapters 5–6, 28, 29, 31, 34)
statement: Several footnotes signal contrary authority to a proposition the body text states without qualification: offending on conditional liberty as aggravating (fn 1007), enlisting others to lie (fn 1006), full awareness limiting the Verdins reduction (fn 1151), and cooperation as an indicator of remorse (fn 1344); in chapters 29 and 31: strict obedience to orders of doubtful validity (fn 4518), explicit notice of a risk as aggravating (fn 4681), phoenixing (fn 4723), corporate remorse (fn 4728), recording a conviction for serious OHS offending (fn 4760) and separate OHS penalties for different duties (fn 4784); in chapter 22: when a duty of care is owed to an adult (fn 3432), the lower culpability of negligent killers (fn 3436) and the denunciation and (usual) imprisonment of a killing despite provocation and family violence (fn 3473); in chapter 28: duration as a feature of drug offending (fn 4326, Quah: the character of the possession, not its duration, matters); in chapter 34: that an intention to die does not reduce deterrence (fn 5071) and that foreign incursion offences are not a “species of terrorism” (fn 5027). Handling: when the reasoning relies on one of these propositions, add “the Manual notes contrary authority (fn N)”; do not fail the reasoning.

Several footnotes signal contrary authority to a proposition the body text states without qualification: offending on conditional liberty as aggravating (fn 1007), enlisting others to lie (fn 1006), full awareness limiting the Verdins reduction (fn 1151), and cooperation as an indicator of remorse (fn 1344); in chapters 29 and 31: strict obedience to orders of doubtful validity (fn 4518), explicit notice of a risk as aggravating (fn 4681), phoenixing (fn 4723), corporate remorse (fn 4728), recording a conviction for serious OHS offending (fn 4760) and separate OHS penalties for different duties (fn 4784); in chapter 22: when a duty of care is owed to an adult (fn 3432), the lower culpability of negligent killers (fn 3436) and the denunciation and (usual) imprisonment of a killing despite provocation and family violence (fn 3473); in chapter 28: duration as a feature of drug offending (fn 4326, Quah: the character of the possession, not its duration, matters); in chapter 34: that an intention to die does not reduce deterrence (fn 5071) and that foreign incursion offences are not a “species of terrorism” (fn 5027). Handling: when the reasoning relies on one of these propositions, add “the Manual notes contrary authority (fn N)”; do not fail the reasoning.

title: Suicide pact manslaughter: non-custodial sentences (22.3) vs manslaughter as a Category 2 offence (22.1.1)
statement: 22.1.1 makes manslaughter a Category 2 offence for adult offenders; chapter 22 lists suicide pact manslaughter as one of three manslaughter offences, and 22.3 says a suicide-pact sentence may release the offender without a custodial component, relying on a 2008 decision that predates the Category scheme. The Manual does not say whether the statutory suicide pact offence is within Category 2. Handling: for an adult offender and offending on or after 20 March 2017, mark its Category 2 status unresolved; a non-custodial proposal gets a caution, not an error.

title: Manslaughter: “failing to explain the killing” listed among gravity factors vs no adverse inference from silence
statement: The manslaughter gravity list includes failing to explain the killing or its circumstances, with no direction; elsewhere the Manual bars an adverse inference from the offender’s failure to give evidence on the plea save in rare and exceptional circumstances, and does not reconcile the two. Handling: the factor may bear on how the circumstances are assessed, but the exercise of silence must not aggravate (caution).

title: Sexual offences: “the maximum in force at the time of the offending” (24.1) vs applying a later reduction (5.1.3)
statement: 24.1 says the relevant maximum is the one in force at the time of offending, not at sentence; 5.1.3 requires a court to apply any later reduction (subject to its exception where the maximum was reduced and then increased again before sentence to the same magnitude or higher) and to disregard any increase. Historic sexual-offence tables include reductions (e.g. Level 6 from 7½ to 5 years in 1997). Handling: audit.maximum_applicable applies 5.1.3; the 24.1 guide never fails a sentence on its own; show this caution for historic sexual offences.

title: Rape: “suspended, non-custodial, or substantially reduced term” (24.1.8.2) vs Category 1 and the abolition of suspended sentences

title: Provocation as a sentencing factor: confined in causing-injury cases (25.2.1), not so confined in homicide (22.2.5)
statement: In causing-injury cases provocation is limited to words or deeds by the victim that induce the offender to lose control and offend almost immediately (25.2.1); in homicide, as a sentencing factor, it is not limited by the common-law test for reducing murder to manslaughter (provocation causing the accused to lose control, and capable of causing an ordinary person to lose control), may be cumulative, and may count where the conduct was excessive (22.2.5). The Manual does not explain the difference. Handling: apply each statement to its own offence class; where both arise in one sentencing exercise, show a caution.

title: Parole offending: no s 16(3B) order where parole is not cancelled at sentence — but s 77(7A) deems cancellation at sentence
statement: 3.3.3 says that where parole has not been cancelled at the time of sentencing, no s 16(3B) order (cumulation or concurrency) can be made without breaching s 5(2AA); it also says s 77(7A) deems parole cancelled at the time of sentencing whenever a prison sentence is imposed for an offence committed on parole. The Manual does not say when the “not cancelled” case arises once s 77(7A) operates, and 8.4.1 states the parole cumulation default without the cancellation condition. Handling: intake asks whether parole was cancelled before sentencing. Yes → the s 16(3B) default applies (exceptional circumstances to displace it). No → no s 16(3B) order; caution, not error. Unknown → unresolved.

title: State term after a Commonwealth sentence: “commences immediately after” (2.4.7) vs “no later than” (8.4.1)
statement: For an offender serving a Commonwealth sentence, 2.4.7 says the new State term must commence immediately after the federal term (or the end of its non-parole or pre-release period); 8.4.1 says the commencement must be no later than that point. Handling: error only if the direction is later than the limit (both readings agree); caution if earlier (partly concurrent), since 2.4.7 would not allow it.

title: Considering parole: “should not consider whether the offender might be granted parole” (3.3.3) vs “may consider” (8.3.3.2)
statement: 3.3.3 says a court should not consider whether the offender might be granted parole at the end of the non-parole period; 8.3.3.2 says a court may consider the possibility of release on parole, its rehabilitative potential and the offender’s suitability in fixing a non-parole period. Handling: fail only speculation about future executive action used to shape totality or the head sentence; allow parole-related reasoning in fixing the non-parole period (caution, cite both).

title: General deterrence for charges that could have been dealt with in the Children’s Court: “unclear”
statement: The Manual says it is unclear whether general deterrence applies where charges that might have been dealt with in the Children’s Court are dealt with in a superior court, and that it is “likely” to apply where punishment beyond that available under the CYFA (or s 32(3)(b)) is necessary. 10.1.2.1 adds CNK v The Queen: a child in the Supreme Court because charged with attempted murder, acquitted of it and convicted of other uplifted offences, had to be sentenced on the remaining uplifted charges as if exclusively governed by the CYFA, and general deterrence was held not relevant when sentencing children; the Court later clarified that it applies (possibly ameliorated) where CYFA dispositions are inadequate and adult custody is necessary. The Manual does not reconcile CNK’s first holding with a higher court’s power to impose a sentence under the Act where CYFA dispositions are inadequate (flag.cyfa_disposition_power), nor either holding with the “unclear” of 4.2.1. Handling: if the offender could have been dealt with in the Children’s Court, any reliance on general deterrence → caution, stating whether punishment beyond the CYFA or s 32(3)(b) is considered necessary; for a child, heavy reliance on general deterrence without that finding (or a finding that adult custody is necessary) remains an error, because general deterrence has minimal relevance when sentencing a child (audit.youth_principles (4), audit.purposes_balance (1)). Where a child is before the higher court only because of a charge of which they were acquitted (CNK), a disposition outside the CYFA → caution (this flag; audit.youth_principles (8), on the fact intake.court records), never error on this ground.

title: “The parole sentence has no role to play” (3.3.3) is supported only by authorities in a line that Bowen overtook
statement: The statement “Beyond that, however, the parole sentence has no role to play …” is supported only by Dickson and Waugh (fn 493), cases the Manual lists in the line of authority (fn 485) that Bowen overtook, Waugh being “expressly disapproved” (fn 488). The Manual does not say whether the statement survives Bowen. Handling: caution when relying on the “no role” limb; apply Bowen (consider both sentences and the entire period).

title: Each charge and its form
statement: A sentence must be imposed for each offence; the maximum and any scheme (category, standard sentence, mandatory minimum) follow the offence; representative and rolled-up charges have special rules; summary jurisdiction and the two-year summary cap turn on the class of offence; an inchoate offence is not a standard sentence offence and a relative maximum needs the primary offence; the CCE scheme turns on Schedule 1A and transaction values; federal charges are outside scope. Several gates turn on per-charge classes that the register does not carry and the Manual lists only for some offence chapters (e.g. 27.5.1, 28.7; a schedule 1 sexual offence for a DATO; a Schedule 1 offence for forfeiture); otherwise, without a stated class the gate must caution, not decide silently from the offence name (for a DATO on a 24.1.1, 24.1.2 or 24.1.4 offence the app also does not propose one unless the user states it is not a schedule 1 sexual offence: flag.dato_sexual_offence_scope). Historic provisions not in the register (e.g. ss 45(2A), 47A) carry Category 1 status, for an offender 18 or older, for offending from 20 March to 30 June 2017 (cat1.historic_sexual_provisions).

title: Plea and its timing; sentence indication
statement: The court must consider whether and when the offender pleaded guilty; timing affects the discount; a plea that produces a less severe sentence of a listed form (custodial; imprisonment; CCO of two years or more; fine over 10 penalty units; aggregate fine over 20 penalty units) requires the s 6AAA statement; a not guilty plea is never aggravating; a guilty plea to at least one imprisonable offence is a DATO condition; a sentence indication on which the plea was entered binds the judicial officer who gave it.

title: Natural person or body corporate
statement: Fine maxima differ for a body corporate (five times the natural-person maximum, stated for Crimes Act offences in 5.1.1 and generally in 12.2: flag.body_corporate_fine_multiplier; 2500 penalty units summarily) and directors may be made liable; for a Level 2 offence a fine may be imposed on a body corporate as an alternative to imprisonment (12.1).

title: Prior and subsequent convictions; serious offender and CCE status; pending charges
statement: Priors are relevant to several purposes (not to aggravate); some statutes turn on them: serious offender status needs qualifying convictions that resulted in imprisonment or youth detention, proved beyond reasonable doubt; CCE offender status needs findings of guilt for CCE offences within 10 years; pending charges may justify deferral or being taken into account. A dismissal has the same effect as a conviction for proceedings for a subsequent offence; a prior Category A or B conviction engages the exceptional-circumstances requirement for youth detention where the current charge is a Category B serious youth offence (a Category A charge engages it without any prior); prior unlicensed or disqualified driving may justify a longer disqualification; a previous s 61(3) offence doubles the mandatory disqualification.

A dismissal has the same effect as a conviction for proceedings for a subsequent offence; a prior Category A or B conviction engages the exceptional-circumstances requirement for youth detention where the current charge is a Category B serious youth offence (a Category A charge engages it without any prior); prior unlicensed or disqualified driving may justify a longer disqualification; a previous s 61(3) offence doubles the mandatory disqualification.

title: Status at the time of offending and sentences being served
statement: Offending on parole or bail, prison offences and escape engage presumptions of cumulation; offending on conditional liberty or contrary to orders may aggravate; totality applies to sentences being served. An offender serving the non-parole period of a prior sentence needs a new single non-parole period (with the allowance for the parole sentence served and no double-counted pre-sentence detention); no term may be cumulated on a life sentence imposed, being served or paroled from; an offender serving a Commonwealth sentence needs a commencement direction within the s 16(4) limit. Orders in force at sentencing limit what can be imposed: the CCO maximum term and total hours, youth detention maxima across occasions, one DATO at a time and no DATO for an offender on parole or subject to a higher-court sentence, a previous AEO for the offence, concurrency of licence orders; CCO conditions must fit any intervention orders.

title: Time already served
statement: Time served must be declared (the whole continuous custody from arrest where s 18(6) applies, excluding non-declarable periods); it is deducted from a combination sentence’s custodial part (affecting the one-year ceiling) and from youth detention unless otherwise ordered; undeclarable custody may be weighed under the Renzella discretion.

title: Victim status, vulnerability and relationship
statement: Victim status triggers mandatory minimums and Category 1 for some offences (only if the status and the offender’s knowledge or recklessness are proved beyond reasonable doubt); vulnerability and family violence context bear heavily on gravity; breach of a family violence intervention order or offending in front of children increases gravity.

title: Harm and victim impact
statement: Harm resulting directly from the offence must be considered whether or not foreseeable; disputed harm used to increase the sentence must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. A DATO cannot be made where the offence involves the infliction of actual bodily harm (unless, in the Magistrates’ Drug Court, the harm was minor); compensation draws on the injury and loss facts.

title: Circumstances of the offence
statement: The statutory gravity factors and the offence-specific guidance require these facts; mandatory minimum schemes turn on gross violence or single punch features proved beyond reasonable doubt and on the offender’s role; some maxima are higher only if a statutory condition is established.

statement: Parity requires any significant difference to be rationally explained, comparing all components.

title: Mental impairment and expert evidence
statement: Verdins, the Category 2 impaired-mental-functioning exceptions, mandatory minimum special reasons and mental health orders all require evidence of the condition at the relevant time and its effect. The mental health orders distinguish: a court assessment order needs only an apparent mental illness, a court secure treatment order an actual one at sentence; intellectual disability alone is not “mental illness” and an RTO or justice plan condition needs a DHS Secretary statement or specification.

title: Addiction and intoxication
statement: Addiction and intoxication bear on culpability, rehabilitation and the choice of sanction. A DATO needs a dependency on drugs or alcohol that contributed to the offence (balance of probabilities). An alcohol exclusion order is mandatory only where a conviction is recorded for a relevant offence, the offender was intoxicated by liquor (“intoxicated” refers to the consumption of liquor), the intoxication significantly contributed, and there has been no previous AEO for the offence.

title: Personal circumstances
statement: Childhood deprivation must be considered; employment history indicates rehabilitation prospects; ill health matters if it makes imprisonment more burdensome; third-party hardship needs exceptional circumstances (but see flag.third_party_hardship_exceptionality); Koori Court participation may mitigate. Whether to record a conviction requires the impact of a conviction on economic or social wellbeing or employment prospects; the need for a licence bears on the disqualification period.

title: Character, remorse and restitution
statement: Good character must be taken into account if established (subject to the child sexual offence exception); remorse must be proved by proper evidence; restitution is mitigating.

title: Cooperation with authorities
statement: Assistance or an undertaking to assist affects the sentence, must be announced and recorded, and is an exception to the Category 2 and mandatory minimum regimes.

title: Delay
statement: Delay may mitigate on either limb (unfairness, rehabilitation), each requiring some evidence; its cause matters.

title: Conditions of custody; deportation risk; custody at sentence
statement: Protective custody and onerous conditions are relevant on evidence of actual effect; deportation is relevant only with evidence of its likelihood and impact; a court assessment order requires that the person is not in custody pending sentencing.

title: Offences taken into account and uncharged conduct
statement: Admitted pending offences may harden (not lengthen beyond the maximum) the sentence; uncharged conduct may not be punished as a separate or more serious offence.

title: Driving-related facts (licence orders; driving-linked guidance)
statement: Serious motor vehicle offences require disqualification with a minimum period (cancellation for a Victorian licence or permit holder; the form follows the licence status); conviction for dangerous or negligent driving while pursued by police, and for vehicle theft, also requires disqualification; RSA s 61(3) requires cancellation and disqualification (4 or 2 years for a first offence, 8 or 4 for a subsequent one, depending on whether a conviction is recorded); other offences connected with driving allow discretionary disqualification. “Arising from driving” also decides whether the NCSI-by-driving guidance applies to a s 24 charge (s 24 is a generic offence).

title: Financial circumstances, property and claims
statement: Means bear on a fine’s amount (after deciding to fine) and on compensation; the onus is on the offender to put material before the court about their financial circumstances. Confiscation and compensation orders interact with the sentence: each is made on application (personal injury compensation only on the injured person’s application); an offender relying on lawful acquisition must present credible material; the court may not take into account the automatic forfeiture of a serious drug offender’s property; personal injury compensation must be reduced by any VOCA Act award; own-motion property compensation is available only where the hearing commenced on or after 31 January 2013.

title: Reports
statement: A pre-sentence report is required before a CCO (other than a work-only CCO of 300 hours or less — the Manual also says “less than 300 hours”: flag.cco_work_only_300_hours) or youth detention, including the youth justice centre route for protected-official offences; a therapeutic order in place of imprisonment for those offences needs a psychiatrist’s or registered psychologist’s report; electronic monitoring needs a positive PSR statement; a CSTO needs the authorised psychiatrist’s report recommending it; reports do not control the sentence; medical reports should not opine on sentencing principles.

title: Prosecution notices that statutory schemes depend on
statement: The 10-year manslaughter minimum applies only if the prosecution gives notice that it intends to apply for it; the DPP may apply for an indefinite sentence only after filing a notice of intention on the day of conviction or within five working days (the court may also act on its own initiative, with its own notice and adjournment steps).

title: Offender’s consent or agreement to orders that require it
statement: A CCO requires the offender’s informed consent; an adjourned undertaking requires the offender’s agreement to give it; a DATO requires written agreement to the order and to comply with its treatment and supervision part, and informed written consent. Without the fact the order can only be proposed conditionally.

title: Serious youth offence categories (youth detention)
statement: Before making a detention order for a young offender charged with a Category A serious youth offence, or a Category B one with a prior Category A or B conviction, the court must be satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist. The Manual does not list the offences in each category (flag.serious_youth_offence_categories), so the user must supply them; unknown → caution.

title: Sentencing after a retrial: the previous sentence
statement: When sentencing after a retrial the court must have regard to the sentence previously imposed; it is not bound by it, but cases where the second sentence may permissibly exceed the first will be rare (time may have changed the offender’s circumstances).
